Publisher: Unknown, late 19th century.
Country of publication: India, Calcutta, late 19th century. Script: Bengali. Title: Phetkāriṇītantra.
Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Deity,
who blazes with wrath, vomits forth fire,
burns the creation, and devours the sons of Diti.
I bow to the terrible Kṛtyā, who roars aloud, wailing piteously, and who is the fierce Kālī of hunger. 1/1.
Unmattabhairava, Nārasiṃhaḍāmarabhairava, the form of Śiva, Mālinī, and the Yamalatantras beginning with Asitāṅga. (1.2)
Having examined the *Siddhayogīśvarī Tantra*, the *Yoginījālaśambara*, and the ritual procedures for *kṛtyā* [sorcery], the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra* is composed. (1.3)
The Supreme Goddess Mātṛkā, whose nature consists of the fifty phonemes, is said to have given birth therein to each [of the letters] from Śiva and Śakti. (1.4)
All these constituent parts (kalās) of hers, numbering fifty, exist for the sake of accomplishing the phonemes;
from them alone have arisen those phonemes which belong to Viṣṇu and Śiva. (1.5)
These forms, joined with their respective powers, are described in sequence:
first Keśava is proclaimed, and after him Nārāyaṇa is considered. (1.6)
Then there are Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, the one renowned as Trivikrama, Vāmana, and Śrīdhara. (1.7)
He is remembered as Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara;
as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. (1.8)
These have been declared as those born from vowels; now those born from consonants are described:
Cakrī, Gadī, Śārṅgī, Khaḍgī, Śaṅkhī, and Halī. (1.9)
Then Musalī, Śūlī, Pāśī, and likewise Aṅkuśī;
Mukunda, Nandana, Nandī, Nara, Narakajit, and Hari. (1.10)
Kṛṣṇa is likewise declared to be Truth, the Eternal, and Śauri;
he is renowned as Śūra, Janārdana, Bhūdharas, and Viśvamūrtika. || 1.11 ||
Vaikuṇṭha is likewise proclaimed, as well as Narottama, the powerful one;
then Balāgraja, Bāla, Vṛṣaghna, and Vṛṣa as well. (1.12)
He is celebrated as Haṃsa, Varāha, Vimala, and Nṛsiṃha;
likewise as Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, and Kṣamā. (1.13)

Peace (śānti), Action (kriyā), Compassion (dayā), Intelligence (medhā), Will (icchā), Faith (śraddhā), as well as Modesty (lajjā), Fortune (lakṣmī), Sarasvatī, Affection (prīti), and Delight (rati)—these are considered the vowels (svaras). 1/14.
She is supernatural power, prosperity, and purity; devotion, intellect, and understanding; forgiveness; she is Rāmā, Umā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Vasudhā, Vasudā, and the Supreme. (1.15)
Parā, Parāyaṇā, Sūkṣmā, Sandhyā, Prajā, Prabhā, Niśā, Amoghā, and Vidyutā—these are the Śaktis who grant all desires. || 1.16 ||
All of them bear the conch and the discus, possess the luster of clouds, and wear yellow garments;
beginning with Keśava, they abide within their own respective limbs, their forms adorned by their Śaktis.
These are proclaimed as having smiling faces and possessing the luster of lightning;
Kāntā, Kṣāntā, Kīrti, and the others hold a lotus and the gesture of granting fearlessness in their hands. (1.18)
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, Amareśvara, Arghīśa, Bhārabhūti, Maulīśa, and Śālvakoṭara. (1.19)
Jhiṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara, Akrūra, Mahāsena, and Svaraja are the forms of Rudra. (1.20)
Then there are Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka, Śivottama, Ekarudra, Karmeśvara, Ekanetra, Ūrdhvakeśa, and Caturānana. (1.21)
Ajeśa, Sarvasomeśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāruka;
Ardhanārīśvara, Śyāmā, Kānta, Āṣāḍhin, and Daṇḍin. 1/22.
Adrimāṇa, Meṣa, Lohita, and likewise Śikhī;
Chagalaṇḍa and Dviraṇḍeśa, as well as Mahākāla and Kapālī. (1.23)
Bhujaṅgīśa, Pinākīśa, Khaḍgīśa, and likewise Cakra;
Śveta, Bhṛṅgīśa, Nakulī, Śiva, and likewise Saṃvartaka. (1.24)
These Rudras, born from their respective classes, have faces resembling vultures;
their bodies are embraced by beloved ones, and they hold skull-bowls and tridents in their hands.
Pūrṇodarā, Virajā, and immediately after her Śālmalī; likewise Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā. (1.26)
Sudīrghamukhī, Gomukhī, the ninth is Dīrghajihvikā, then Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and also Vikṛtamukhī. (1.27)
Jvālāmukhī, as well as Ulkāmukhī, Śrīmukhī, and Vidyāmukhī—these, born from the vowels, are the powers of the vowels (svara-śaktis). || 1.28 ||
Mahākālī and Sarasvatī, endowed with all perfections;
Gaurī, Trailokyavijayā, and likewise Mantrāntaśaktikā. (1.29)
Bhūtamātā, Lambodarī, Bhāvinī, Nāgarī, as well as Khecarī, Majjarī, Rūpiṇī, and Vīriṇī. || 1.30 ||
Kākodarī, Pūtanā, and Bhadrakālī are also Yoginīs; as well as Śaṅkhinī, Gajjinī, Kālarātrī, and Kubjinī. (1.31)
Kapardinī, Vajriṇī, Jayā, Sumukheśvarī, Revatī, Mādhavī, as well as Vāruṇī and Vāyavī. || 1.32 ||
Another is Rakṣopadhāriṇī, and likewise those called Sahajā;
Lakṣmī, Vyāpinī, and Māyā are known as the Śiva-śaktis. (1.33)
Residing within the limbs of Rudra, they possess a brilliance like that of the Javā flower; their forms are beautiful with passion, and their arms are likewise bound by red lotuses and skull-cups.

The auspicious analogies for Mātṛkā, whose essential nature is that of the primordial source (puṃprakṛti), are distinguished by the measures (mātrā) and by names such as the three genders and so forth, while others are cruel. (1.35)
Mantras ending in *huṃ phaṭ* are considered masculine; those ending in *svāhā* are feminine; and those ending in *namaḥ* are neuter—thus are the mantras said to be of three kinds. (1.36)
Furthermore, they are considered to be of two kinds through the division into mantra and vidyā:
those mantras whose deities are male, and likewise those vidyās whose deities are female. (1.37)
Male mantras, neuter mantras, and female mantras are to be employed for killing, pacification, and malevolent rites; thus they should be recited by practitioners. (1.38)
The gentle mantras known as the Pradhānas should be joined with the rite of cruelty;
for there was the mantra called Haṃsa, which is the syllable of the Supreme Self.
Thus, through the elision of the syllable "haṃsa," he attained non-duality; by the disappearance of the letters of the word "haṃsa," he emerged after piercing through his own throat. (1.40)
And that primordial sound, endowed with the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, gave rise within the three worlds to the three Vedas and the three qualities (guṇas). (1.41)

The three fires, the three times, the three humors, and the three musical notes—these, beginning with Dhruva, have attained the state of the ocean of excellence within the Great Sound (Mahādhvani). 1.42.
The letter *u* is said to be Kuṭila, and the letter *ma* is indeed Kāla;
the letter *la* is Indra, the powerful one, and *ha* is called Haṃsa. (1.43)
Vindhyavāsinī and Māyā are the letter *i*, which represents the two breasts;
Māyā and Lañjā are the syllable *krīṃ*, while *huṃ* is called the *kūrca*. (1.44)
"Dviṭhaḥ svāhā" is declared [as the mantra]; Kālāgni is the pervasive Aṅkuśa;
"Phaṭ" is the Astra-mantra; from this, Brahmā [is established] starting from the right ear, and Śiva [is established]. 1/45.
The letter *sa* is Bhṛgu and Prāṇa; alternatively, it is Vāṇī and Pāvakāśana.
The letter *ra* is Nāgeśa and Ujjvalana; the letter *ra* is said to be the Moon. (1.46)
The syllable *e* is said to be Bhaga, and *u* is called Śiva; these two are declared to be the right and left [hands]. The syllable *ṛ* is proclaimed to be Pāśin. (1.47)
The Lolākṣikā is the letter *la*, and the letter *ha* is Nakulīśvara;
Brahmā, seated upon Indra’s throne, is the Trimūrti and Manmatha. (1.48)
The syllable *drauṃ* is the light (*jyotis*) consisting of the three principles (*tritattva*). *Hrīṃ* and *huṃ* are declared to be the "tuft" (*kūrca*) and "wrath" (*krodha*), respectively.
The letter *ya* is renowned as the wind (*vāyu*), and it is described by the wise as the cloud (*jīmūta*). (1.49)
The syllable following fire (ra), joined with the great letter (ma), belongs to the lineage of Nṛsiṃha;
it is the letter sa, like the moon in its left eye, a planet released from the crescent moon.
This very stainless seed-syllable has been declared by Kaulinī; one should install it with devotion.
It has been stated that it provides protection against the fear of ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and ceṭakas. 1/50.
The third letter after *hsau* is said to be *hsau*, which is to be known as Sadāśiva;
*ha* is declared to be the Void (*śūnya*) by Bhairava and the others who are composed in meditation. (1.51)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Treasury of Mantras," in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The second chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
Now I shall describe the procedure for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the sequence beginning with rites for pacification (śāntika).
In rites for pacification (śāntika), it should be square; and in rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), it should indeed be circular. || 2.1 ||
A triangle is prescribed for malevolent rites (abhicāra), while a pentagon is considered for killing (māraṇa);
a hexagon is for deluding (mohana), and a heptagon is considered for paralyzing (stambhana).

Likewise, for the destruction of enemies, an eight-cornered [pit] is prescribed, while for the removal of disease, a nine-cornered one is considered appropriate; however, for the fire-oblation (homa), one should have a single pit measuring exactly one cubit.

One should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) out of sand, measuring four finger-breadths in height, and shaped either as a square, a triangle, or a circle, provided with three girdles (*mekhalā*). (2.4)
A quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the east bestows the attainment of sovereignty;
that known as the "womb" (yoni), located in the southeast corner, is recommended for the scorching of enemies.
A half-moon shape in the southern direction is intended for the destruction of enemies;
a triangle in the south-western corner increases the diseases of foes. (2/6)
In the western direction (Vāruṇī), however, there is always the circle that increases longevity, prosperity, and nourishment;
in the northwestern direction (Vāyavī), there is the six-cornered [circle], which is beneficial for the destruction of enemies. (2.7)
In the north (saumyā), there is the pool named Padma, which bestows prosperity, wisdom, and nourishment upon men;
in the northeast (aiśānī), there is an eight-cornered pool that grants all desires.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The Third Chapter. Now I shall describe the rules for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; listen attentively.
The *sruk* should be thirty-six finger-breadths long, and the *sruva* twenty-four finger-breadths.
The face, the neck, and the altar are likewise [measured] by seven and eight [units] respectively;
the staff, measured by its length and circumference, is twenty-four finger-breadths. (3.2)
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be four fingers wide and two fingers high;
its circular excavation should be four fingers deep and one should dig it to a depth of two fingers.
The girdle (mekhalā) should likewise be two finger-breadths [in width]; one should contemplate the remainder as the decorative ornament.
One should make the altar (vedī) three finger-breadths in width at the front and rear of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

The opening, measured by the tip of the little finger, should have a depth of two finger-breadths and a capacity of one karṣa; it should be dug in mud and shaped like a deer's footprint. When the flowing ghee emerges, [it is ready]. (3.5)
The handle is twenty-two finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths in diameter;
the ring at the base and tip of the vessel should be like that of the *sruva* ladle, and it should be made of gold.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles may be made of gold, silver, or copper; they may also be made of wood, or even of iron or *kāraskara* wood. (3.7)
The Vilva tree is for the son of the Lord of Nagas; these two are established for minor rites.
Sandalwood, Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Cūta, and Vikaṅkata [are used]. (3.8)
The *śamyā*, *āmalaka*, and *sāra* wood, as well as *palāśa*, are the types of wood [to be used].
One should perform the ritual bath according to the rules with the weapons, the limbs [of the mantra], the roots, and the vidyās. (3.9)
Having come to the place of worship and having offered the *arghya* to the Sun, one should properly perform the worship of the door with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (3.10)
Having performed the worship of the bronze bell and covered the door with a cloth, the pure practitioner, wearing the sacred thread upon his hand, should face the northeast. (3.11)
Having sat down, one should assume either the lotus (padma) or the auspicious cross (svastika) posture;
and for the sake of knowledge, the seeker of learning should perform everything with a concentrated mind while in the lotus posture. (3.11)
Facing either east or north, or facing west for one desiring prosperity, according to the sequence to be described here. (3.12)
Then, seated, having wiped both hands with the *praṇava* and having placed the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) upon the fingers in due order.
One should perform the binding of the directions in all quarters with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), creating a protective enclosure like a wall of fire on all sides by means of that mantra. (3.14)
One should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) with either the mantra or the syllable Om (praṇava).
The knower of the mantra should utter the Praṇava with a single vowel sound.
Having filled the abdomen with air and remaining there for as long as possible, this indeed becomes prāṇāyāma known as pūraka, which fills the body. (3.16)
Having covered all the limbs and being free from inhalation and exhalation, one should remain like a full water-pot; that is the *kumbhaka* breath control. (3.17)
The knower of mantras should likewise exhale the breath with one [finger] and fill it with the other;
having released the union of exhalation, he should expel that breath through the exterior. (3.18)
This is declared to be the prāṇāyāma called recaka; there is no doubt about this.
Having circumambulated the knees, neither too quickly nor too slowly, [one performs it]. (3.19)
The snapping of the fingers is declared to be one *mātrā*;
then, indeed, the inhalation (*pūraka*) is performed with twelve *mātrās*. (3.20)
Therefore, exhalation (recaka) is performed with double that measure;
likewise, there are three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), each consisting of a triad.

The wise, by means of the *praṇava*, should draw out from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) the function of the *liṅga*—consciousness residing in the heart which is the witness of all—and place it outside. (3.22)
Having encapsulated [the deity] with that very [mantra], one should place it upon the head;
[one should likewise purify] the body, both external and internal, which is devoid of consciousness. (3.23)
Having meditated upon the syllable *yaṃ*, which is smoke-colored and situated in the center of the navel-mandala, within the middle of the wind-mandala, one should purify by means of it. (3.24)
Then, by means of the vital breath (jīva), which has the nature of fire and is situated within the circle of fire, one should burn that heap of ashes until it takes on the form of a body. (3.25)
One should meditate upon a reddish orb located between the eyebrows or situated at the heart;
it is white, shaped like a half-moon, and endowed with two lotus feet.
Remaining there, one should cause [the elements] to be flooded by the syllable *va*, which has the form of nectar;
having placed the earthly seed-syllable, one should contemplate the sphere of space (*vyomamaṇḍala*).
Having divided [the body] into two parts with the Praṇava, one should place the form of consciousness there above the head and unite it with consciousness.
Then the practitioner of mantra should contemplate himself as being bathed in nectar, newly born and stainless, in the form of the deity. (3.29)
Having recollected the seers (ṛṣi), meters (chandas), and deities (daivata), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
It is threefold: placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), placement of the hands (karanyāsa), and placement of the body (dehanyāsa). (3/30)
Divided by the distinctions of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal through its qualities, that [ritual] is threefold:
the first is the placement on the hands (karanyāsa), while the placement on the body (dehanyāsa) is the middle.
The third [stage] shall be the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa); such is the determination of the scripture.
Having encased the syllable Oṃ with the mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa). (3.32)
First, the hand-nyāsas (karanyāsa) are performed starting from the elbow and ending with the little finger;
then, having placed [the mantras] upon all the limbs, one should do so both in direct order and in reverse order.
Starting from the right thumb and likewise proceeding to the left thumb, there exists for mantras an innate reversal known as *saṃhāra* (dissolution). (3.34)
Beginning from the right thumb and extending to the little finger of both hands, this placement is known as *sthiti*, which brings great prosperity. (3/35)
The arising of the ritual placement (nyāsa) is held to proceed from the head down to the feet;
however, that which proceeds from the feet up to the head is the dissolution (saṃharaṇa). (3/36)
The procedure for the abdomen is placement; the state of abiding within the heart occurs during the placement of the syllables of the mantra—this indeed is the supreme sequence. (3.37)
The sequence of placement for the six limb-mantras should be performed in the heart, the head, the crest-position, the arms, the sides, the directions, and the two eyes. (3.38)
The wise know that in the Śaiva and Śākta traditions, the limb-mantras end with the weapon-mantra (astra);
likewise, in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, they are said to end with the eye-mantra (netra) for both ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship (pūjā).
The two syllables "Ṭha" should be applied according to rule upon the heart, not on the head;
"Vaṣaṭ" is said for the crest-lock, and "Hum" is traditionally taught for the armor. (3.40)
"Vauṣaṭ" is said for the eyes, and likewise "phaṭ" is to be applied [for the weapon].
Those four fingers, excluding the thumb, [are placed] on the heart and the head. (3.41)
For the crest (śikhā), it should be a mere fist with the thumb forming the nose;
for the navel, it is formed by all the fingers; and for the binding of armor (kavaca) on the two hands, it is likewise. 3/42.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the three fingers beginning with the index finger on the eyes, and with both palms on the hands,
one should then bind the directions with the hands.
When the five limbs are prescribed using the tips of the thumb and index finger for the directions starting from the east in sequence, then one should omit the eyes. (3.44)
In the case of mantras whose limbs [auxiliary parts] have not been mentioned, the limbs should be fashioned either word by word or even letter by letter;
or else, all the limbs may be formed from the mantra as a whole.
For an ascetic, there should be the placement known as "origination" and that called "dissolution";
[one should place] the seers, meters, and deities upon the head, face, and heart. (3.46)
Having remembered [the deity] at the beginning of the recitation and having paid homage to oneself, one should then perform worship;
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should enter the lotus of the heart.
Then, having meditated upon the deity there, one should worship them mentally according to the sequence [prescribed] by means of mantras and various auspicious ritual substances. (3.48)
In that same sequence, the mental sacrifice is thus described;
or else, one should not utter the mantra aloud, but rather remember the mantra solely with the mind. (3.49)
One should display the mudrās there and meditate upon the supreme deity; in that case, invocation is not desired, as the mental worship is performed within the heart. (3.50)
Having propitiated [the deity] with mental devotion, one should then perform the external worship;
having performed the purification of the place and the purification of the materials, one should purify the vessels. (3.51)
One should arrange the *arghya* vessel and other items upon them according to the prescribed rite;
then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), one should [worship] one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) there.
One should worship with supreme devotion through rites prescribed by rule:
the seat, the invocation, the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and likewise the water for sipping (ācamana).
Bathing, clothing, and sacred threads, as well as all kinds of ornaments;
likewise, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food, and libations. (3.54)
One should perform worship with these eighteen services: garlands, ointments, salutations, and dismissal. (3.55)
Accompanied by the Śaktis, the Mūrtis, and the Lokapālas, this union with the Pīṭha-mantras is called the Nityayāga (the eternal sacrifice). // 3.56 //

The sacrifice performed with the entire *pīṭha* alone, without the external enclosures (*bahirāvaraṇa*), preceded by the recitation of mantras, is the intermediate daily sacrifice (*nityayāga*). (3.57)
Accompanied by the fire-rite, oblations, and ornaments, as well as the supreme worship joined with the purification of materials. (3.58)
Having offered the time while omitting the fire-ritual (agnikārya), yet including all the ritual services (upacāras), this is remembered as the middling form of worship. (3/59)
Setting aside the splendor of garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as various other rituals, worship performed solely through the application of merit constitutes the lowest form. (3/60)
One should prepare uśīra and sandalwood for the vessel alone, along with jasmine, camphor, kakkola, bahumūla, and tamālaka. (3.61)
Having thus ground them according to the rule, one should cast them into the water for rinsing,
along with tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice, barley, paddy, and sesame seeds.
One should place clarified butter, white mustard seeds, and flowers into the arghya vessel;
it should always be combined with honey, sugar, ghee, curd, and milk.
Having prepared the madhuparka, one should offer it according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, [one should provide] uśīra, kuṅkuma, māṃsī, and sandalwood.
Murā, hrīvera, kuṣṭha, and aguru—these are indeed declared to be the eight ingredients of the fragrant paste for Viṣṇu. (3.65)
With rocanā, kapikā, kuṅkuma, māṃsī, tvak, and aguru-candana—this is the sixth Vaiṣṇava fragrance, which is recommended for the Śaiva and Śākta [traditions]. (3.66)
A seat, a welcome, the arghya offering, water for the feet, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, further water for sipping, a bath, garments, and ornaments. (3.67)
One should employ perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise prostration; these are the sixteen services (upacāras) for that worship. (3.68)

The worship consisting of five services (pañcopacārikā pūjā) comprises the offering of water for honor (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), a seat (āsana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for sipping (ācamana), and so forth, beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya). // 3.69 //
Worship is said to be threefold; one should resort to one of these:
having meditated upon [the deity] worshipped with the mind, [one should offer it] through the left nostril. (3.70)
Having formed a *añjali* with the *praṇava*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon a seat of wood or a funeral pyre;
then, by means of the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should effect the presence [of the deity]. (3.71)

Then one should effect complete cessation with the mantra and the armor-mantra; having made [the deity] face oneself with the *praṇava* and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), [one should proceed]. (3.72)

Then, as with one's own body, one should prepare the water for the feet and other offerings for the body of the God; the water for the feet (pādya) should be given to the feet, and the respectful offering (arghya) is offered to the head.
There should be water for sipping (ācamanīya) in the mouth and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) there;
one skilled in mantras should again give water for sipping to the face. (3.74)

Thinking, "I shall prepare the water for the feet for him," one should arrange the water for the feet and other offerings, joined with this mantra beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. (3.75)
At the beginning and at the end of the worship, the preceptor should offer these—water for the feet, the arghya offering, and water for sipping—with the root mantra alone. (3.76)

Since the dismissal (*visarjana*) and the re-absorption (*āropaṇa*) into oneself are required, the sequence for that [process]—beginning with the mandala and so forth—is intended [to be explained] after sipping water (*ācamya*). (3/77)
With his two hands holding flowers, the practitioner should thus meditate on the Lord;
having entered the sacrificial ground, O God, he should then recollect the oceans. (3.78)
Then one should meditate on the God in the mouth, and immediately thereafter in the heart—the God who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, with a gracious countenance and eyes. (3.79)
In that manner, having unified oneself with that deity, one should contemplate;
when the dismissal is elsewhere, then one should offer the primary arghya.
One should dismiss [the deity] with the words, "Stay as you please and go elsewhere.
However, the dismissal [of the deity] by the teachers is not desired anywhere other than that [specific location]. (3.81)
But right there, one should offer [the oblation] with both hands as before;
having performed the recitation according to one's ability, as well as three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). (3.82)
Furthermore, having released the limbs in this manner, one should dismiss the deity;
when the knower of mantras sees something impure at the time of recitation, [he should do so]. (3.83)
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the remaining rites;
and when the practitioner himself is pure, he should then recite the mantra. (3.84)
Having bathed as before and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should recite [the mantra] again;
I shall now describe these preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) here. (3.85)

A twice-born person performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite should first subsist on food properly obtained through alms and so forth, and he should perform his recitation (*japa*) during the daytime alone. (3.86)
Subsisting on vegetables, barley-gruel, and chickpeas along with ghee, or else on curd, roots, or fruits, one should take this meal every day. (3.87)
Likewise, celibacy has been prescribed, as well as bathing at the three periods of the day;
one should especially perform the worship of the deity in the forenoon. (3.88)
Barley, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, solid food, and sacrificial oblation—each preceding one among these is more highly recommended as food for the accomplishment of mantras. (3.89)
All mantras should generally be employed with the syllable *praṇava* at their beginning;
one should remain seated on the prescribed seat, restrained in speech, and with a mind focused on nothing else. (3.90)
One should perform the recitation of mantras preceded by saluting the guru;
[one should visit] sacred fields, holy fords, forests, groves, temples, rivers, and lakes. (3.91)

These places—a hut or a secluded spot—are the ones that bestow the accomplishment of mantras; for through the recitation of the mantra within one's conduct, it becomes one with the nature of the deity. (3.92)

On the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, during eclipses and other such occasions especially, whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is ten times more distinguished than loud recitation (uccaiḥ). (3.93)
The whispered recitation (japa) performed with the tongue is a hundredfold [more effective], while the mental recitation is a thousandfold;
through ten hundred-thousand recitations, a mantra consisting of a single syllable attains success.
One should perform the recitation (japa) according to the increase of syllables; for others, one should combine [the counts].
At the junction of the rosary beads, the ritual of recitation should be performed with a mantra that is two or three times the number of seed-syllables (bīja). 3/95.
Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are known as *mālāmantras*;
mantras consisting of more than ten syllables, or half that number, are designated as *bījas*. (3.96)
Mantras bestow accomplishment in old age, while *mālāmantras* do so in youth;
those mantras consisting of five syllables grant accomplishment in childhood, and other mantras [grant it] beyond that.
They know that for all [rites], the fire-oblation and the libation consist of a tenth part of the recitation;
if one lacks the materials, ghee is used in the oblation, but if one is unable [to perform even that], one should recite everywhere. (3/98)
The recitation of the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth should be one-tenth of that of the root mantra (mūlamantra).
In the event of inability to perform the prescribed fire-oblation (homa), the recitation should be double. (3.99)
O beloved, for those recitations and fire-offerings for which no specific number has been stated by me,
the number eight thousand is prescribed for both the recitation and the offering.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the offering (bali) with the mantra ending in "svāhā";
one should perform prostration and worship with the mantra ending in "namaḥ. (3/101)
Having joined the name at the end of the mantra with the words "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*), one performs the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
No specific number is prescribed for the recitation (*japa*) or the fire-oblation (*homa*), though eight hundred and more is recommended.
The rites for nourishment and other purposes should be commenced according to the specific day, lunar day, and astrological conjunction; that procedure shall now be fully explained by me. (3.103)
The fifth, second, third, and likewise the seventh lunar days,
when conjoined with the day of Mercury or Jupiter, are highly esteemed for rites of pacification.
The sixth, when joined with Jupiter and the Moon, as well as the fourth,
the thirteenth, the seventh, and likewise the eighth and ninth, are recommended for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika).

The tenth and eleventh lunar days, when joined with Sunday or Friday, as well as the new moon, the ninth, and the first day of the lunar fortnight, are for the purpose of attraction (ākarṣaṇa). (3.106)
The full moon day joined with the slow-moving planet [Saturn] is for the rite of inciting hatred;
likewise, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and the eighth day when the stars are dim. (3.107)
For the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), the lunar days are auspicious, especially during the evening twilights;
namely, the fourteenth, the eighth, and likewise the new moon day of the dark fortnight. (3.108)
These [days] are also recommended for the rite of killing on a Mandāraka day;
likewise, the fifth and tenth lunar days when conjoined with the day of Mercury or the Moon. (3.109)
The full moon day (paurṇamāsī) should be known as the lunar day for the rite of immobilization (stambhana).
One should perform auspicious rites when there is the rising of benefic planets, and inauspicious rites when there is the rising of malefic planets.
In a fierce rite, killing is performed during the *riktā* lunar days, on Sundays, and during the *mṛtyu-yoga*;
starting from sunrise, this occurs sequentially during the ten *ghaṭikās*. (3.111)
The seasons—known as spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—should occur day by day within each day and night. (3.112)

The winter season is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), spring for rites of subjugation (vaśya); the cool season (śiśira) is to be known for rites of immobilization (stambhana), and summer is declared for rites of inciting enmity (vidveṣa). (3/113)
The rainy season is to be known for the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), and autumn for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
One should draw the diagram for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*) during the rising of Aquarius, Leo, or Scorpio.
Rites for hatred, eradication, and so forth should be performed during the ascensions of Capricorn, Cancer, Aries, and Libra;
while rites for subjugation, pacification, and nourishment should be performed during the ascensions of Aries, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces. (3.115)
One should perform the killing of an enemy and their suppression through methods such as sowing dissension when the eighth sign is reached;
one should write for subjugation (*vaśya*) in the forenoon, and for inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*) at midday. (3/116)
Peace and nourishment are accomplished during the twilight hours, while killing is performed at the time of dusk;
one should write for paralyzing at midnight, and for attracting before the break of day. (3.117)
The wise man should draw whatever other auspicious work is to be done at dawn;
subjugation is performed in the east (Indra), and eradication in the southeast (Agni), as well as all malevolent rites.
In the south, there is enmity toward the Rakshasas; in the directions of Varuna and Soma, there is peace;
in the region of the Maruts, there is the destruction of one's lineage; and in the northwest, there is strife and suppression. (3.119)
One should perform the prescribed auspicious rite for the state of Brahman;
for subjugation and attraction, one should write on birch bark, and for eradication, one should write on a banner.

Having inscribed [the mantra] upon the skin of a donkey, one effects enmity; upon elephant hide, one effects immobilization; and having inscribed it upon the garment of a deceased person, one brings about death by fever and other afflictions. (3.121)
In a dispute, one should perform rites such as paralyzing; even on a stone slab, one may effect delusion.
For subjugation, one uses saffron, camphor, gorocana, and turmeric. (3.122)
With the ring finger, one should write for immobilization and attraction;
with one's own blood, for inciting enmity; and with the blood of a crow, for killing. (3.123)

One should perform delusion with blood from a person full of hatred, and expulsion with the blood of a camel; likewise, one may effect both hatred and expulsion, as well as killing, with the feathers of a crow. (3.124)
One should visualize the red color for subjugation, attraction, and immobilization;
one should visualize the red color for neutralizing poison and for immobilization. (3.125)
One should contemplate white for pacification, nourishment, and invigoration; yellow for rites of immobilization; and smoke-colored for rites of eradication. (3.126)
In the case of driving away [an enemy], the seat has the luster of a *śakragopa* insect; for killing, it is black in color; however, the white-colored seat is declared to be *sāttvika*. (3.127)
That which stands on the path of vehicles is yellow and proclaimed as rājasa;
that which stands on the measure of the staff is fierce, black, and is called tāmasa. (3.128)
The *sāttvika* [mantra] is for those desiring liberation; the *rājasa* is for those desiring sovereignty;
the *tāmasa* is for the destruction of enemies and the warding off of all diseases. (3/129)
For the sake of pacifying all calamities, one should contemplate the Tāmasa [form]:
the Rudras, along with the Tārkṣyas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rakṣases, and Kinnaras. (3.130)
Piśācas, bhūtas, lords of daityas, siddhas, kimpuruṣas, and gods—the portions of all mantras are traditionally said to be fifteen. (3.131)
Some say there are eighteen [types] considered for all men:
the two-syllable *kartarī*, the three-syllable *sūcī*, and those with four syllables. (3.132)
The mallet and the pestle have five colors; the chains have six; the armor has seven; the trident has eight; and the supreme [weapon] has nine. (3.133)
The spear (śakti) is said to consist of ten [syllables], and the axe (paraśu) of eleven;
the discus (cakra) consists of twelve phonemes, while the thunderbolt (kuliśa) should consist of thirteen. (3.134)
The nārāca and bhuśuṇḍī weapons are formed with fourteen syllables;
the lotus with sixteen syllables; and the scissors for cutting mantras likewise. (3.135)
The *sūcī* is described by its specific division; the *mudgara* is known for use while eating;
the *muṣala* is for agitation; the *śṛṅkhala* is for binding; and the *krakaca* is for cutting. (3/136)
One should employ the *śūla* for killing, the *śakti* for paralyzing and the act of attraction, the *paraśu* for inciting enmity, and the *cakra* for all rites. (3.137)

The *kuliśa* is prescribed for joining [mantras], the *nārāca* for breaking through enemy forces, the *bhusuṇḍī* for killing, and the *padma* for rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*). (3.138)
The wheel, however, is the coloring rite; one should not employ it in this manner for the higher [levels].
Although it has been shown in some instances, it contradicts both the principles (tattva) and the scriptures (āgama). (3/139)

Since the rules for the practical application of mantras such as the thousand-syllable mantra have been shown, listen now to me regarding how the recitation of mantras should be performed according to one's desire. (3.140)
The addition of a name at the beginning of a mantra is proclaimed as the "sprout" (pallava);
it is used for killing, neutralizing poison, and subduing planetary influences and spirits. (3.141)
For the rites of eradication and inciting enmity, a sprout is indeed recommended.
The placement of the name at the beginning of the mantra and so forth is designated as "yoga. (3/142)
In rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, expiation, purification, delusion, and illumination, the wise employ the yoga. (3.143)
He is said to be employed in the rites of paralyzing (stambhana), eradication (uccāṭana), piercing (udbheda), and creating enmity (vidveṣa).
When the mantra is placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name, it is called "obstruction" (rodha). (3.144)

In bringing about the presence of the mantra, in warding off all diseases, and in pacifying the afflictions of fever, planetary influences, poison, and the like, it is called "obstruction" (rodha). (3.145)
In the case of delusion (*sammohana*), that same [method] applies, as well as the syllables of the mantra's name;
when they are separated by intervals of one [syllable], that is proclaimed as "interlacing" (*grathana*). (3.146)

That should be employed for pacification, with the name placed at the beginning and end as Manu prescribed; that is called "encased" (saṃpuṭa), and it is defined for use in the rite of pinning (kīlana). (3.147)

In the divine *stambha*, *mṛtyuñjaya*, and *rakṣā* [mantras], there is a *saṃpuṭa* [structure] consisting of one syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) for each syllable of the mantra, in due order. (3.148)
That [syllable] is said to be Vidarbha for the rites of subjugation and nourishment;
thus has the sequence of yoga been declared by the wise for all undertakings. (3.149)
One should employ *huṃ* for binding, eradication, and hatred when they are combined;
*phaṭ* for cutting; and *huṃ phaṭ* for warding off obstacles and seizing spirits. || 3/150 ||
In rites of minor action and the like, women are employed, while eunuchs are used elsewhere;
*vauṣaṭ* is for nourishment and satiation, and *sanikṛntatau* is for awakening. (3.151)
One should recite "svāhā" in the fire-ritual (agnikārya) and "namaḥ" everywhere during worship;
[these are used] for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, causing hatred, attraction, expulsion, and killing. (3.152)
One should employ *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* in their proper sequence.
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), causing distress (*santāpa*), and fever (*jvara*), one should employ *svāhā*. (3.153)
The wise should employ "Namaḥ" for the pacification of anger and for peace, and "Prīti" for attraction;
they should use "Vaṣaṭ" for enchantment, stimulation, nourishment, and the conquest of death. (3.154)
The syllable *hrīṃ* causes the destruction of affection; likewise, *vaṣaṭ* is used for cutting, killing, driving away, and inciting hatred, as well as when making offerings to the fire. (3.155)
In the matter of making known the mantra, *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed for both gain and loss.
The classes of mantras are threefold, according to whether they are feminine, masculine, or neuter. (3.156)
Feminine mantras end with the "wife of fire" (svāhā), neuter mantras end with "namas," and masculine mantras are said to end with "huṃ phaṭ" in rites of subjugation and eradication. (3.157)
A mantra that predominantly consists of the syllables *tāra* (om), *agni* (fire), or *anya-viyat* (other than space) is said to be fiery (*āgneya*).
The remainder are lunar (*saumya*); these two are praised for use in fierce and gentle rites, respectively. (3.158)

A mantra belonging to Agni may become gentle (saumya) if it is generally accompanied by "namaḥ" at the end; likewise, even a peaceful mantra becomes fierce (raudra) if it is embellished with "hūṃ" and "phaṭ. (3.159)
A mantra, whether asleep or awakening, does not bestow accomplishment; for O Left-Armed One, sleep occurs when [the breath] flows through the left, and waking when it flows through the right. (3/160)
If the mantra of Soma were to belong to the Fire-manu through a complete reversal, one should know that at the time of awakening, both mantras bring about the results of both. (3/161)
But during sleep, one should not speak; in the rite of *stobha*, one should cause the doors to be obstructed.
Having performed the *dhāraṇā* of Agni, one should perform the possession (*āveśana*) in due order. (3.162)
Having performed the *māhendrī* concentration, one should commence the withdrawal;
having fixed the mind right there on the south, one should perform the act of slaying. (3/163)
One should begin the rite of causing enmity, expulsion, destruction, and the making of one hunchbacked;
this occurs in the right part of the *ādhāra* through the conjunction of poison and the planets. (3/164)
A person should paralyze an army and undertake their undertakings;
likewise, legal proceedings against an enemy should be conducted right there on the left side. (3/165)
Having fixed the mind on the point [bindu] in the southern part, the wise one should practice for the sake of pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and the enchantment of women. (3/166)
One should accomplish the vidyā for the rite of sorcery (abhicāra) on the left side;
having fixed the mind upon the pericarp of the foundation (ādhāra), one should practice it there. (3.167)
One should accomplish the *sārasvatī* siddhi as well as other *śākteyī* siddhis;
the *pauṣṭikī* siddhi is incomparable and bestows the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha. (3/168)
The pericarp within the heart is attained by one of steady mind;
it consists of a square, a half-moon, a triangle, and a hexagon. (3.169)
And they are well-rounded, with the shapes of spheres such as the earth and so forth, in sequence;
yellow, white, red, blackish, and smoky-colored. (3/170)
There, the seed-syllables beginning with *u* cause one to fall into hell;
however, in the center of the navel is the mandala of wind, conjoined with its seed-syllable.
One should maintain there the consciousness characterized by the specific nature of air;
one should contemplate a triangle, the Piṅgalā, as the fire-maṇḍala within the heart. (3/172)
One should maintain there the consciousness as the fire element on all sides; in the ritual manual, the Maheśvara mandala is called the Earth mandala. (3.173)
There, one should meditate upon the pillar of consciousness endowed with its [mantric] bundle;
and on the forehead, an half-moon marked by two white lotuses. (3.174)

One should maintain consciousness therein and contemplate it in the form of water; having performed this visualization during the deliberation, one should conceive the earth as submerged on its southern side. (3/175)
The garment is said to be red, and the turban is remembered as red;
the circle of the sky is marked with six dots belonging to the wind-god.
A triangle, provided with a svastika and conjoined with the aperture of fire;
a lotus for water, and a square with a thunderbolt for earth. (3/177)
Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī—these are said to be, in order, the six deities of action; one should worship them at the beginning of the ritual worship and other rites. (3.178)
The directions of Īśa, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni are considered [the presiding deities].
Having understood the deities of the directions, time, and so forth, one should accomplish one's ritual acts. (3.179)
Now I shall describe the postures according to the prescribed ritual:
the lotus posture (padmāsana) for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), and the auspicious posture (svastikāsana) for rites of pacification (śāntika). (3.180)
Likewise, the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana) is used for attraction, nourishment, and inciting enmity;
the half-svastika (ardhasvastika) for eradication, while the half-sthāpana-pārṣṇika is for immobilization.
Likewise, for killing and immobilizing, the vikaṭa posture is proclaimed;
for subjugation, the bhadrāsana is taught for them, and now follows their meditative cultivation.

The six mudrās should be known in sequence as those called the lotus, the noose, and the mace; and those named the club, the thunderbolt, and the sword, for the rites of pacification and so forth. (3.183)
In rites for pacification, nourishment, and subjugation, she is endowed with supreme beauty, radiant with all ornaments, and has attained the fulfillment of her desires and aspirations. (3.184)
The deity should be properly meditated upon with a face like a perfectly serene lotus;
likewise, even in the act of attraction, one should proceed as if drawing fish with a hook. (3.185)
In the case of attraction, it is like one being drawn toward a goal; in the case of aversion, like one being rebuked by people;
and in the case of killing, like a thief being dragged away by people while being torn apart with clubs. (3.186)

For the purpose of subduing or expelling an enemy, one should visualize him as an owl possessed by a crow; for the purpose of paralyzing, one should imagine him as being crushed by a stone like a blade of grass or a leaf. (3/187)
Struck by the king’s men like an axe by a thief, or by a tiger, he is rendered powerless when it comes to killing again. (3.188)
Having mounted any corpse whatsoever, with his lips bitten together in rage, the mantra-practitioner should then perform the rite, just as in the case of cruel rituals. (3.189)
Having fashioned a rosary from pearls or even from crystal,
one should recite the mantra for the sake of its accomplishment during rites of pacification or those that are mixed.
One should perform recitation with coral and diamond gems for the rites of subjugation and enrichment;
one should perform recitation with gems from the tusks of an elephant in rut for the rite of attraction. (3.191)
And in a battle of the dead, one who desires the destruction of an enemy should make a rosary from the teeth of a brave man and a donkey, and perform the recitation. (3/192)
Having observed a rosary made from the hair of an enemy, horsehair, or the sinews of a corpse, one should recite [the mantra] for the purposes of causing hatred or expulsion. (3.193)
One who desires the destruction of an enemy should fashion a garland from the teeth of a donkey and a corpse that has died in battle, and then perform the recitation. (3.194)
It is performed with conch shells and gems for the attainment of dharma, desire, and wealth;
and one should recite the mantra with lotus seeds for the attainment of all desires and aims. (3.195)
A mantra recited with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows all fruits; a cord made from lotus fibers is recommended for rites of pacification and nourishment. (3/196)
For attraction and eradication, a rope made from the hair of a horse's tail is used;
for killing, a rope made specifically from human sinews is supreme. (3/197)
For other rosaries, an auspicious cotton string made with twenty-seven beads bestows liberation. (3.198)
A rosary consisting of fifteen beads is prescribed therein by the seers of reality at the outset as that which bestows the fruit of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*). (3.199)
Worshipped with exactly one hundred and eight [offerings] in all rites, one should recite the mantra for attraction using the middle finger and the thumb. (3.200)

One should perform the recitation with the thumb and forefinger for the rites of inciting hatred and expulsion; one should perform the recitation with the thumb and little finger for the rite of slaying an enemy. (3.201)
One should perform the recitation with the thumb and the ring finger during other rites;
however, one should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers in this manner. (3.202)
If a recitation is performed without using the thumb, it shall be fruitless.
For the rite of subjugation, one should recite facing the east; for malevolent rites, facing the south. (3.203)
In the west, one should find the giver of wealth; in the north, it shall be for pacification.
It will effect longevity, protection, peace, or even nourishment. (3/204)
Thus, having addressed the Pradhāna, one should offer prayers until the emission [of the seed-syllable]. (3.205)
Having addressed the deity, one should write the mantra—which has that deity as its agent and expresses the name of what is to be accomplished—containing the seed-syllable (*mantrabīja*) within it.

If the mantra of the subordinate deity (*upadevatā*) or of the limbs (*aṅga*) consists of a single syllable, one should write that very syllable all around. This sequence should be understood for the initial writing of general mantras and so forth; however, in the case of recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and the like, having made such a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one proceeds in the same manner at the conclusion of the rite, such as the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
"One should pray"—this is the secret.

For the accomplishment of sacrifice, the fire-oblation (homa) for pacification and nourishment should be performed by those who achieve the rite in an eight-sided, square, circular, or lotus-shaped [fire-pit]. (3/206)
Then, it should be performed with either the face turned as before or with a gentle face;
however, for attraction, it is done in a wind-pit (vāyukuṇḍa) while facing the northern direction.

For the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), one should offer oblations into that pit facing either the southwest or the north; or, for the rite of driving away (*mārutaka*), one should face the southeast or [the northeast] in that pit.

For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations facing north; for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), he should face the southern direction and offer oblations into the southern sacrificial pit (*yāmyakuṇḍa*) using the specific means for that purpose.

For the warding off of planetary influences and spirits, one should offer oblations into a pit marked with a vajra while facing the northwest; for subjugation, one should offer into a pit shaped like a womb (yoni).
In a pit marked with a vajra, one should offer oblations facing east during the rite of immobilization (stambha).
I shall also describe the substances according to their respective ritual requirements.
In rites for pacification (śāntika), however, milk, ghee, sesame, and milk are used in sequence;
furthermore, the creeper known as Amṛtā and milk-rice (pāyasa) are prescribed therein. (3.212)
Next, I shall describe the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) in rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika):
through bilva leaves one obtains a kingdom, and likewise through jasmine flowers (jātī). (3.213)

One desiring a daughter should offer oblations with parched grains (lāja); likewise, one desiring a son with lotuses; one obtains prosperity through curd; and food through offerings of grain soaked in clarified butter.
One should offer oblations with five-colored flowers soaked in clarified butter;
one obtains clothing of that same color from the Night Goddess—of this there is no doubt. (3.215)
For the sake of prosperity and to pacify great poverty, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with milk, or ghee, or lotuses soaked in honey. (3.216)
Through a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) with ghee, bilva, and sesame seeds, one obtains peace and a treasure;
for attraction, however, one uses salt and priyaṅgu, along with those [substances] prescribed for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
One seeking subjugation [should offer] *jātī* flowers; for attraction, those born of the *karavīra*; likewise with cotton, *nimba*, buttermilk and the like, or even with new hair. (3.218)

For the purpose of driving away (uccāṭana), the wise one should offer oblations with crow feathers; for bewitching (mohana), with seeds of the mad-datura plant; and for killing (māraṇa), with poison and blood.
And one should offer goat’s milk and its ghee, as well as the seeds of cotton and even the bones of men;
likewise, the flesh of the victim, along with his nails, hair, and human marrow. (3.220)
Desiring to slay an enemy, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations after unifying [the elements];
for the sake of killing a donkey, one should sprinkle it with garlic and blood. (3.221)
One should offer oblations with clarified butter or oils for the purpose of slaying an enemy;
for the purpose of eradication, one should offer oblations with *rohī* seeds mixed with sesame seeds, or with barley.
For all malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one should offer oblations with pungent oils, seeds mixed with husks and thorns, cotton seeds, and mustard seeds blended with sesame. (3.223)
With cruel *kākolūka* leaves, *kāraskara*, *vibhītaka*, *marīca*, *sarṣapa*, and the milky sap of the *arka* plant, along with pungent trees, [the rite] is accomplished. (3.224)
One desiring death should perform the rites with pungent oils and the milk of the *snuhī* plant;
those desiring long life should do so with ghee, sesame seeds, or mango shoots. (3.225)
One should instantly destroy fever with mango leaves smeared with milk;
likewise, one should use *guḍūcī* together with the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra for the pacification of elephants and horses. (3.226)
One should offer oblations with white mustard seeds to remove sudden diseases of cattle;
likewise, one desiring rain should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of cane and their leaves.

Having offered oblations with *puṣṭikara* seeds, one obtains nourishment; with *putrajīva* seeds, one obtains a son; and by offering oblations of ghee and *guggulu*, one attains the status of a master of speech.
Through flowers produced from the *mallikā*, *jāti*, *vidruma*, *nāga*, and *punnāga* trees, as well as through Sarasvatī, there is accomplishment and likewise the fulfillment of all aims. (3.229)
One should offer oblations with milk or even with salts for the purpose of warding off rain;
likewise, one should offer red flowers, apāmārga, aṅkola, and subhadraka. (3.230)
With these [flowers] sprinkled with honey, the mantra-practitioner may effect subjugation;
likewise, with dry leaves blown by the wind or with wood struck down by lightning. (3.231)
Likewise, by means of camel bone and *avakushta* [seeds], there is the eradication of an enemy;
as well as with *dūrvā* grass, *guḍūcī*, cow’s ghee, sesame seeds, and rice. (3.232)
The wise man should perform a rite for peace with oblations of rice and fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood;
first, he should recite the mantra at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) for the sake of liberation from sin. (3.233)
This mantra bestows accomplishment upon one whose body is purified;
yet a mantra that has not been meditated upon or worshipped does not become well-accomplished, nor does it grant its favor.
A mantra that has not been recited does not grant success; one that has not been offered in oblation becomes a source of misfortune.
Thus, worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offering constitute the fourfold set of ritual actions. (3.235)
Every day the practitioner should perform this himself if he desires accomplishment:
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should meditate on Śiva; at the conclusion of the meditation, there is again the recitation. (3/236)
The knower of mantras, engaged in recitation and meditation, attains success quickly.
[These trees are] known as Kāraskara, Kṣīrāmalaka, Udumbara, and Jambu. (3.237)
Khadira, kuṣṭha, karaca, pippala, nāgara, rohiṇī, palāśa, lakṣa, kāmbaṣṭha, bilva, arjuna, and vikaṅkata. (3.238)
The mantra is Sārasika, Moṭa, Ārūḍhāgni, Sadāgati with the bindu, and likewise Tumburu with Parākrānta and Īśa. (3/239)
The vowel *ī* is called *svaramāyā*, while the vowel *ā* is said to be the noose (*pāśa*).
*Krom* is the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and *huṃ* is the wrath (*krodha*); *i* is Viṣṇu, who is both supreme and non-supreme. (3/240)
The first [letter] with the bindu is said to be the end of the creation-group (sṛṣṭivarga), namely *ha*.
When joined with two or even many [other letters], it is called a *piṇḍa*. (3/241)
The letter *ī* is the illustrious Mahāmāyā; the letter *e* is known as Bhaga;
the dot (*bindu*) is the Moon and the Vessel (*kuṇḍa*); and the nasalization (*anusvāra*) is called the syllable *huṃ*. (3/242)

The vowel *i* is said to be the emission of the *kalā*; *ha* is proclaimed as the fire of time (*kālāgni*). The final letter of the temple (*ma*) and the wrathful one (*krodha*) are the principle (*tattva*), remembered as *kṣa*. (3/243)
The semi-vowels y, r, l, and v, as well as the sibilants ś, ṣ, s, and h, are internal;
others declare that the letter l and the vowel e are external. (3/244)

In this manner, the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the final letter of the twelve powers (*śakti*), such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others, beginning with Kālī, will now be described. That very name [of each power] is its designation; here, the designation of the letters should be understood according to the vowel. Enough with this brief indication. When the enemy is to be slain, it is not otherwise; such is the established doctrine.
With a mind thus agitated, one should likewise perform [the rite] excluding the Brāhmaṇas. (3.245)
If one does not attain success due to the obstruction of a powerful opposing karma, one should perform the rite again two or three times. (3.246)
One who is utterly struck down by fate should not undertake worldly activities;
there is no fault whatsoever in this, though he may incur ridicule. (3/247)
Having understood the supreme procedure for practice in its general form, one should perform it according to the specific rite therein, and not otherwise. (3.248)
Thus ends the third chapter, the General Chapter, in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The Fourth Chapter.
Now I shall proclaim the foremost and most excellent mantra of the cocks, just as the sole Guru of the Kṣapaṇas [did], for the benefit of the worlds. (4.1)
That which was previously mentioned as ending with the letter *na*, followed by the sixth vowel (*ū*), and possessing a *bindu*—this is called the *Kukkuṭa*;
this mantra is repeated, and the word is repeated again, followed by the previous mantra ending with *na* and the fifth vowel (*u*). This mantra is said to bestow longevity.
The bestower of glory, wealth, all happiness, good fortune, and prosperity.
This fifteen-syllable mantra has been declared to have Kukkuta as its presiding deity;
all that is the splendor of the deity, augmented by the power of Śakti. (4.3)
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk, upon a supreme island with a ground of gold and jewels,
delightful on its surface with a gentle breeze from soft sand and jewels strewn incessantly—
therein stands a pure, towering tree, bearing a multitude of jewel-like fruits.
It was devoid of even a single golden lattice, yet possessed leaves of many kinds, variegated and shimmering with numerous jewels.

One should further meditate upon that [deity] as presiding over it, with limbs exceedingly radiant and most beautiful, his face adorned by a crest, and his claws and feet as sharp as those of a cock. (4.5)

He whose face is the six-faced god (Kārttikeya), whose belly is the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī), whose back is the destroyer of Time (Śiva), and whose two feet are the elephant-faced god (Gaṇeśa) on his left and right;
he whose wings are the celestial trees and who wears a beautiful chain made of jewels— [to him I bow].
May that very cock bestow upon us all the qualities of attraction and the rest. 4/6.
Dwelling eternally upon the lotus-hand of Gaurī, with his body resting upon her face,
radiant with every ornament, moving his feet, and skilled in the flapping of wings; golden-hued,
with a beak of jewels and a neck adorned with shimmering circular gems, he is of beautiful form.
May that red-crested one, the bestower of all perfections, protect us from all people. 4/7.
Alternatively, the cock that dwells upon the tip of a palmyra tree on the jewel-island in the midst of the ocean is dear to all;
delightful as an altar, enriched with every ornament, and well-served by the immortals, it quickly brings others under its control. (4.8)
For the sake of preliminary service for that [deity], having performed a great worship of the Lord in a Śiva temple containing a single liṅga, he sits facing north. (4.9)
One should perform the preliminary rites of the mantra on a mountain peak, by a riverbank, in a temple of Śiva devoid of cattle, or in a place provided with a western door. (4.10)
Having bowed to the Guru mentally, one should prepare a seat;
then one should perform the purification of the hands, the purification of the body, and the three claps of the palms. (4.11)
Afterwards, the wise one should perform the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra;
thereafter, he should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Praṇava.
One should first arrange the *mātṛkā* and afterwards perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
One should then specify that very mantra which is the first of the bird-mantra. (4.13)
Having uttered the second word, one should perform [the rite] with the head itself;
and having placed *vīṃ* at the crest, one should place the third syllable of *vana-pakṣin*.
Having uttered the fourth state (turiyapada), one should apply it to the eyes;
the six limbs are prescribed as being joined with the "beak" weapon (cañcvāstra).

Pūḥ! To the heart, *namaḥ*; [with repetition] to the reality (*tattva*) of you, *svāhā* to the head. Pūḥ! To the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; [with repetition] to the reality (*tattva*) of you, *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*). 4.16.
PŪṂ: for the three eyes, Vauṣaṭ; PŪṂ: for the palms and backs of the hands, Astra, Phaṭ.
One should assign Namaḥ, Svāhā, Vaṣaṭ, Huṃ, and Vauṣaṭ in their respective order. (4.17)
The wise practitioner should sequentially place the *pūm* syllable and other *pūm* syllables in the center of the forehead-bindu, as well as in the eyes and the ears. (4.18)
One should place [the mantras] in the two nostrils, in the mouth, in the throat, as well as in the heart, in the stomach, in the region of the navel, in the penis, and in the private parts. (4.19)
One should perform the placement [of mantras] pervading the head and other parts with the entire mantra.
Having thus performed the placement upon the body, one should meditate on the Bird whose nature is Śiva.
Having worshipped the deity mentally with the sixteen types of service (upacāra),
and having made a formal petition through external yoga, one should diligently satisfy the deity.
Having meditated upon that deity Kukkuṭa, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times;
having offered libations a hundred times, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) will be accomplished. || 4/22 ||
The knower of mantras should perform the desired rites—such as protection, causing enmity, paralyzing, and driving away—by means of this mantra. (4.23)

Having written [the name] interlaced with the mantra within a vessel of salt, ending with the syllables of the person to be acted upon (sādhya), and having established the vital breaths (prāṇas) therein, if one recites it one hundred and eight times and then holds [the vessel], that person comes under one's control. (4.24)

If one gives betel-leaf to a woman after reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eight times before eating it, she will become eternally submissive; through this instruction, she will laugh and bestow upon him all desired enjoyments and wealth. (4.25)

Furthermore, he who recites the mantra five hundred times, having applied it to the preparations of various kinds of food and drink, brings even one named Kanaka, along with his lineage, under his control until death. (4.26)
The root [of Citrā] together with radish and mustard oil, the bark and flower of the two types of Citrā, the seed of Hastikarṇa along with its potency, water from within one's own nostril,
and the Rauhiṇa leaf— these five parts, when combined together in a vessel, [form the remedy].
Or rather, for a man, that [staff] is held as punishment; but for a woman under his control, this [staff] is the god of love.
If one recites the Hayamāraka root mantra one hundred and eight times and casts it upon the head of someone for seven nights, that person shall become submissive. (4.28)

Having inscribed this mantra, interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), upon birch bark, and having fashioned an effigy from clay mixed with *kaulālī* earth, one should place it in the heart and install the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) therein;
then, having recited [the mantra] at the three junctions of the day for a full day, or alternatively, having stirred it with the juices of *guṇḍī*—
Once anointed, one will certainly become submissive, even in other future births. (4.29)

One who holds upon his head, with palms joined in reverence, a stalk of flowers over which the mantra has been recited one thousand and eight times, will certainly become beloved in all the world; such indeed is the excellent practitioner of the mantra. (4.30)

Likewise, one should bear the *chada* leaf, the *vallī* creeper, and *lakṣmī* flowers; thus, through the recitation of the *musaliśa* mantra, one becomes prosperous, a bringer of auspiciousness, and beloved. (4.31)
Madhuka, the goddess Dūrvā, Haṃsā, and likewise ghee—just as [these are effective], what need is there to mention the root of the Varaṇa tree, let alone among human beings? (4.32)
By combining ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one part respectively with the anusvāra and the eye (the letter *i*),
and joining them in sequence starting from the *añjali* [mudrā], the entire region is brought under control.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for each [ingredient], having combined them and ground them into ten portions, and having formed them into pills and recited [the mantra] over them one thousand and eight times, the application of a *tilaka* made with these pills serves to delight women and men. This [ointment] is like collyrium held in the hand, mixed with camphor and applied with a wick lit by the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilā*), containing various medicinal herbs. It has been consecrated one thousand times.
One should perform this daily for a full year to bring the entire world under one's control; such is the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

Having meditated upon oneself as a cock by means of the power of one's own *gaṇa*, and having bound the target by the neck with a chain, one should recite the mantra of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). (4.34)

For three nights, remaining vigilant during the middle of the night for a thousand times, at the end of the fourth crowing of the cock, he should [utter] the name of the person to be accomplished and the ritual action. (4.35)
One who desires subjugation should recite [the mantra] while joined [in yoga] at all times; beginning from the third watch of the day, one should thus recite over a woman languid with passion. (4.36)
With her garments dampened by perspiration and her mind agitated by passion, her secret parts and hips were moist with sweat, and her clothes and ornaments had become loose. (4.37)
With her footsteps faltering as she moved, her bodice bristling with thrills of horripilation, her sighs heated by the fire of passion, and the sprout of her lower lip parched; 4.38.
With her mass of hair disheveled, her eyes rolling as she stumbles, and her hands joined in salutation, she comes to the mouth of her dwelling at night. (4.39)

Having inscribed this mantra— interspersed with the *sādhya* [name] and the *praṇava*, together with the ritual action— within the leaf of a betel nut using a stylus, and having performed the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*),
one should recite it eight hundred times over a plaster made from the milky sap of the *arka* plant, after an interval of three nights.
Heated by the flame of the lamp's fire, Urvaśī herself would take refuge with the two uru-śīs (thighs).

Having written this entire mantra, enriched with the lineage of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), upon birch bark, and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (infusion of life) for it, one should then recite it one hundred and eight times for three nights.
Then, having separately cast this mantra into honey, clarified butter, and milk, one should recite it again.
One attracts the desired woman from even the realms of the Nāgas and other worlds before long. || 4/41 ||
Having written this mantra, together with the person's name and action, upon a shallow dish with *rocanā* at night, and having performed one hundred and eight recitations while fanning it with air,
one should heat a fire made of *khadira* wood, facing away from that [dish], which has arisen from his own body.
And a woman, as treacherous as the impetuous speed of an elephant in rut, approaches the fire. (4.42)
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one who recites [the mantra] interwoven with the name of the target three thousand times over three days will certainly attract the desired person.
Thus is the summoning.
Likewise, one should grind monkey hair and asafoetida upon the hide of a donkey;
the mantra, recited seven times, should be interwoven with the name and the ritual action. (4.44)
Furthermore, by means of that [incense], there arises a fragrance between two people who are affectionate; even those who are hostile, or even those who are affectionate, become divided. (4.45)
One should write the mantra, interwoven with the name and the ritual action, upon a palm leaf smeared with poison;
having made it into two pieces, one should bury them on both banks of the ocean.
With this mantra, one should perform a thousand oblations at the conclusion of the rite in a fire of *khadira* wood;
thereby, even two sick people shall come to hate one another.
Thus ends the rite for creating enmity.

Having written the name of the target person enclosed within the mantra at night on a mirror and a clay dish, one should bury it at a crossroads after reciting the mantra one thousand times while holding one's breath. 4/48.
This immobilization will certainly come to pass for all the worlds; there is no doubt in this matter.

Having fashioned an image—or alternatively, using charcoal from a cremation ground as clothing—one should properly establish it with the wind [mantra], with the name placed within the heart, with the mantra on the forehead, and with the wind situated in the testicles; having recited that over a thousand times, or even ten thousand times, one should burn the garment.

One should write it after recollecting [the deity]. In a cremation ground, there is the paralysis of speech for one who has a wife. Having written the mantra—enclosed within the name of the person to be acted upon—upon a pair of bricks, and having performed a thousand recitations at midnight during the night, the mantra becomes established with life-force;
this is an extremely sharp binding. For paralyzing, it is thrown into extremely sharp water.
Having written the mantra upon a kila made of *citā* wood, together with the ritual action, the name,
and the recitation performed three thousand times, one should then bury it on the path to ward off the *jāla* [obstacles].

Having assumed the form of a *nimb* tree at night, one should perform this mantra—consisting of the name of the enemy joined with the *yūṃ* syllable—and having recited it nine thousand times and accomplished it with the eight [offerings], one should then bury it on the road to block the enemy army. (4.50)
Thus ends the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*). Now, the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*):
Having recited [the mantra] over charcoal from a funeral pyre under the asterisms of Maghā, Ardra, Mūla, or Pūrvaphalgunī, this [charcoal] is prepared and cast into a fire situated on a funeral pyre.
And having burnt that [mixture] combined with [the substance of] existence here, one should write the name of the enemy at the top of the mantra and the pair of karmas.
Having recited the mantra eight thousand times on a Tuesday coinciding with the fourteenth lunar day, O Śivā, one should cast [the substance] and shake it;
having recited the mantra three thousand times according to the sequence of the ritual, it becomes enriched with the power of the rite.
Having performed the rite of giving, one should cast it upon the head of the enemy.
One will certainly and swiftly uproot that enemy by reciting this mantra over a red-hot coal during the asterisms of Maghā, Aśleṣā, Mūla, or Puṣya,
while inserting the name of the enemy therein.
It is like a mantra, wrapped [in cloth], and recited eight thousand times.
Having scattered [the mantra] at the four cremation grounds to cause destruction in the enemy's house,
one should recite the mantra together with the ritual action and the encapsulation (saṃpuṭa).
Having recited it one thousand times, one should bury it in the house of enemies.
And at that door, eradication occurs swiftly;
having cast out the nest of crows into the fire located in the *pitṛbhu* (southern) quarter, one should recite the mantra over the enemy mixed with those ashes. (4.55)
Having written the name of the person against whom the rite is directed at the top of the mantra, one should uproot the enemy after reciting it eight thousand times;
this should be performed on another Tuesday that coincides with the fourteenth lunar day.
It is enriched by the sequence of actions and recited one thousand times with the Anu-mantra.
Having recited the mantra, one should cast it upon the head of the enemy;
this will certainly and swiftly cause the enemy to be eradicated.
This is the "Funeral Pyre Meteor" rite, using the name and karma of the enemy.
And one whose leaf has been touched [by him], having recited [the mantra] a thousand times. || 4/57 ||
One should cast an owl at the door; within seven days, it shall cause the enemy's eradication.
Furthermore, one should take a stake made of funeral pyre wood, inscribed with the name and the ritual action, and [recite the mantra] eight thousand times.
One should bury in the enemy's house that which has been consecrated with the mantra; it causes their expulsion in an instant.
One should write the mantra on a piece of *kāraskara* wood using soot from a funeral pyre stirred with the juice of *unmatta*, using a crow’s wing as the pen.
One should write the mantra, which is as beautiful as the fruit of the *kākavandhyā* plant, encased within the name of the ritual action.

Having dispatched his life-breaths into this [object] which is smeared with the eight poisons of an enemy and rendered effective, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times right there, either in a cremation ground or at a crossroads. (4.60)
If one buries it in the enemy’s house or casts that water upon the head of the foe,
he will either go to another land or, being constantly afflicted by disease, go to the other world.
Thus ends the rite of eradication.
The fourth chapter.
The fifth chapter:

Having written the mantra interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) on a palm leaf, and having placed it within two effigies (*puttalī*), one should perform the recitation of the mantra a thousand times while focusing the mind on the vital breath (*pavana*).

Having killed [the victim] smeared with pungent oil in a fire ignited in a cemetery that blazes like one of the insane, and having remained there during the night-watch of the bear (the seventh watch), one may cause delusion or death for a duration of three days. || 5/1 ||

If one recites [the mantra] while presiding over an image fashioned from the wood of the *sādhyākhya* tree, even a thousand repetitions will cause [the target] to be pinned down in a cremation ground.
With a weapon, one pierces the limb [of the target] once the mantra has been mastered.
Whatever limb of even the enemy of mountains (the elephant) perishes, [it is consumed by fire].

Having fashioned an effigy from clay mixed with the dust from the footprint of an enemy’s offspring, one should write this mantra— accompanied by that person's name and their specific deed— upon the heart, the head,
or the feet of that figure using charcoal obtained from a cremation ground.
Having placed this wind [mantra] upon his heart, he should quickly recite it two thousand times.

And always, facing the southern direction, one should offer into the blazing fire of the cremation ground— kindled by the ten causal factors— the oil produced from *tīkṣṇa* (mustard) after having first extracted it from a doll struck a hundred times with a weapon; or alternatively, one may do so under the constellation of Nairṛti.
"The minister has heard that the city of the Lord of the Dead (Yama) will certainly be reached by this enemy."
On a Tuesday, having taken clay from an anthill,
one should draw the image of the enemy on a leaf,
establish its vital breaths, and smear it with poison.
One should offer oblations in a cremation ground for the purpose of destruction. (5/5)
Having fashioned an image of the enemy out of cow dung, one should draw it upon a palm leaf, with its heart [inscribed] and the mantra interlaced within it.
Having placed it upon the effigy,
one should properly set down a silver vessel, or else an earthen pot, filled with cow dung.
In that case as well, the wise man should cast the written leaf into the cow-dung water upon which the life-force of the enemy has been established.
At the end of the three junctions of the day, one should recite [the mantra] over that [object] as long as its shadow remains;
having seen that shadow of the enemy in water mixed with cow dung, one should remain concentrated. (5.9)
Whichever limb is terrifying in one's own heart, one should cut that very limb [of the enemy] with a weapon; that part of the enemy will perish within seven days—of this there is no doubt. (5.10)
If [the line] is severed at the heart, the belly, or the throat, death will occur;
if there is a wound on the head caused by a weapon, he will suffer from a disease of the head.
