Ginger, *citraka*, asafoetida, black pepper, *ārohī*, long pepper, *mandāra* smoke, and mango—this is declared by the wise to be poison. (5.12)
Kākamācī, āmalakī, audumbara, jambu, khadira, kṛṣṇā;
vaṃśa, pippala, nāga, rauhiṇa, nalina, samudra, and sārikā. (5.13)
Haridrā, nimba, kuṭaja, vikaṅkata, kadamba, and the bark of bakula; vañjula, panasa, arka, śamī, kadamba, nimba, and prakāśamūla. (5.14)
Then, he who recites the mantra a thousand times with devotion, using *kapimāṃsī* flowers during the ritual of recitation, shall attain the abode of Ramā. (5.15)
Having recited [the preceding mantra] equally, one should recite the mantra of the cock-form one hundred and eight times;
for the mantra of Maheśa, when it takes the form of the cock-mantra, is equal to a thousand [recitations]. (5.16)
And for one endowed with these five [qualities], the palace is fulfilled through various means such as the fulfillment of desires within a single year. || 5/17 ||

Having meditated upon a cock as the form of the Lord at dawn every day with a joyful mind— or else having herself become Māyā— she repeatedly circumambulated him from all sides in front of her own city, while he supported the earth with his feet.
Whoever should mutter this with devotion, he shall attain [the goal] like Upendra, or indeed cause him joy. || 5.18 ||

Meditating on his own mantra, one who recites it while visualizing [the deity] covering with fragments of jewel-like fruits a palm-leaf fan shattered by his beak, shall bring even an enemy under his control like Indra himself. (5.19)
Meditating upon the jewel that appears as a mere fault, a fallen half-leaf from one's own tree, yet a precious gem of immense value;
and having certainly recited the mantra, he attained abundant and mature prosperity filled with jewels. (5.20)
Joyfully scattering streaks of golden dust and soil upon the ground, chirping with delight, and scratching heaps of grain with its claws and feet,
it— whose crest was slightly curved and whose brilliance was to be contemplated— [beheld] the reddish [sun].
He who mutters [the mantra] over the neck [of a vessel], that person's house becomes filled with grain and other riches. (5.21)
This "Ten-Fold Medicine," spoken ten times by this sage and worn upon the head after being recited,
removes misfortunes and dispels the fears of disease, poison, and malevolent spirits.
It is an extreme means of subjugation for those who worship it, and a source of great delight.

Having written only the name [of the person] upon a birch leaf, one who has recited [the mantra] one thousand times according to the rules protects that entire object— whether it be water, fuel, leather, or a water-skin— in three ways.
One should quickly protect the person endowed with the recitation of the *dhūr* mantra. || 5/23 ||
He who knows the cock consecrated by the *manu* of rice and recited one thousand times will conquer in battles, like a cock or a swan. (5.24)
Having quickly touched [the image] and meditated upon the Thousandfold One, one should recite the mantra over a cock;
he will immediately conquer those [enemies] in battle along with their soldiers and clawed weapons. (5.25)
What is the use of much talk here? Whatever is desired is accomplished immediately by this *mantra*.
Before long, the stainless Kamalā takes up residence in his home. (5/26)
Thus spoke the mendicant sage named Kukkutānala, who had cast down the faction of the enemies that were the elements, who was devoted to the recitation of this mantra,
and who was a devourer of all, casting aside the wings of the mass of misdeeds.
His own faction consists of those who have been wounded while protecting virtuous people who bowed down before him. 5/27.
He is a wish-fulfilling tree for all seekers of their desired objects, and he is skilled in attracting and delighting the best of gods, men, and women.
Then the Ananta [letter] joined with the Bindu, followed by the pair of Puṃkolis;
then the Śakti [letter] Vāṃ, and then the pair of Puṃkolis, Vigala. (5.29)
One should extract the syllable *cu*, which is Varuṇa enriched by that very Ananta;
one should then extract Krodha—that beautiful mantra of the cock. (5.30)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Kukkuṭeśvara," in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The Sixth Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Śambhu, various kinds of mantras have been indicated to me by you previously."
Now I wish to hear about the goddess Mucchiṣṭapūrvikā.
Śambhu said:
Listen, O Goddess of excellent hips; I shall describe that Goddess, by the mere knowledge of whom a man becomes composed of wisdom (vidyāmaya). 6.2.
The Goddess said:
Ā PŪ KOLI PŪ KOLI VĀ HRĪ PŪṂ KOLI VIGALA CU VĀ HU HU.
What is the procedure for this, and what is its fruit? [Explain] to me according to the nature of this vidyā.
O Lord, please tell me with effort that which was declared as a secret.
Śambhu said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the procedure and the results, such as eradication and so forth;
even stationary poison, O Goddess, is destroyed by the power of this knowledge.
Now, O beloved, I shall further proclaim another goddess who is most secret—the Mātaṅgī goddess, preceded by Ucchiṣṭa, who bestows all supernatural attainments (siddhis). 6.5.
The Goddess who removes all sins and is free from all defects—by knowing that Goddess, calamities come to an end. (6.6)
O Goddess of the gods, it conquers poison—whether stationary, mobile, artificial, or born of the body—and whether it resides in one's own limbs or those of another. (6.7)
This is the supreme knowledge, the highest wisdom, which removes all sins;
it bestows heaven, grants liberation, and yields the fruits of sovereignty and happiness. (6.8)
"O Goddess, this vidyā, which was previously mastered by me and which overcomes poison, purifies even the sin of killing a Brahmin when recited but once. (6.9)
This [goddess] is the destroyer of all sins and the bestower of worldly prosperity;
if one should ever remember the Goddess while having an unwashed mouth, [she grants these fruits]. (6.10)
Then, O Goddess, one becomes as if having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), even though no ācamana has been performed;
the unfortunate truly becomes fortunate, and the sorrowful becomes happy. (6.11)
Even a barren woman obtains a son who lives for a hundred years;
the destitute man acquires wealth, and the fool shall attain knowledge. (6.12)
Whatever accomplishment one prays for, that very thing one shall obtain by force;
O charming goddess, listen as I explain the procedure. (6.13)
O Goddess, immediately after eating, even without performing the ritual rinsing (ācamana),
the practitioner should first offer the bali-oblation with the root mantra.
Then, having meditated upon that Goddess, one should recite the mantra for the attainment of one's desired goal.
Listen to the mantra, O Great Goddess; I shall tell it to you exactly as it is. (6.15)
O Goddess, one should likewise utter the word "ucchiṣṭa," then "cāṇḍālinī," and immediately after that, one should proclaim "sumukhī. (6.16)
O Mahāpiśācinī, after that follows the seed-syllable of shame (LĀM), and thereafter,
the three *ṭha* syllables joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*.
O Great Goddess, this twenty-four-syllable Vidyā, which bestows all accomplishments and grants all goals, is accompanied by the Visarga. (6.18)

Neither the lunar day nor the asterism is prescribed, nor is fasting enjoined; neither the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), nor the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), nor the placement according to the castes (*varṇanyāsa*) is taught. (6.19)
For him in whom this mantra abides, there is no fault from women, nor obstacle, nor impurity, nor restriction; he is not overcome by obstacles. (6.20)
O Sovereign of the World, I shall describe her meditation exactly as it is:
she is seated upon a corpse, clothed in garments of red silk.
Adorned with red ornaments, decorated with necklaces of *guñjā* seeds, she has a beautiful face, is sixteen years of age, and possesses full and elevated breasts. (6.22)
The best of mantra-knowers should meditate [on her] with a skull and a chopper in her hands, having the form of supreme light, through the union of the left and right [channels]. (6.23)
Having offered the bali-oblation with the remnants [of food], one should recite [the mantra] with the mind fixed upon it.
One who desires success in this [practice] must perform the recitation using only the remnants. (6.24)
All perfections arise for one who recites while remaining in a state of ritual impurity (ucchiṣṭa).
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall proclaim that which bestows fruit. 6/25
For the sake of the sudden accomplishment of her purpose, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) and a libation (saṃtarpaṇa);
having composed oneself, one should draw a square mandala upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The knower of mantras should worship the Goddess in the maṇḍala with the root mantra;
then, having taken the arghya from the fire, [he should worship her] as she stands established in the form of fire.

Having meditated upon the Goddess, one should perform a fire sacrifice with curd, white mustard seeds, and rice according to the procedure of one thousand repetitions; thus the king becomes subject to one's will.
He who performs a fire-oblation for the Goddess with the flesh of a cat attains the supreme knowledge that brings all scriptures under his control.
One should perform a fire-oblation with the meat of a goat mixed with honey, according to the procedure of one thousand repetitions; thereby, the attainments of wealth come to pass.
One who desires knowledge should perform oblations with sugar, honey, and milk-rice;
indeed, for him the fourteen branches of learning will surely become perfected. (6.31)
O Great Goddess, by performing a fire sacrifice with the garment of a menstruating woman, along with honey and milk-rice, one may bring the three worlds under one's control.

One should perform the fire sacrifice with *nāgavallī*, honey, and clarified butter; by means of ten thousand repetitions according to this single method, the *siddhividya* will certainly be attained.
With the fresh flesh of a cat, together with ghee and honey, the summoning of the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas will certainly succeed. (6.34)
By performing a fire-oblation with the flesh of a hare mixed with honey, one obtains knowledge, wealth, and excellent women.
By means of *dhūstūra* and *arka*, the knower of mantras, having offered oblations into the funeral fire with the feathers of a cuckoo and a crow, shall destroy his enemies. (6.36)
The knower of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice for the eradication of enemies in a fire made of funeral pyre wood, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should perform the fire sacrifice continuously with the feathers of an owl and a crow;
thus one shall cause the enemy to hate one another, becoming agitated by mutual strife and arrogance. (6.38)
By means of an oblation of owl feathers, the miscarriage of a noble woman may be brought about;
one who is composed should perform the oblation according to the rite of one thousand. (6.39)
By offering bilva leaves with clarified butter continuously for one month, even a barren woman may obtain an excellent son who lives a long life. (6.40)
O Goddess, by offering a red bandhūka flower mixed with honey, even for an unfortunate woman, good fortune and happiness are forcibly bestowed. (6.41)
O Dear One, whoever rises early in the morning and performs a fire-oblation day after day, offering one hundred and eight hibiscus flowers with clarified butter, [attains the desired fruit]. (6.42)
By practicing this for six months, the summoning of gods, gandharvas, and mortals, as well as maidens born of the nāgas, will certainly be accomplished. (6.43)
Afflicted by desire, they come by force and embrace him with vigor;
for this, an oblation is performed with sesame seeds mixed with milk-rice (pāyasa) for the sake of the vidyā. (6.44)
One attains the Great Vidyā, which abounds in the words of a multitude of scriptures;
one should diligently perform the fire-oblation with honey and the flesh of the Ruru deer. (6.45)

Know her, O Goddess, Great Goddess, as one possessed of knowledge and wealth, who has brought the weapons and scriptures under her control; she is the bestower of the fruits of the Vāmācāra path. (6.46)
Through the practice of right conduct, she will not fail to bestow her fruit;
and after every meal, one should offer her a bali-oblation day by day. (6.47)

O Dear One, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while using the remains of food as an offering, whether in a forest thicket, a cremation ground, an empty house, or at a crossroads. (6.48)
O Goddess, by the offering of *vāli*, she certainly becomes manifest.
This goddess was recited by me while desiring the form of Bhairava. (6.49)
Thus has this goddess, who removes all sins, been described;
by the recitation of her mantra, O Goddess, one is freed from all sins. (6.50)
"There is no defilement by remnants; he shall certainly become pure.
Thus spoke the Goddess Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī, renowned throughout the three worlds. (6.51)
No other knowledge whatsoever proceeds; listen, O fair-faced one!
Listen, O Goddess, to the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) which accomplishes the time of the sacred observance (samaya). 6/52
Śaṅkara said:
"There is no need for a lunar day (tithi), nor a constellation (nakṣatra), nor should one worship the Sādhya deities and others;
this is renowned as Mahāvidyā, which culminates in the initiation of Śiva. (6.53)
O Goddess of gods, the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is worn by practitioner men;
one should worship the Goddess, who was perfected by Mahādeva, with the remains of the offering (ucchiṣṭa).
Nor should one remain without having understood this most extensive and detailed work;
for what is the use of much speaking, O Goddess? One might even accomplish the three worlds [through it]. (6.55)
This mantra should always be remembered by one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
A person should offer oblations with milk, rice mixed with molasses, and fish.
One shall obtain long life, wealth, sons, and the eighteenth [knowledge], which is learning;
this must be guarded with effort and should not be told to anyone. (6.57)
Devotion to the Guru must be practiced through both body and wealth;
O Goddess, neither public scandal nor any other sin remains in the mortal world [for one who does so]. (6.58)
O Goddess, having enjoyed happiness in the other world, the practitioner should proceed by leaping;
now hear the lore which has the fortnight as its sole essence, the giver of wealth as its sole essence, and the lore itself as its sole essence. (6.59)
The wish-fulfilling cow on earth, providing all assistance, the essence of the ultimate truth, and possessed of great majesty.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Commentary on Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī," in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), according to the Bhavasiddhalakṣmīmata.
The seventh chapter: This application of Dhūmāvatī is now written by me.
The seed-syllable of Dhūmāvatī consists of the letter *da* (the last of the dental class), followed by the Lord of the Directions (*va*), and the Bindu (*m*), ending with the *dviṭha* (*pha*). (7.1)
The mantra of Dhūmāvatī is proclaimed as that which effects the subjugation of enemies;
the knower of mantras should fashion it joined with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). 7.2.
The sage is Pippalāda; the meter is Nivṛt; and the deity is Vivarṇā—fickle, black, tall, and clad in soiled garments. (7.3)
With disheveled hair, harsh in appearance, a widow with sparse teeth, mounted upon a chariot whose banner is a crow, and with her breasts hanging down. (7.4)
Her eyes were exceedingly harsh like the rays of the sun; she shook her hand and was endowed with excellent qualities.
Her voice was very loud, she wore matted hair, and her gaze was crooked. (7.5)
Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, terrifying, and a bringer of strife—one should meditate upon her as being of such a nature, and thereafter perform the ritual action. (7.6)

The knower of mantras should form the limbs [of the deity] by means of that [seed-syllable] joined with the fourth consonant, combined with the sixth vowel, and endowed with the six long vowels. (7.7)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*, the practitioner of mantra,
intent on fasting, should recite [the mantra] day and night in an empty house.
In a cremation ground or even in a forest, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while remaining silent;
during the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, one should wear a turban and remain dressed in wet clothes.
Having drawn the yantra over the object to be accomplished and having established Śiva therein, one should worship Him;
then, having seized hold of Śiva by means of the name of the enemy, one should mutter the mantra.
An enemy beyond a thousand leagues away is seized by fever;
there shall be pacification of that fever through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or even with milk.
Having written the first syllable of the mantra, one should then write the name of the enemy;
the sage should thus write the name of the enemy in the accusative case following the mantra. (7.12)
By reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times in the forest, the death of the enemy will certainly occur;
having written the name of the foe upon a leaf at night in the forest upon a yantra. (7.13)
The destruction of the enemy occurs through ten thousand recitations of the mantra;
having burnt a crow in the cremation fire and taking its ashes, they should be consecrated with the mantra. (7.14)

By means of the ash from a cremation ground, one should immediately effect the eradication of an enemy in the eight directions named after the opposites; then, one should place the Śiva-mantra over him.
Having written down the names of adversaries, one should perform the rite during the dark fortnight;
one should offer incense of buffalo milk, which causes calamity for the enemy.
Assuming the form of a buffalo in a dream, one should strike down the enemy;
one should place the two nostrils of the barren woman's hand above the enemy. (7.17)
Standing in water, the practitioner should recite the mantra; by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, he shall destroy his enemies.
Having fashioned a linga with cremation-ground ashes, he should worship it with flowers and other offerings. (7.18)
Peace arises from the offering of milk oblations into the fire of the funeral pyre's wood;
by the offering of dust-incense, Kālikā appears in the form of a vulture. (7.19)
Having approached, one slays the enemy through peace [rites] using the incense of *nirmālya*;
with the incense of a boar's tail, one may destroy her who has the form of a sow. (7.20)
Through incense made from the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, pacification occurs and not otherwise;
pacification of all malevolent sorcery arises through the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (7.21)

O Goddess of the gods, having written the syllables of the name with milk or with the three sweets (madhuratriyaya), one should pierce [the ground] with a stake from a milk-tree; then, having recited the mantra while writing [the name],
one should engrave it in two places and bury it— this is the rite for the eradication of enemies.

Having offered oblations to the twice-born with clarified butter sprinkled with the dust from his two feet, and having performed the fire-sacrifice (homa) with the ashes of the funeral pyre while reciting that mantra, one's desires will be fulfilled in that very manner. (7.22)

One should draw [the mantra] with the syllables of that [name] combined [with the seed-syllable], together with the eight vowels of Vāyu, in the northwest (vāyavya) for the purpose of uprooting their lineage, vomiting it upon their heads or into their enemy's houses; having made the ten syllables of the enemy red, one should cause it to dwell there.
And its powder, having been empowered by the recitation of the thousand-syllable mantra, is placed upon its sprouts. (7.23)

Having recited [the mantra] in a dwelling, or in a cremation ground, or where flower-offerings have been discarded, or within the range of one's feet, or on the ground where donkeys dwell, or in a haunt of spirits, or at a crossroads. (7.24)
Having brought sugar from a saline wasteland, from a place that deludes the earth, or from a flowering dwelling, the practitioner, naked and facing south, [should perform the rite]. (7.25)
Having thrown a clod of earth into a cremation ground, one should likewise roast it in a fire there;
one should then recite the mantra over that powder a hundred thousand times and cast it into the enemy's house.
In the midst of the army, there shall be the eradication of all their factions.
One should place grains of rice in an ant-hill at the level of one's feet.
One who knows the mantras should offer oblations of food mixed with ghee for seven nights at night;
such a person wanders over the entire earth like a crow until death.

Having fashioned an image of the enemy under the birth-constellation of that foe, the knower of mantras, having performed the consecration of life-force and pierced its vital points with thorns, [should proceed]. (7.29)
Having repeated the mantra with iron [objects], one should enclose it with those to be described;
having recited it over the previously mentioned pebbles, one should constantly heat them.
Within seven nights, even his eradication will certainly occur.
Now, having drawn the two figures of a dog and a boar upon both sides of the army...
The two objects to be accomplished should be infused with the mantra on occasions such as the rising of a Tuesday;
[this is done] by the practitioner using the juice of *dhustūra* mixed with charcoal from a funeral pyre.
Having tied him by the mass of his hair to the back of a bull, one should mutter that [mantra];
having summoned the enemy to a cremation ground, one should bury him in his house at night. (7.33)
Even between Gaurī and Śaṅkara, there would be immediate enmity.
One should write the name of the target, interspersed with the syllables of the mantra, upon the bark of an Aśvattha tree. (7.34)
Having recited [the mantra] for each of those things most dear to another, and having extracted them, one should practice;
pierced by the previously mentioned thorns, one should lead [them] away by touching them a hundred times, a hundred times.
At that very moment, those two become enemies even by name.

One should write the letters ending with the vowels (the consonants) around the perimeter, with the word "poison" (viṣa) in the corners, and the syllables of the mantra surrounding them; in the center, one should separately place the house of wind (the letter Ya) and the person to be acted upon (sādhya).
Reciting the mantra, one should strike with embers produced from gold upon cotton and salt on a Tuesday or a Saturday; this brings about enmity with the inhabitants of the earthly realm (bhūrloka).
Having assumed his former form and having drawn an image of the enemy, one should wither it;
having recited the mantra at night, one should heat it and suspend it over fire. (7.37)
In this manner, having written [the mantra] with substances for seven days, one should dry it using sky (space),
fire, garlic, datura, asafoetida, white mustard, and wild ginger.
Having thoroughly ground boluses mixed with salt and combined with the liquid of an *unmatta* plant, the mantra-practitioner should write [the diagram] with that and recite the mantra. (7.39)
Having placed the image there, one should constantly offer oblations and recite the mantra;
likewise, one should drive a suitable wooden peg into the center of the sacrificial offering (bali) and [place the image] upon it.

Having kindled the fire with its embers and combined it with the ritual substances, one should perform recitation for seven nights; thereafter, one should first offer oblations into the sacrificial pit in an empty house.
It should be blazing with a triangle and trident, and provided with a girdle and a sanctuary;
there too, one should drive in a stake after kindling the fire as before.
Then the minister should suspend the effigy over the fire,
smeared with the released substance, with its feet upward and its face downward.
Having propitiated with red substances and having kindled [the fire] with fuel-sticks produced from poisonous trees, one should offer oblations into the blazing sacrificial wood within the image.
By means of these initial oblations, the poison undoubtedly departs. (7.44)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Dhūmāvatī," in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The Eighth Chapter.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Śiva, I now desire to hear the mantra of Gṛdhrakarṇā.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, O beloved, I shall tell you the mantra of Gṛdhrakarṇa; listen. 8.1.
Having uttered the word *gṛdhrakarṇā*, one should then say the word *virūpiṇī*;
after that, the word *lambastanī*, and then one should speak the word *mahoragī*. (8.2)
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should utter the word "utpādaya" (arise) above that in the same manner;
these words should be spoken for the sake of repetition, as well as that very mantra.
Having uttered the word "vahnijāyā" (svāhā), the wise practitioner,
intent upon the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, should then recite the mantra ten thousand times for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra.
Pippalāda, the best of sages, is declared to be the Nibṛc-chandas;
the deity is Bhadrakālī herself, who possesses five limbs. (8.5)
Exceedingly fierce, with great fangs, emaciated, tall, and thin-waisted; with eyes of intoxication, heroic, long-nosed, and full of passion. (8.6)
With a smooth and deep resonance, resembling a dark blue cloud, she was ablaze like fire from a frown, terrifying with her great face. || 8.7 ||
With bitten lips, her lips copper-red with rage, possessing long, red body-hair,
her fierce staff-like arms wielding tridents, she devours the worms of hell.
The goddess is clothed in exceedingly red garments, fond of red meat and wine;
her limbs are adorned with a variegated garland of heads as she drinks the wine of blood.
Dancing and laughing, attended by hosts of piśācas, she wandered over the surface of the earth mounted upon the shoulders of piśācas. (8.10)
Born from the mouth of Śaṅkara, the Yoginī beloved of Yoga—such is Bhadrakālī, surrounded by the Mothers. (8.11)
Having meditated and properly propitiated [the deity], one should commence the ritual activity of the mantra;
and whatever has been taught regarding Dhūmāvatī, that one should perform by means of this [mantra]. (8.12)
The ritual application has already been stated; now the specific rule regarding this is being declared:
having recognized that sound from within the forest as a single thread, [one should proceed]. (8.13)
Having taken up a poison tree, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa), having constructed a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) either in an empty house or in a forest. (8.14)
Having kindled the fire with fuel from bilva trees, the wise practitioner should maintain it;
then the mantra-adept, the practitioner, should recite the mantra over a pit made of poisonous wood. (8.15)
The wise man, having made a well-disciplined and steadfast brahmin the presiding witness, should cast one hundred and eight [seeds] into the fire. (8.16)
Having stationed brave warriors with swords in hand in all directions and having performed the protective rite, one should worship the Fire-god while filled with wrath. (8.17)
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, the practitioner of mantra, having placed the tip of a staff into the fire,
should perform oblations with white mustard seeds during both the morning and evening sessions.
Having firmly placed the tip of the sacrificial ladle into the fire,
the wise practitioner should then offer two thousand oblations with white mustard seeds sprinkled with that [liquid], after first dismissing the fire with the offering of a bali.

One should meditate on the form of the Goddess as resembling the fire of universal destruction, red-colored with fierce eyes, with a lion impaled on the tip of her trident, wearing a garland of the heads of young men, possessing sharp fangs,
her upper hand occupied with a flaming torch, her mind reeling from intoxication by the honey of blood, and most terrible.
The host of enemies was made to cry out loudly by the terrible sound of the staff of stone held aloft in his hand.
Having whirled the torch with his right hand before the face of the enemy, he should move far away and then cast it forth while remaining established in the fire of wrath. (8.21)
O observer of the great vow, having gone quickly to that sacred ford while restraining your speech, you must certainly bathe, become pure, and stand in water reaching up to your neck. (8.22)
That man, being composed, should mutter the Durgā and the Sāvitrī mantras one thousand and eight times, or otherwise a hundred times each. (8.23)
Having crossed over and then covered [the area], he went to the abode of the gods for the sake of great delusion;
having gone there, he performed a grand worship of the Discus-wielding Lord.
Taking hold of both feet, the wise one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
having recited that many, he should have himself consecrated with a jar by virtuous persons. (8.25)
Having given the sacrificial fee according to the rules, one should perform the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
Having meditated upon Durgā, one should mutter her mantra a hundred thousand times, and likewise that of Sāvitrī.
Having performed the consecration for those two, one should feed the twice-born according to one's ability;
having given a sacrificial fee according to one's means, the practitioner becomes perfected. (8.27)
This application of Rudra’s staff is terrible and a destroyer in battle;
it was indeed fashioned by Hara in the past during the war between the gods and the asuras. (8.28)
Although I am unable to explain its full ritual application, nevertheless, I shall describe the mere procedure for such rites as inciting hatred, expulsion, and so forth. (8.29)
A wise person should engrave the name of the enemy a thousand times with *vibhītaka* fruits;
having recited the mantra a thousand times, he should bury it in a cemetery. (8.30)
Exorcism would occur swiftly, and even death; how much more so for human beings, O best of the twice-born? This must not be performed by the wise. (8.31)
In the same manner, one should indeed draw that very [triangle] facing downwards within the triangle;
having recited the mantra over a dhattūra seed-stalk and smeared it upon that spot.
"One should utterly uproot enemies like dust blown away by the wind.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Gṛdhrakarṇā," in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Śiva said:
Now I shall fully declare the great mantra of Bhadrakālī.
Listen, O Supreme Goddess; attend with full attention.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the palace (prāsādabīja), one should utter the word "Kālī";
then, having spoken the word "Mahākālī," one should follow it with a pair of *kila*s.
This great mantra of Bhadrakālī ends with the word "ṣaḍagnivallabhā";
having propitiated it, one should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
"Hauṃ Kāli Mahākāli Kili Kili Phaṭ Svāhā"—with this mantra, the rosary should be consecrated one hundred and eight times;
one should meditate upon this Great Goddess Bhadrakālī, the remover of fear. (9.4)
Emaciated by hunger, with sunken eyes and a face as dark as soot, her hair disheveled and weeping, she cries out,
"I am not yet satiated; I shall make this entire world my single morsel," as she holds in both hands a fierce noose resembling the flames of a blazing fire.
May Bhadrakālī, whose teeth resemble the fruit of the jambu tree, remove fear and protect me. 9.5.
And here the ritual application (prayoga) should be performed as declared in the General Chapter;
the mantra of Aśeṣakālikā has been taught for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose. 9.6.
This goddess, the Great Goddess, who effects the subjugation of enemies, should be meditated upon according to one's desire; she bestows the accomplishment of dharma, kama, and artha. (9.7)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Bhadrakālī," in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The Tenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the rule for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the attainment of merit;
it directly bestows all accomplishments and destroys even great sins. 10.1.

By the gods for the sake of divinity, by the Siddhas for the sake of attaining the power of moving through the sky, and by the Gandharvas, Dānavas, and Yakṣas for the sake of accomplishing their respective goals.
It is always frequented by serpents, Rākṣasas, mortals, sages seeking liberation, those driven by desire, those devoted to dharma, and those longing for wealth.
O Sage, I shall describe that goddess known as Dakṣiṇā according to her true nature:
Oṃ, she has a terrifying face, is formidable, has disheveled hair, and possesses four arms. (10.4)
She is dark-hued, divine, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
and holds in her lower left lotus-hand a sword with a head freshly cut off.
Her right hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
she possesses the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise naked. (10.6)
She had a garland of severed heads suspended from her neck, smeared with dripping blood,
and was terrifying with a pair of corpses used as earrings.
She had terrible fangs and a gaping mouth, with full and elevated breasts;
she wore a girdle made from a multitude of hands belonging to corpses, and her face was smiling.
Her face was made radiant by streams of blood flowing from her two corners of the mouth;
she was of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, and a dweller in the cremation ground.
She has prominent teeth, her mass of hair is adorned with hanging pearls that extend to the right,
and she is seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
She was surrounded on all four sides by auspicious jackals howling with terrible cries,
and together with Mahākāla, she was intent upon the practice of inverted sexual union.
Having thus meditated upon Kālī, who dwells in the abode of the cremation ground, with a face serene with happiness and a lotus-like countenance smiling—
I shall proclaim her mantra, which bestows all desires:
(krī krī krī hū hū hrī dakṣiṇe kālike krī krī krī hū hū hrī svāhā). || 10/13 ||
The first letter of the [first] group situated in fire (the letter *ra*) conjoined with the digit of passion (*ratibindu*);
then the triple-guṇa (the syllable *oṃ*); then a pair of *kūrca*s (the syllable *huṃ*); and then a pair of *lajjā*s (the syllable *strī*). || 10.14 ||
"Then again, as before, [the mantra] 'dakṣiṇe kālike ca'—the wise know this mantra to be joined with two *ṭha*s. (10.15)
This twenty-two-syllable mantra bestows all accomplishments upon men;
herein there is no requirement for purification and the like, nor is there any concern regarding friends, enemies, or defects. (10.16)
Nor does it require a great deal of effort regarding time, place, and so forth;
nor does it involve much expenditure of wealth, nor does it cause physical affliction. (10.17)
The practitioner who contemplates this [mantra], which grants the fulfillment of all desires, will always have every accomplishment in his hand; of this there is no doubt. (10.18)
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, arises in the assembly;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants are defeated. (10.19)
For even kings fall into servitude; what then of other people? [One cannot expect] coldness from fire, the freezing of water, or the cessation of the sun's movement. (10.20)
He is capable of reversing day and night, as well as [the consequences of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, and approaching those who should not be approached. (10.21)
It quickly takes away everything; one should therefore contemplate only the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Through speech, one becomes equal to Vāgīśvara, and through wealth, one becomes a lord of riches. 10.22
To women he was equal to Kāma, and to his enemies he was like Yama;
he was beloved by all people here and increased their fame. (10.23)
And before that, a man attains the difficult-to-reach state of the Goddess;
having become possessed of the splendor of the moon and sun, he shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas.
And much more of this kind could be said again;
for him who remembers Ghoradakṣiṇā, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain. (10.25)
One should contemplate her with a serpent as a sacred thread, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
and with matted locks of hair, standing in the presence of Mahākālī.
Having likewise meditated upon the Goddess with the pair *kūrcalajjā* and the two seed-syllables at the end, one should worship her with red flowers.
Constantly pierced by the arrows of desire, shameless and agitated, women abandon their respective husbands and always embrace him alone. (10.28)
Having meditated upon her as red in color, holding a trident in her hand, bearing a single trident, and stationed near Mahākāla, [one should worship her] with beautiful yellow flowers. || 10/29 ||
Having worshipped Kālikā, one should likewise apply [the mantra] at the end as well;
thus, the summoning of both the stationary and the moving always succeeds.
Whether it be in heaven, the netherworld, or whatever else exists upon the surface of the earth,
he draws everything toward himself, just as Mahākāla has commanded.
Having thus meditated upon the tawny-colored [deity] with two arms, holding a ritual knife in the left hand and a skull-cup in the right, indeed at the end of everything there is only this pair.
Having recited [the mantra] in this manner, one should worship her with black flowers;
indeed, death occurs for that person for whose sake the rite is performed. (10.33)
The Piṅgākṣī expels, the Kekarī terrifies,
the Muktāsyā puts to flight, and the Ghūrṇitā drives one mad.
When enraged, she causes agitation; when armed, she brings about accomplishment. When enraged, she causes contraction; when deceived, she creates opposition. (10.35)
If a person is to be led toward whatever state of being, they should meditate on themselves as abiding in that state;
in this regard, everything should be performed while contemplating only the state of being. (10.36)
One should not perform *uccāṭana* (driving away) here; rather, *surata* (the rite of union) is prescribed everywhere.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, and having performed the daily obligatory rites during the day, [one should practice]. (10.37)
Sleeping naked at night, engaged in sexual intercourse, or with hair disheveled—by these means all perfections (siddhis) are attained. (10.38)
Stambhana (paralysis), mohana (delusion), and especially vaśīkāra (subjugation)—
a man who gazes upon another's wife while naked should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times.
He was indeed the abode of all sciences and always a master who had reached the further shore;
by the mere sight of him, disputants were considered to have lost their luster. (10.39)
His speech may be of every kind, consisting of both prose and verse;
or else, the man may have disheveled hair and consume sacrificial food (haviṣya).
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times; this is remembered as the rule for each ritual procedure.
Having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should perform the invocation with the appropriate portion.
He who thus engages in sexual union shall be endowed with wealth, grain, and sons;
he will indeed become the best among all those possessed of knowledge—of this there is no doubt. (10.42)
A man who, beholding the vulva of a woman in her season, mutters this mantra ten thousand times, will find that even his speech as a child becomes composed of prose and verse. (10.43)
His speech indeed issues from his mouth composed in metrical verse;
it should always be recited during sexual union for the sake of liberation from great sins.
Having gone to a cremation ground, with disheveled hair and naked, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims. (10.45)
Having settled a preta in that very place, the best of mantra-knowers, remaining silent and intent upon terrifying [the spirit], should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. (10.46)
He attains the supreme accomplishment, which is very difficult even for the gods to obtain:
attraction, subjugation, eradication, and likewise awakening. (10.47)
Stambhana (paralysis), mohana (delusion), bhāsana (illumination), and likewise drāvaṇa (liquefaction);
eloquence, wealth, and indeed the state of having many sons. || 10/48 ||
Indeed, one attains the state of having many lovers and being beloved by all;
one even attains the power of moving through the sky and divinity itself. (10.49)
There is neither old age nor death, neither disease nor fear;
there is no terror for the human being, nor the falling away of speech or body. (10.50)
Alternatively, he shall eternally possess the twenty-four siddhis by [offering] thousands of bilva leaves smeared with the blood from his own body.
Having worshipped the Goddess in a cremation ground with flowers of the *arka* tree mixed with semen a thousand times, one shall attain equality with Vāgīśa.
Having worshipped Kālī in a cremation ground, one attains all perfections;
he becomes wealthy, powerful, eloquent, beloved by all women, and wise. (10.53)
There is no doubt in this matter, according to the words of Mahākāla:
having brought a woman to the cremation ground, such as a courtesan well-adorned with fine garments... (10.54)
Having sprinkled the mantra with hibiscus flowers, one should then meditate upon Caṇḍikā, her limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste and adorned with red flowers.
Then, having gone there, he shall obtain the kingdom if she does not cause him fear;
furthermore, he should lie upon a bed in the cremation ground, seated upon a corpse.
One should repeatedly recite the mantra in every way, or likewise ten thousand times, with semen and similarly with one's own hair. (10.57)
And by washing the vulva of a woman who has engaged in sexual intercourse, as well as with the blood of a ram, the blood of a buffalo, and indeed human blood; 10.58.
By means of the blood of a rat or a cat, eloquence arises for him;
he attains wealth, and all accomplishments are produced. (10.59)
By his speech he would be a living soul, by his wealth a lord of riches, by his command even the king of the gods, and by his beauty the god of love himself. (10.60)
For this wind, accomplished through power, is the achiever of the meaning of all principles;
once accomplished, it always offers the sacrificial oblation of flesh along with bone.
The flesh of a rat, a cat, a sheep, and even that of a buffalo, as well as the bone of a corpse, should be offered together with liquor. (10.62)
One should offer into the cremation ground the hair of a cat cut by one's own nails that has come from a broom; by doing so, one shall become a master of all accomplishments.
Having prepared one hundred excellent leaves smeared with a woman’s menstrual blood,
the wise man should recite the mantra over each one individually and then offer them as an oblation.
Having indeed fashioned the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the form of a vulva (yoni), measuring one span (vitasti) in height, one cubit (hasta) in width, and likewise one cubit in depth below; 10.65.
In that regard, the rite of establishing the fire must indeed be performed by the Brahmin;
he should offer the first oblation to the god Mahākāla.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter, cooked rice, meat, and blood;
especially with black flowers mixed with clarified butter, and even with semen.
One should likewise offer the meat of a Ruru deer with clarified butter, boiled rice, blood,
and even raw flesh and such, in the cremation ground for the ancestors.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, pure and with a restrained mind, one should perform this during the day for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (10.69)
At night, even during sexual union, one should truly act naked with hair loose;
this should be performed with effort for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (10.70)
The rule for all twice-born classes here is said to be for the daytime;
likewise, it is declared that for Śūdras, the great practice is seen to be at night.
Whatever one desires in the mind, that one obtains constantly;
one should offer oblations to Mahākāla with effort, and thereafter to the Goddess with diligence. (10.72)
Having carefully divided the mantra into three parts, the best of practitioners [should offer] meat, blood, skin, hair, nails, rice, and milk-rice.
Clarified butter (ājya) should be offered with great care for the sake of all accomplishments;
having performed it in this manner, one attains the highest perfection. || 10.74 ||
Whatever one desires in the mind, that one obtains constantly:
divinity, the state of a dānava, and likewise the status of a siddha or a cāraṇa.
Having offered [the oblation] constantly, one who is thus ever-vigilant attains [the goal] eternally.
Now I shall describe the unsurpassed ritual for the worship of the Goddess:
one should first draw a triangle, and then another triangle upon it. (10.76)
At its end is a nine-cornered [figure], and in its center one should place Śivā;
thus, one should indeed encircle it with fifteen spokes using lines.
An outer eight-petaled lotus should be made, adorned with four doors;
then, one should place [the deities] in the corners starting from the east, proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having again placed Kālī, Kapālinī, Kulvā, Kurukulvā, Virodhinī, and Vipracittā on the outside of the hexagon; || 10/79 ||
One should place Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, and Dīptā in the third triangle;
likewise, one should place Nīlā, Ghanā, and Balākā in the other triangle.
In the other triangle, the wise one should likewise place Mātrā, Mudrā, and Mitā;
all of them are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, and adorned with garlands of severed heads. (10.81)
And holding a threatening gesture with their left hands, they are smiling;
outside of that, at the base, are Brāhmī and likewise Nārāyaṇī.
Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, Aparājitā, Vārāhī, and likewise Nārasiṃhī are to be worshipped. (10.83)
Then, in the center, within the triangle, one should install the Goddess Dakṣiṇā and likewise Mahākāla; this is remembered as the prescribed ritual.
For all the goddesses as well, there shall likewise be offerings and worship, and unguents prepared according to one's means. (10.85)

The worship of all [the deities] must always be performed three times each. I shall now explain, in due order, the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).

The knower of mantras, having first joined [the limbs] with the six long vowels and preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), should place the six limbs upon himself three times, once, or as he pleases. (10.87)
With fifty syllables, one should likewise join the heart, the two arms, the two shanks, and the ten directions. (10.88)
The best of those who know mantras should perform the complete ritual of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) five, ten, or seven times with the root mantra, once it has been purified. (10.89)
Then, one should indeed meditate upon her of the previously described form as Ghoradakṣiṇā,
accompanied by the circle of Yoginīs and joined with Mahākāla.
Having performed worship with self-restraint, he should also present the bali offering;
having set aside the bali, he should offer the naivedya in the southwest (nairṛtya) direction. || 10/91 ||
Having duly offered the goddess into his own heart,
the wise man should carefully wear the remains of her offerings (nirmālya) in a clean place.
The practitioner of mantra, pure and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
likewise, being impure at night, he should likewise recite it one hundred thousand times.

The practitioner of mantras should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part [of the recitation], and likewise perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the consecration (abhiṣecana). The procedure for both the fire-oblation and the libation has been duly explained. (10.94)
Having thus worshipped the Goddess who burns away impurities, having offered the bali-oblation according to the rules, and having likewise gratified and consecrated her,
whatever desire one’s mind conceives for its own welfare in the world of mortals—
Having reached that very state, he proceeds along the path of each successive stage, which is sought after by yogis. || 10/95 ||
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is cited as its meter (chandas);
the goddess Śmaśānakālikā is the deity, and *krīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), while *hūṃ* is the power (*śakti*). (10.96)
The application is for the sake of all accomplishments.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*, in the description of Śmaśānakālikā.
The eleventh chapter: Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, adorned with the crescent moon, the Daughter of the Mountain questioned him as she sat upon his chest.
The Goddess said: O Īśāna, O Omniscient One, tell me: those sages of Bharata, whose wealth is their austerity—having acquired what knowledge did they compose the *Bhārata* and other works? (11.2)
Having heard the secret words of the daughter of the mountain, the Supreme Lord embraced his beloved and, honoring her, said, "Excellent! Excellent! (11.3).
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O virtuous lady, to this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) which burns the fuel of ignorance;
having attained which, great-souled beings [succeed] in virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.
The poets of pure intellect considered nothing to be impossible;
yet you speak in debate that speech which paralyzes even the most eloquent opponent.
Knowledge is an enemy that causes the ruin of the wise through the offering of sacrifices;
it leads to the laughter of the assembly members by means of impure chatter and the like. (11.6)
One may bring under one's control a debater, a king, or even a minister;
through the mere knowledge of this mantra, a fierce intellect is produced. (11.7)
Omniscience arises from recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Merely by placing [the mantra] upon the tongue, even a fool becomes a skilled poet. (11.8)
With her feet set in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, she tramples upon the heart of a corpse with a terrifying, loud laugh;
supreme, with hands holding a sword, a blue lotus, a flaying knife, and a skull-cup; born from the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*;
short-statured, with a massive matted lock of hair that is dark blue and tawny, and bound by fierce serpents.
Having cast her own dullness into the skull-bowl, Ugratārā herself destroys the ignorance of the three worlds.

Having bowed to Tārā, who follows the Great Cīna tradition and delivers one from the three worlds, one shall possess unimpeded intelligence regarding the scriptures, be victorious, and become a lord of speech. (11.10)
I shall describe the method for its accomplishment, which is my means for attaining omniscience;
every time is auspicious, for no inauspicious time exists anywhere.
And there is no fault regarding day or night, nor at twilight or the dead of night;
nor concerning clothing, seat, standing place, house, body, touch, and so forth, or water. (11.12)
One should not seek purification here; one should move with a mind free from conceptual construction.
Here there is no dependence on perfected beings and the like, nor is there any fault regarding friends and others.
Whoever should thus contemplate the Goddess, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires, eloquence consisting of prose and verse shall arise for him in the assembly. (11.14)
By the mere sight of him, disputants are considered to be deprived of their luster;
even kings submit to servitude—what need be said of other people? (11.15)
One should always worship the Goddess, even when unclean from bathing or having just eaten;
at midnight, in a pure place, one should cause an offering to be presented with the mantra. (11.16)
One must never harbor hatred toward women; rather, one should especially honor them.
Having placed a large conch shell at the site of recitation, one should perform the *japa* while holding it upright. (11.17)
While approaching, touching, or looking at a woman—even one who has not yet reached the age of puberty—he should offer appropriate oblations and edible substances according to his preference. (11.18)

Having offered meat, fish, curd, honey, milk, vegetables, ghee, sugarcane products, and all other kinds of food beginning with cooked rice, one should perform the recitation while consuming [the remnants]. (11.19)
There is no restriction regarding direction or time, nor any restriction regarding fixed postures and so forth;
there is no restriction of time for the recitation of mantras, nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings of bali.
In this practice of the great mantra, even if one acts according to one's own will as prescribed by the rules, no unrighteousness arises; rather, through that, great merit is produced. (11.21)
Here, acting according to one's own will is prescribed; one should conduct oneself with a bold mind, considering one’s purpose accomplished and with a contented heart. (11.22)
One should worship with fragrant white and red flowers, with petals,
with bilva leaves, maruvaka, and other auspicious flowers, excluding tulasī.
In a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads— staying there, the yogi should accomplish the practice of Tārā, the savior from the three realms of existence.

Having received the mantra according to the prescribed rite and having likewise satisfied the preceptor with gifts of cows, land, gold, clothing, and other such items, to the full extent of one's wealth; || 11.25 ||
Even while seated on a soft turban or upon other soft seats, one may attain supreme accomplishment by relying [on this practice]. (11.26)
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should then contemplate the universe as empty;
[one should contemplate] oneself as untainted, stainless, pure, and identical with Tāriṇī.
Then, one should meditate on a red lotus arising from the syllable ĀḤ in the intermediate space;
furthermore, one should meditate upon a white lotus above that, arising from the syllable ṬĀṂ.
Above that, one should again meditate on the syllable *i*, resembling the color of a blue lotus; then, one should visualize a knife born from the syllable *huṃ*, adorned with the seed-syllable.
One should meditate upon her above the perpetrator, oneself as Tāriṇī—
terrible, with feet in the pratyālīḍha stance, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
She is short-statured, pot-bellied, and formidable, with a tiger skin wrapped around her waist;
she is endowed with fresh youth and adorned with the five mudrās.
Adorned with three eyes shaped like the orb of the rising sun, four-armed, with a protruding tongue, of terrifying form, and bestowing boons. || 11.32 ||

One should meditate on her holding a sword and a cleaver in one hand, and a blue lotus and a skull-cup in the left; she has a single tawny, fierce matted lock, and is adorned with Akṣobhya upon her crown. (11.33)
The Sumukha, the Caturasra, the Vṛtta, and the Gomukha—these are renowned as the five mudrās, known as the Yonimudrā, and are saluted. (11.34)
She was situated in the midst of a blazing funeral pyre, possessing terrifying fangs and a formidable appearance;
her face was smiling with intense absorption, and she was adorned with the ornaments of women.
The yogi who is perfected in the essence of contemplation upon her, who dwells within a white lotus inside the waters that pervade the universe, shall become a great poet.
Even one who is dull-witted, if he is a fool yet intent upon the power of contemplative cultivation,
attains his desired speech through one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra.
This great three-syllable mantra, ending with *phaṭ*, resides in the heart;
though joined with five rays of light, it is the burner of the fuel of ignorance. (11.38)
I shall describe the method for its extraction, which is the cause of my omniscience:
first, having placed the letter 'sa' along with 'pa', it is adorned with the fourth vowel. (11.39)
One should then give the syllable *stṛṃ*, mounted upon the letter *ra*, radiant and blazing, adorned with the lunar drop (*bindu*), and embellished with the fourth vowel.
Then one should join the syllable *haṃ* conjoined with the long vowel *o*; after that, one should add the syllable *phaṭ*, making the mantra complete for the attainment of success (*siddhi*). (11.41)
With a steady mind, the wise one should conceive himself as a great poet;
through the constant practice of cultivation, he will become a god—of this there is no doubt. (11.42)
With his hands and feet adorned by very pure nails like spears, joyful in mind yet silent toward the ornaments of others,
he was a devotee of the feet of Hari, Hara, and the Lotus-born Brahmā.
He becomes an inhabitant of Sarasvatī for a long time. || 11/43 ||
If, after the expansion of many thousands of births through the performance of meritorious deeds,
one becomes a human being dependent upon a guru for a long time,
and having somehow obtained this Manu, [one fails] to [serve] him as a disciple—
One should give it to one's eldest son, who is the ornament of his own family. || 11/44 ||
One should never give it to one who delights in evil, nor ever to one who lacks devotion;
one should give it to one devoted to the guru, to one who is peaceful, and to a worthy recipient who is self-controlled.
After careful consideration, O Manu, [the kingdom] should be given even to the eldest son if he is disciplined;
but to what other son, or to one of a different lineage, should such great prowess be entrusted? (11.46)
If the practitioner recites this [mantra], having recited it with honey for three days, he should place it upon his tongue.
If he recites it, it has been mastered.
If he does not recite, it does not mean that he is ignorant. || 11/47 ||
The disciple should always serve the lotus-feet of the Guru with a spirit of devotion;
he should be entirely submissive to him in every way.
For how could that man, born of pride, ever [attain] this mantra?
He becomes in this world the destroyer of the dualistic tenets of disputants. || 11/48 ||
One should always conceal both this mantra and the guru;
for by such [secrecy], the vidyā becomes potent, whereas it would become powerless through disclosure.
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
therefore, one should always regard him as even greater than one's biological father. (11.50)
The man who knows this mantra shall never be a fool;
by performing its worship, he becomes renowned throughout the three worlds. (11.51)
On whichever day one obtains the *manu*, if there is a gain on that day, one certainly experiences the reversal of both good and evil actions. (11.52)
Through instruction, the limb-mantras and likewise the offering-mantras must be known by the wise; for success comes from the attainment of this mantra. (11.53)
Whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold [more effective], while mental recitation is a thousandfold;
through a garland of great conch shells, the desired success is attained without delay.
Whatever conduct is prescribed in a particular mantra, such is the dharma therein;
by means of that, one becomes successful, attaining either heaven or even liberation. (11.55)
One must not entertain delusion in this regard, for it results in the loss of accomplishment.
One should always maintain a pure mind; thus, accomplishment shall be granted as liberation.
One may bring the king's wife under control through a specific ritual service;
the king by mere recitation; and the entire world by means of an oblation.
Thus, O Daughter of the Mountain, this manifestation of Nīlasarasvatī has been shown by me to you, just as it was previously revealed by Brahmā to us.
When a practitioner who has mastered the mantra places his hand upon the head of even a fool, he quickly bestows [power] such that the fool, too, composes verses. (11.59)
In the mantra of Nīlasarasvatī, which removes obstacles to poetic composition, lack of faith is the second [obstacle], and there is nothing else that causes an obstacle. (11.60)
She who always bestows grace upon those who worship her, Nīlasarasvatī, will especially manifest through my grace in the Kali Yuga. (11.61)
Even if he possesses little knowledge, eloquent scholars will honor him,
just as they look upon the Teacher Vācaspati when seeing such a knower of mantras.
Merely by knowing the mantra, two powers arise: instantaneous poetic inspiration that cannot be surpassed by others. (11.63)
Knowledge said to the Brahmin: "I am your treasure; guard me.
Do not give me to one who is envious, so that I may remain most powerful. (11.64)
But to whichever Brahmin you know to be pure, self-restrained, and a celibate student— teach me to that one, who is like a guardian of a treasure and is free from negligence.

O Dear One, if the attainment of this mantra should occur through the power of past karma (*adṛṣṭa*), it is a human effort within one's own lineage; a wise person should not transfer it to another lineage. (11.66)
One obtains knowledge, the Vedas, fame, long life, and many sons;
that is the abode of Śrī and Sarasvatī where the Manu Sārasvata resides.
In the deep water of a lotus pond during the grip of darkness,
one should quickly retrieve a wooden staff with one's teeth and fashion a ritual peg (kīlaka) from it.
With that [substance] smeared with honey and ghee, one should write the root mantra, which bestows success, in the center of a circle of vajras upon a lotus leaf.
Having cast those [flowers] into a square sacrificial pit,
one should also offer oblations of a thousand red-hued lotuses soaked in milk and water.
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should likewise utter the pair of words "Padme," then say the word "Mahāpadme," and after that, the word "Padmāvati. (11.71)
One should offer the bali-oblation with the mantra "Māye svāhā" as performed previously;
he who performs the rite in this manner will certainly become a swift poet. (11.72)
Then, at midnight, one should constantly offer an oblation at a crossroads;
having first uttered the Praṇava, and after that the Hṛllekhā mantra.
At the end of the word *ekajaṭe*, one should utter the great sound;
having addressed the Lord of Yakṣas with the word *pataye* following [the name], [one says] *mama*. (11.74)
Having uttered the word *upanītam*, say "baliṃ gṛhṇa" twice;
having said "gṛhṇāpaya" twice, [place] "mama" at the end of every word.
One should utter "śāntiṃ kuru padaṃ" and immediately thereafter "paravidyām";
one should say "dvidhākṛṣya" and twice "truṭaṃ chindhi. (11.76)
Then, beginning with "sarva" and followed by "jagadvaśamānaya," this mantra—"māyā svāhā"—is for the purpose of attaining success in rites such as the offering of oblations (*bali*). (11.77)
It wards off hostile armies, planetary afflictions, misfortunes, diseases, and malevolent spells;
or else, one may apply honey and parched grain to the tongue of the child.
Just as one would previously pierce [the skin] with a golden needle after cutting the veins,
the mantra-practitioner should write the root mantra upon the lip of the person using white dūrvā grass.
By the mere utterance of these words, a child shall become eloquent and a swift poet;
by merely reciting it a hundred times, a man who applies a tilaka of *rocanā* [becomes so]. (11.80)
Having performed [the rite], the mantra-practitioner should bring under his control, like himself, whomever he beholds;
taking charcoal from a cremation ground on a Tuesday night. (11.81)
Having wrapped it in black cloth, one should bind it with a red thread;
having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should cast it into the enemy's dwelling.
Within seven days, this great expulsion of them occurs:
one should write the mantra on human bone with turmeric mixed with alkali. (11.83)
If one recites [the mantra] a thousand times at night on a Sunday and casts it into someone's house, death will come upon that person within three months.
There may be loss of crops in the field, or loss of speed in the horse;
the knower of mantras should write [the diagram] on birch bark with lac juice upon a pair of female genitals.
In the center of that, one should then write the root mantra joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya),
as well as the vowels in their sequential order and the consonants beginning with 'ka' according to their proper sequence.
One should employ this yantra, which is joined with the eight groups [of letters], and one should carefully wrap it with a yellow cloth. 11.87.
One should tie it with a silk thread as an ornament for the neck of children;
for women, it is bound on the left hand, and for others, on the right hand. (11.88)
Even a barren woman obtains a son, and one who is destitute becomes wealthy;
this protection was formerly bound for the sake of knowledge by Gautama and others. (11.89)
For the sake of fame, by other kings desiring victory in battle—
thus has this been declared by the noble ones of the Gautama lineage, the nature of the mantra-varṇas as spoken for the benefit of all people.
By the power of its realization, there shall be the attainment of all desired goals without exception, and one may abandon any other effort for the sake of even more rapid poetic composition. (11.90)
Now I shall fully explain to you the unsurpassed procedure for worship:
first, having consecrated the water, one should then perform the washing of the feet.
Having sipped water twice and tied the topknot, one should then perform the purification of the ground;
having driven away the obstacles, one should perform the consecration of the ground with mantras.
Having drawn the yantra and consecrated it with flowers, speech, body, and mind,
and having sat upon a soft seat, one should write the *māyā* syllable on the eastern petal.

One should write the second seed-syllable in the south, *phaṃ* in the north, and *ḍhaṃ* in the west; one should write the *tāra* seed-syllable in the center and perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Then, having meditated on the *māyā* syllable, red in color, at the navel, one should contemplate the body—which is of the nature of sin—as dried up and consumed by the fire born from it. (11.95)
Having meditated on the syllable *hrīḥ*, yellow in appearance, in the heart, one should then contemplate the ashes being blown away by the wind arising from it at the forehead. (11.96)
Having soaked those bones with the nectar produced from that [kūrca] which has the luster of snow, one should contemplate oneself within them. (11.97)
Free from all defects, stainless, and of the nature of the deity;
it has the seed-syllable as its pericarp, arising from seeds, extending through the waters that pervade the universe.
Short and dark-complexioned, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a corpse situated in the midst of a funeral pyre;

round-faced with three reddish eyes, adorned with Akṣobhya upon her crown, endowed with the five mudrās, wearing a garland of human heads, with a single tuft of hair (*ekajaṭā*), and possessing ten fierce faces.

I praise her who is joined with a fierce young woman, who is restless, trembling, and fickle; who wears a tiger-skin as a lower garment, who holds a sword, a dagger, and a blue lotus, who possesses a bright skull, and who has a large belly. || 11.99 ||
Having thus meditated upon oneself, one should perform the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs;
thereafter, the worship of the hands and limbs is performed with the seed-syllable enriched by the six long vowels.
Having first invoked and established [the deity], and having offered the *arghya*, one should anoint [the image];
and having addressed Śrīmadekajaṭā with the words "O Vajrapuṣpa," [one should proceed]. (11.101)
One should worship again with the root mantra ending in *agnipriyā* (namas) along with the *satārā* (oṃ).
Having offered perfumes and other articles, one should present the *bali* offering. || 11.102 ||
First, one should worship Akṣobhyavajra and Tāriṇī upon the head;
one should scatter vajra-flowers with the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā). || 11/103 ||
Likewise, the mantra-practitioner should worship Vairocana, Śaṅkha, Pāṇḍava, Padmanābhaka,
and Asitābha on the four petals starting from the eastern direction.
One should worship Nāmaka, Nāmaka, and Pāṇḍava along with Tārā in the four corners starting from the southeast, using their respective mantras in due order.
Having worshipped Padmāntaka and Yamāntaka at the eastern gate,
and likewise Vighnāntaka, one should worship Narakāntaka.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra while meditating, neither too high nor too low;
having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), and having paid homage and praised the Goddess, he should dismiss her. (11.107)
One should draw a very beautiful eight-petaled lotus with cow-dung, surrounded by a city-gate (bhūpura) enriched with many jewels; this is the yantra consisting of Ekajaṭā.
One should always offer the worship of the goddess Valī and other rites at night;
by the grace of the goddess Tārā, all such acts attain imperishability. (11.109)
Having uttered "Śrīmadekajaṭā," one should say "accept the vajra-flower";
then, having pronounced [the name] beginning with Tārā and ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā), one should perform the worship.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the section on the venerable Ekajaṭā within the illustrious Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The twelfth chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Mahākālī.
By the mere knowledge of which, nothing remains unachievable on earth. || 12.1 ||

The two Krodhas are likewise joined with the fire of dissolution (ra), blood (ru), the downward-moving (dha), and the upward-haired one (ī), combined with Nāda and Bindu. Thus, again, are the two Krodhas. (12.2)
"Seize the beast by its foot! O armor, weapon, fire, and beloved!"—this fourteen-syllable mantra of Mahākālī, beginning with the syllable *dhruva*, has been proclaimed. (12.3)
(“Oṃ phreṃ phreṃ hūḥ hūḥ, seize the victim! Hūḥ phaṭ svāhā!
Another mantra, preceded by Tārā and others, is proclaimed as being like a fire that consumes all transformations;
one should extract two *hara*s, two *stambha*s, and two *kīlaya*s. (12.4)
This other mantra, beginning with *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*) and ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), has been declared;
regarding its ritual placement (*nyāsa*), purification (*śuddhi*), and the [assignment of] seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, no further deliberation is required here. (12.5)

Then, having devoutly worshipped Kālikā— accompanied by her messenger-goddesses (dūtīs) stationed in the directions starting with the east— in a black pitcher filled with black water, [one should proceed].

She has five faces, is exceedingly fierce, and possesses three eyes on each face; she holds a spear, a trident, a bow, and arrows, as well as a sword, a shield, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The goddess, adorned with serpent ornaments, holding [weapons] with her right and left arms, bearing the crescent moon, possessed of matted locks, and terrifying with her lolling tongue. || 12/8 ||
Her skeletal frame was fleshless and swollen, adorned with a garland of skulls;
her body had a wildcat for a sacred thread, and she was surrounded by spirits and vetālas.

Having thus meditated upon her whose limbs are smeared with marrow, fat, and grease, and who is mounted upon a great corpse, one should accomplish the desired goal that resides in the mind— that which bestows success.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā as the eighth. (12.11)
These [goddesses] are situated upon the pitcher-marks from the east up to the northeast;
then, in the pericarp, is the Goddess who removes the fear of Mahākāla.
When the fire has been restrained by the utterance of the name and the supreme [fire] has been fully kindled,
one should, while enraged, offer the enemy as an oblation while muttering the mantra of the Goddess.
The fuel consists of *picumarda*, *vibhītaka*, and *citraka* wood; along with *hara*, poison, *rājiṇṭha*, *kakaja*, and *ālavalā*. (12.14)
Whether in one's own house or in a cremation ground, by means of a fire-oblation of *vibhīta* wood and charcoal,
combined with the application of the *Kālikā* mantra, one destroys the enemy within seven days.
Uccāṭana should be performed in the afternoon, and likewise, māraṇa at twilight;
standing in the southern direction, facing south toward the village or other location. (12.16)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śrī Phetkāriṇī Tantra, concerning the two mantras of Mahākālī.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mantra consisting of fragrance,
by the mere knowledge of which nothing remains unattainable in the three worlds.
One should utter the mantra beginning with "Rudrajāyā mahāyoginī," then say "Gaurīpade," followed by "Bhuvanabhayaṅkarī," ending with the armor syllable (huṃ). (13.2)
One should [worship] the Weapon-Yoginī with the mantra consisting of half [of the seed-syllable] joined with the six long vowels;
then, with the other half, the Heart; and then, in sequence, the Armor and the Head with the [remaining] Weapon-mantra.
The sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) is thus remembered as consisting of the crest, armor, eyes, and weapon;
Aṅgiras is the seer (ṛṣi), and the goddess Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas).
And [the goddess] Siṃhavaktrā, who causes fear among the spirits;
having spoken thus, "Next is the deity Mahākṛtvan," one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
She has the face of a lion, a black countenance, and pendulous breasts;
her mouth is formidable with fangs, she has three eyes, and she blazes brilliantly on all sides.
Clad in a black garment, possessing a radiance equal to smokeless fire,
with hands like lotuses holding a trident, a wheel, a mace, and a skull-topped staff.
Having meditated upon the Kṛtyā with her large tongue constantly lolling and terrifying with eyes like lightning, the best of mantra-knowers should worship her according to the prescribed rite.
Having meditated, one should worship Kṛtyā with red flowers for the purpose of subjugation; likewise, in rites of killing, she is black and worshipped with meat, blood, and liquor.
And Kṛtyā, Madanā, Sarvakullā, Svacchādanī, as well as Bhīṣaṇā, Śrīmatī, and likewise the supreme Pratiṣṭhā. (13.10)
The wise one should worship the Vidyā in sequence upon the eight petals:
first, on the eastern petal, is she named Śāṅkarī, endowed with white-colored garments. (13.11)
She has two arms, a gentle countenance, and holds a noose and a goad; she is auspicious, and on her right side is the one named Abhiṣikā, who has a protruding tongue and a face like nectar.
She is black in color with red hair, adorned with red garlands and unguents;
she has four arms and holds a blazing trident and a skull-bowl while uttering the lion’s roar.
In the west is the goddess named Vāruṇī, golden-hued with a smiling face, holding a sword in her hand, wearing a garland of heads, and adorned with all ornaments. (13.14)
In the north is the one named Bhīmikā, who wears a golden garland, has brilliant white fangs, always bestows fearlessness, and causes terror to those who seek the four aims of life.
Having performed worship, the practitioner of mantra should daily recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
thereafter, its application must always be carried out by the practitioner.
Having discerned the proper time, one should have an image made of beeswax, twelve finger-breadths in size, including the nails and hair of the enemy. (13.17)
In the heart [mantra], there is the name and the syllable *phaṭ* for all rites:
"The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of such-and-such a person are here; the life-force (*jīva*) of such-and-such a person is established here. (13.18)

(Āṃ krīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ) O beloved of Agni, bring here all the senses of such-and-such a person, as well as the speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breath of such-and-such a person!
Having thus established the vital breath (prāṇa), one should then smear the image with black pepper.
Having tied the hair of a dead Brāhmaṇa and that of a Caṇḍāla separately to her two feet, she should be suspended upside down from a gateway made of Kāraskara wood.
Below that, there is a triangle provided with a girdle where the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is located;
having established the fire there in the evening and strewn it with reeds and grass, [one should proceed].
One who intends the killing of another should prepare an oblation using fuel-sticks of *vibhītaka*;
he should offer into the fire parched rice of the *nicula* tree and the feathers of a crow and an owl. (13.22)
Having commanded, "Tear him apart! Wither him! Kill him!", the person should then perform a fire-oblation one hundred and eight times.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, having duly propitiated Kṛtyā in the presence of the fire, [he said]:
"This seizing of my throat, whether it occurs far away or even nearby," (13.24)
Having said, "May all attain satisfaction," one should present the food offering;
then, having protected the fire according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the observance for nine nights.
The corpse of the deceased remains as long as the weapon-rite for the dead is not obstructed.
Having ground black pepper and white mustard with the milk of the sun-plant (arka), one should stir it in water while reciting the mantra, meditating upon the enemy with a fixed gaze. (13.26)
Having stepped upon that enemy with the yoga-step while wearing a black upper garment, and having meditated upon this thunderbolt-spear, one should hurl it down upon him. (13.27)
Within nine nights, the enemy dies; of this there is no doubt.
This occurs when *vibhītaka* fruits soaked in oil are offered into the fire of the funeral pyre at Harasiddhi.
It is indeed the truth declared by the Gaṇas that while fighting, the enemy is slain;
having fashioned an image of the foe upon a pure board of *sādhyakṣa* wood. (13.29)
Having ground black pepper with the milk of the *arka* plant, one should apply it right there;
having uttered the syllable "phaṭ" at the heart, [one should do so] in a well containing the remains of Śiva's offerings (*śivanirmālya*).
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having recited the mantra a thousand times,
one should immediately perform an immersion and carry out its protection.
Having recited the mantra according to the prescribed rite, one should pierce [the enemy] with the lion-mudrā;
within six months, the enemy shall die at both twilights.
Then, having taken a dry leaf of the *vaibhītaka* tree that has been blown up by the winds,
