the practitioner of mantras should write with the blood of a black cobra.
One should employ the seed-syllable of Vāyu at the end of the name of the enemy;
by burying it in his house, he will surely wander about like an elephant. (13.34)
By means of dry leaves blown by the wind, wood felled by lightning, camel bones, funeral pyre embers, and charcoal, the eradication of an enemy shall occur. (13.35)
A wise person should perform a rite for peace using dūrvā grass, guḍūcī with its fragrance, ghee, sesame seeds, rice, food offerings, and palāśa wood fuel.
One should worship Lakṣmī with bilva fruits and leaves, and likewise for the sake of prosperity (Śrī) with nandyāvarta flowers;
one should also worship with vajra flowers, apāmārga, charcoal, and subhadraka.
One should perform the rite of subjugation with these [substances] sprinkled with the three sweets (madhuratraya).
This has been stated in the Auśanasa Tantra; now the day (vāra) for this is also being told.

Having performed the rite of pacification according to the prescribed rule, one should recite this "Parimala" mantra one hundred and eight times daily; it brings about the alleviation of great diseases.
Remaining with a one-pointed mind, one should mutter the supreme mantra that brings the world under control;
in one's mind, one should contemplate the Kṛtyā, mounted upon an elephant and unwearied.
It removes the fear of thieves, tigers, wild beasts, water, and other such dangers;
by merely hearing it once, it destroys all sins. (13.41)

By drinking water consecrated with this mantra while remaining constantly composed, one becomes wise and eloquent; and by performing the consecration while reciting it [the same result follows]. (13.42)
Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, even poison becomes nectar for a month, a fortnight, two months, six months, or likewise for a year. (13.43)
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
Now, I shall describe in detail the sequence of the ritual for the Great Peace (Mahāśānti).
It bestows all accomplishments, is meritorious, destroys all sins,
eliminates the defects of all planetary influences and the like, and is the cause of success.
It is the weapon of all mudrās, the destroyer of all misfortunes, the crusher of untimely death, and the constant increaser of victory. (13.46)
It bestows longevity, purifies, and grants nourishment, prosperity, good fortune, and subjugation; it grants sons and fame, and destroys misfortune and impurity. (13.47)
It is the pacifier of great diseases and the destroyer of epilepsy; [it subdues] yoginīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, kuṣmāṇḍas, and pannagas. (13.48)
In that place, the ḍākinīs and others do not specifically remain;
therefore, O child, one should worship Kṛtyā according to the prescribed ritual.

One should draw a sixteen-petalled lotus joined with a yoni and marked with a bindu; having drawn an eight-petalled lotus in its center, one should place the letters beginning with *pa* in their proper sequence. (13.50)
In the center of that, while recollecting the root mantra, one should draw a hexagon;
within it, one should draw the disc of the moon, and above that, one should draw the image.
In its center, one should draw a tortoise adorned with a garland of flowers;
in its center, one should place the Kṛtyā, endowed with all the [prescribed] characteristics.
One should worship according to the prescribed rule and offer milk-rice (pāyasa);
having placed the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, in eight jars around [the central deity].
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodheśa, Unmattabhairava, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra is remembered as the eighth. (13.54)

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should worship the Kṣetrapālas outside of that, ending with the Lords of the World (Lokeśas), and then perform the fire-oblation (homa) before the Goddess.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter, apāmārga, unbroken rice, sesame,
mustard seeds, the tips of dūrvā grass, khadira, and aśvattha wood— eight hundred of each respectively.
One should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa) either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila).
To its right side, one should meditate upon Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rule.
One should place the Goddess in the center of the jar, while visualizing Śrī on the right;
on the left side, one should worship the goddess Hṛllekhā Bhuvaneśvarī.
On his very left side, one should worship Aṇimā and the others;
one should mutter the root mantra ten thousand times, which destroys death.
One should recite the *Parimala* mantra ten thousand times for the expiation of the murder of an embryo;
by reciting it that many times and performing an ablution (*abhiṣeka*), there is the pacification of even great diseases. (13.60)
In this way, the mortal who performs [this rite] shall attain a meritorious state, he by whom the fragrance has been known and which always resides upon his mouth. (13.61)
"For him, nothing remains incurable, nor is there even fear of diseases"—in such extensive tantras, the Parimala mantra is to be known. (13.62)
It brings great peace to men and destroys suffering and poverty;
by its power, a woman mounted upon a horse shall quickly become submissive.
One should place the seed-syllable of Durgā, encapsulated by the Sāvitrī mantra, in equal measure. (13.63)
The desired success will be swiftly attained; there is no need for deliberation here, whether one is afflicted by disease or other ailments oneself or even another. (13.64)
Having begun, the practitioner of mantras should recite; he is immediately and instantly liberated.
From an oblation of grain, there will be grain; with milk, it brings the acquisition of cattle. (13.65)
One obtains Lakṣmī from the Bilva tree; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Having performed [this] on earth before the solar orb, it is as if one has reached the very edge of the world.
One suffering from fever, while burning with internal heat, should stand in water reaching the knees with the face turned downward and meditate on the water as consisting of fire. 13.67.
Having cast [the mantra] a thousand times into the body of the enemy while filled with wrath,
he should, after blazing his hand, touch his heart a hundred times with the lotus-mudrā and other gestures.
The wise one should cause the sprinkling of water itself to be performed against the enemy;
beneath the solar orb, the waters are infused with fire by means of the *vidarbha* mantra. (13.69)
Having reflected upon this, one should meditate on the enemy situated between those two, enveloped by garlands of flames; there is no need for further deliberation here. (13.70)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the glorious Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The fourteenth chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
One should meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, the mother of the elephant-faced one, the universal-formed Bhavānī.
She who ceaselessly feeds the breast of Heramba, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
served by hosts of gods led by Brahmā with joined palms, attended by throngs of Siddhas,
adorned with a profusion of jewel-ornaments, the consort of Paramaśiva, cloud-colored and three-eyed. (14.1)
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, the wise one should recite her mantra.
Now, O Dear One, I shall fully declare the mantra of Jayadurgā.
By the mere grace of whom one becomes Sadāśiva himself;
having uttered the words "Durge Durge," followed by the word "Rakṣaṇī" (O Protector).
The great mantra of Jayadurgā begins with *tārā* (oṃ) and ends with *vahnijāyā* (svāhā);
having placed the word *pāti* in the middle, the wise practitioner should install the words of the mantra.
This protective rite of Jayadurgā, accompanied by the armor-mantra, has been declared;
having meditated upon oneself as dark-complexioned, three-eyed, and four-armed. (14.5)
A person should mutter that [mantra] which bears tridents upon conchs and discs and possesses a fierce form, during battle, in legal proceedings, and for the sake of victory and so forth. (14.6)

One should daily worship Jayā, Śrī, Nityā, as well as the sword and the dagger. The mantra of Jayadurgā has been declared; now another mantra is being told. (Oṃ durge durge rakṣaṇi svāhā hūḥ hūḥ hūḥ). 14.7.
Having uttered "Namo Bhagavatyai," after [the name] Jvālāmālinī,
[the mantra] beginning with Tārā and ending with Dviṭha (Phaṭ) is proclaimed as being surrounded by a host of vultures.
Oṃ, homage; "hṛdayam" is declared [as the heart-mantra], likewise "bhagavati" for the head;
and "jvālāmālini gṛdhragaṇaparivṛte" is for the crest-lock (śikhā). || 14.9 ||
One should place upon the body this armor-mantra, "svāhā astram," joined with its seed-syllable:
(Oṃ namo bhagavati jvālāmālini gṛdhragaṇaparivṛte svāhā).
One should recite this mantra ten thousand or a million times; through such recitation, one becomes victorious. (14.10)
The supreme mantra of Jvālāmukhī is declared to be another mantra, beginning with "ruddhaṃ" from Rudrāṅganā and "jvālāmukhī" from Agnijāyā. (14.11)
"Hrīḥ Svāhā Jvālāmukhi Hrīḥ Svāhā.
Having smeared one's feet with lamp-oil, one should recite this eight thousand times for twenty-three days, beginning on a day sacred to the Guru at midnight. (14.12)
"He gives six [offerings] every day at sunset; of this there is no doubt," as was further stated by Agastya in the Nārāyaṇīya in the past. (14.13)
Durgā may be of nine types, specifically as the Nine Durgās;
one who desires perfect accomplishment should keep her secret and not utter even her name.
Especially for a righteous king and his son, one should perform the rite of the Nine Durgās out of consideration for the gravity of the matter. (14.15)
The king, too, having properly propitiated the knower of mantras with various kinds of wealth, should, out of devotion and constant respect, keep him close at hand for the sake of protection. (14.16)
This should be employed by oneself in times of distress, especially in rites such as killing;
therefore, the mantra-practitioner should diligently perform the act of killing.
When requested by others, the minister should report everything to the king;
having reported it according to the prescribed rule, he should subsequently cause it to be executed by the best of ministers.
Merely by recollecting [this], the mantra-practitioner shall destroy all enemies;
one should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of either a thousand or a hundred [gold pieces]. 14.19
By giving cows, gold coins, or land abounding in grain, one attains all peace and becomes a performer of universal protection. (14.20)
One should perform the rites specifically at the beginning of the meditation according to the ritual procedure for the Nine Durgās; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (14.21)

One should meditate upon her who is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, bearing a conch, a discus, a trident, and a sword, whose mouth is a flame, whose form is terrifying, and who strikes fear into the three worlds. (14.22)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Discourse on Jvālāmukhī Surrounded by the Flock of Vultures," in the *Phetkāriṇī Mahātantra*, within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
Fifteenth Chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
I shall now declare the Āgneya mantra, which accomplishes all aims.
Mārīca Kāśyapa is said to be the son of this Mahāmanu.
The metre here is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is said to be Agni Jātavedas;
[the verses consist] of nine, seven, six, seven, and again eight [syllables]. (15.2)
The ritual of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is proclaimed by means of the seven syllables of the root mantra as follows:

"To Jātavedas, *namaḥ* for the heart; *svāhā* to Soma, the enemy-warder, for the head; *vaṣaṭ* to Veda, who bestows [knowledge], for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *huṃ* to him who protects us on all sides, for the armor (*kavaca*); *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes, like a boat across all difficulties."

*Sindhuṃ duritātyagniḥ astrāya phaṭ.* Thus are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Now the mantra: *Jātavedase sunavāma somaṃ arātīyato nidadhāti vedah | Sa naḥ pariṣadati durgāṇi viśvānāveva sindhuṃ duritātyagniḥ ||* (15/3) For Jātavedas, we shall press the Soma; he casts away the wealth of the enemy. May he carry us across all difficulties, as Agni crosses over dangers like a boat across the Sindhu river. (15/3)
Thus, the Āgneya mantra is to be known as consisting of forty-four syllables. The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are performed with the root mantra itself:
on the thumbs, ankles, shins, knees, the pair of thighs, the hips, anus, navel, heart, breasts, and the two sides. || 15/4 ||
On the back, between the shoulders, at the roots of the arms, on the arms themselves, at the forearms and wrists, and on the palms and soles; || 15.5 ||
The wise one should sequentially place the syllables arising from the mantra upon the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, cheeks, brain, and head.
On the head, forehead, eyes, ears, lips, and tongue;
and on the neck, arms, heart, belly, hips, private parts, thighs, and knees. (15.7)
The wise practitioner should place the words of this mantra upon the shanks and the feet.

In this arrangement of syllables, one syllable is assigned to two locations; likewise, in the placement of the words, one word is recited for the two arms, and one should place one [word] each upon the thighs, knees, shanks, and the pair of feet.
She possesses a radiance equal to a garland of lightning, stands upon the shoulders of the king of beasts, and is terrifying;
she is attended by maidens whose hands gleam with swords and shields,
and who hold in their hands a discus, mace, sword, shield, arrow, bow, bowstring, and the raised index finger of threat.
One should meditate upon Durgā, who possesses the nature of fire, bears the moon, and has three eyes.

On the right side [of the deity] are the discus, sword, arrow, and mace, and on the left side are the conch, shield, bow, and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), or [these may appear] somewhere else.
A person of vast intelligence should recite the mantra consisting of thousands of syllables;
at its conclusion, [one should perform the fire sacrifice] with sesame seeds, white mustard, various roots, and excellent sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*).
With milk-tree wood [fuel], smeared with clarified butter as an oblation and mixed with ghee,
[one should perform] four hundred and forty-four [oblations].
One should offer four thousand oblations into the consecrated fire within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala, whose pericarp is marked with six corners.
One should worship the pedestal of the Goddess according to the procedure that will be described hereafter.

Having prepared the sixfold yantra, having inscribed the seed-syllable of Durgā in the corners, and having arranged the outer paths and so forth— one should [worship] Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, and thereafter Bhadrakālī.
Sumukhī, Durmukhī, Saṃjñā, and afterwards Vyāghramukhī again. || 15.13 ||
Then, one should worship Durgā with the lion-faced form and her nine powers;
the preceptor should offer the seat with the lion-mantra as previously stated.
Oṃ, homage to the lion with adamantine claws and fangs. Having conceptualized the form by means of the root mantra, one should invoke it therein and worship it.
(She who consists of all vidyās, the knowledge of Brahman, is said to be contained within Annapūrṇā. || 15/15 ||
The wise one should worship the six limbs as before upon the filaments;
furthermore, the forms produced from the eight feet beginning with Śrī should be worshipped outside.
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, he who is named Havyavāhana, another named Aśvodaraja, and furthermore the one called Vaiśvānara. (15.17)
Kaumāratattvatejas should be [the first], followed by Viśvamukha and Devamukha;
then [the elements] earth, water, fire, and air, accompanied by "Oṃ" and "Namaḥ" to Ananta.

Having worshipped [the deities] equally in the four cardinal directions, one should again worship their constituent parts (kalās) in the corners; thereafter, one should worship the quartet beginning with Earth in the directions starting from the East.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule the four digits— Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti— in the corners, || 15/20 ||
Having worshipped the power-deities of the letters beginning with *Jā* in the directions starting from the east:
*Jāgatā*, *Tapanī*, *Vedagarbhā*, and *Dahanarūpiṇī*. (15.21)
She who has the essence of camphor, the slayer of Śumbha, moving through the sky immediately thereafter;
she is Vāgīśvarī, the bearer of intoxication, whose form is the moon, and who possesses the speed of thought. 15.22.
Marudvegā, Rātrisaṃjñā, Tīvrakopā, Yaśovatī, Toyātmikā, Nityā, Dayāvatī, and Apahāriṇī. (15.23)
She is the one who transcends, the mother of the Vedas, beloved by Him, and the beloved of Madana;
she is to be propitiated, the giver of joy, the supreme, and the destroyer of the universe.
And the sixth is Daṇḍinī, Tigmā, Durgā, Gāyatrī, Niravadyā, Viśālākṣī, Śvāsodvāhā, and Nādinī. (15.25)
Vedanā, Vahnigarbhā, and likewise Siṃhavāhā;
Dhuryā, Durviṣahā, and after that Adrijā and Tāpahāriṇī. (15.26)
Having abandoned all defects and being free from rivals, one should likewise worship the forty-four world-protectors (Lokapālas), together with their respective vehicles and weapons.
When this mantra has been perfected through such means as worship, the excellent practitioner shall become a master of the fiery weapon; its ritual procedure is now declared.
The mantra recited in reverse order is declared to be the Āgneya weapon (the Fire-weapon).
The seers and other [limbs] of this mantra are proclaimed to be exactly as previously stated.
One should arrange its six limbs in reverse order;
one should perform the placement of the mantra and the placement of the steps in reverse sequence. (15.30)
One should understand the distinctions of meditation through the instructions of the guru and not otherwise;
the arrangement of recitation should be as before, and one should offer oblations according to the previous number.
For his accomplishment, one should perform worship as before with *caru* well-cooked with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), [worshipping] his powers in reverse order. (15.32)
In all cases, the preceptor should perform double the number of recitations of the Gāyatrī;
he should perform cruel rites according to the procedure for the reverse order.
The rites of pacification (śāntika) and enrichment (pauṣṭika) should be performed in the forward order;
at the time of the ritual application, one should recite the eight quarters in the reverse order.
Afterwards, this mantra becomes purified by means of this procedure.
The five-syllabled quarter beginning with Śrī is to be known as having the nature of the organs of cognition. (15.35)
The other [seed-syllable] beginning with *dhū* is remembered as five-colored and consisting of the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
The first [syllable] beginning with *cā* is the third; it is remembered as five-syllabled and composed of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*). || 15.36 ||
The fourth foot, consisting of seven syllables, should be abandoned; it has the form of the element (dhātu).
The fifth foot, preceded by 'da', consists of six syllables and has the form of a wave (ūrmi). || 15.37 ||
Another six-syllabled mantra beginning with *to* is considered to consist of the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*).
Another five-syllabled mantra preceded by *sa* is said to consist of the objects of the senses, such as sound (*śabdādimaya*).
The eighth [syllable] beginning with *se* is to be known as having five phonemes, starting with *va-ca-na*.
Thus, through the union with the principles (*tattva*), the arrangement of the quarters (*pāda*) has been illustrated. (15.39)
The fire-deities, beginning with Tārā, are produced from the syllables of their respective feet;
they are the images of the primary forms, possessing radiance arising from their own specific colors.
With blazing hair and faces, possessing terrifying fangs,
these deities born of the senses are said to have upward-gazing eyes.
The deities arising from the feet of the Bhūtas are proclaimed to have faces turned sideways;
they are produced from syllables that are the forms of the elements and are beautified by the fire of their emergence. (15.42)
Those born from waves have faces turned upward; those born from hair have faces turned sideways. All these women are known as eunuchs, arising from the objects of the senses.
Now, those deities whose colors are described as being directed horizontally or sideways are remembered as facing oneself in propitious rites, while in other rites they are turned away.
The first group of deities has arisen, their faces ablaze;
by means of these, the practitioner may burn the kingdom of the enemy along with its mountains and forests.
A wise person should begin the practice of the weapon-mantra during the asterisms of humans;
one should employ it during the asterisms of Asuras and withdraw it during those of the gods.
The three [asterisms] preceding and following [Punarvasu], as well as Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī—
these the wise call the asterisms belonging to human beings.
Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Mūlā, Ghaniṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā, Citrā, Maghā, and Viśākhā—these stars have Rākṣasas as their presiding deities. (15.48)
Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣyā, Svātī, Hastā, Punarvasu,
Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Śravaṇa are the asterisms presided over by deities.
The deities born from the sense organs are said to have their gaze directed upwards.
One should commence [an action] during the *nandā* lunar days and discharge weapons during the *riktā* days. (15.50)
One should perform the mounting on the Bhadrā day for victory and the unsurpassed Anantya rite;
the commencement is on Tuesday and the conclusion on Saturday. (15.51)
The withdrawal [of the disciple] may take place during the Guru's or Venus's retrogression;
the commencement [of study] occurs when the planets are in fixed signs, and the dismissal when they are in movable signs. (15.52)
The preceptor should perform the withdrawal of the weapon within both [the disciple's and his own] selves;
during the dark fortnight, he should discharge the weapon with fire, and again with the moon.
In the bright fortnight, one should gradually withdraw the weapon back into oneself;
the wise practitioner should perform the emission and withdrawal by means of the sun during both fortnights.

Facing westward, one should accomplish all rites everywhere, including the constellations, trees, and all [deities] bearing the names of those to be accomplished, conjoined with their respective rituals. (15.55)

The mantra-practitioner, using as many fuel sticks as there are syllables in the mantra, each joined with the respective mantra-syllable, should offer them into a kindled fire; thus he shall slay his enemy.
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should [use] the excellent sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the thorn-apple (dhustūra) and the tree known as the poison-tree (viṣavṛkṣa).
Having become self-restrained, one should offer seven thousand oblations individually, smeared with rājī oil; the enemy shall go to the city of Yama.
During the rainy season, one who wears wet clothes should offer oblations for seven nights with black pepper mixed with honey, stirred into an oil of white mustard seeds.
Having written the name of the enemy according to the prescribed rite upon a palm leaf, that foe is seized by a fever equal to the fire of universal destruction.

Having enveloped it with the Āgneya weapon and buried it in the center of the sacrificial pit, one should offer oblations of black pepper while enraged; he [the victim] will then become overcome by fever.
Taking that, one should throw it into cold water; he shall become submissive.
Having ground apāmārga seeds together with black pepper and honey, [one should apply it]. (15.62)
Then, having cast it into very hot saline water, one should boil it;
[it is applied] to the heart, the mouth, and the nose of an image made of *ṛkṣa* wood.
One should sprinkle a little water at a time with a ladle made of *kāraskara* wood while reciting the Āgneya mantra; that person shall soon become afflicted with fever.
Having thrown it into boiling water, one shall slay the enemy without effort;
or, having smeared an image of the enemy with pungent oil at night, [one should perform the rite]. (15.65)
If one recites the mantra in reverse order while the fire is blazing, the victim is immediately afflicted by fever; from performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) with this [mantra], death shall occur.
In salt from the ocean, stirred with asafoetida, poison, and cumin,
one should boil an effigy made from the wood of the tree corresponding to the victim's birth star.
Having turned it face downwards, one should strike its head with a staff made from a poisonous tree and recite the Astra-mantra in reverse order.
Within seven days, the enemy, deluded by fever, shall meet his death,
struck down by the poison seized by the Sun, the chariot-dragon, and the lord of serpents.
Having meditated upon one's own enemy as naked, with limbs smeared with oil, scorched by the rays of the sun, and facing downward, [one should submerge him] in boiling water.
Beholding the Sun, one should offer libations; thus the enemy becomes dear to Death.
One should meditate on her holding a mace and a trident, with the luster of a dark cloud at the time of dissolution.
Having offered oblations of cotton seeds and nimba leaves soaked in the fat of a ewe, the preceptor shall cause enemies to hate one another by means of this mantra. (15.72)
Having meditated upon the terrifying goddess, who bears a raised index finger and a trident, [one should offer] sprouts from poisonous trees combined with buffalo ghee. (15.73)

Having performed the oblation, the knower of mantras instantly causes the enemy's army to vanish by meditating upon the Goddess as previously described, using the four substances beginning with black pepper.
One should offer oblations for three days with [substances] sprinkled with the blood of a goat; this will effect the eradication of the enemy's army—of this there is no doubt. (15.75)
Having meditated upon Durgā, who holds a fire-spit and blazes like the fire of universal destruction,
[one should perform the rite] with seeds produced from the *dhustūra* plant, smeared with mustard oil.
Having offered oblations, one should delude the enemies with black pepper and mustard seeds;
one should meditate upon Durgā, who resembles the fire of destruction at the end of time and who wields a trident and a sword.
One should offer oblations with the best sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the *nakṣatra* tree, saturated with wound-healing oils; within a month, one shall destroy the enemy.
Mounted upon a lion, she rushes toward the fleeing enemy,
discharging arrows released from her bow that are filled with mouths of blazing fire.
Recalling Durgā as she releases [the waters], one should offer libations with warm water;
by gazing at the orb of the sun, the eradication of the enemy shall occur.
The mantra-practitioner should likewise touch his heart for the sake of his own protection;
he should visualize [the goddess] as one who destroys even the most difficult diseases, holding a mace in her hand.
One should offer oblations with excellent fuel-sticks of *nimba* and *vibhītaka*, soaked in buffalo ghee, which possess a luster like a garland of lightning, using parched grain.
Or else, by means of *kodrava* grains, there shall be the immobilization of the enemy's army.
One should meditate upon the mantra of Gāli-Durgā, who is red in color and holds a noose and a goad.
[This is performed] in a fire kindled with salt, honey, and wood from the tree of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). (15.83)
One who knows the mantra should perform oblations at night for seven days; he shall thus bring kings under his control.
He should meditate upon Viśvadurgā as red in color, holding a noose and a goad. (15.84)
The practitioner of mantra who offers oblations at night with blossoming *kalinī* flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water, the entire universe shall come under his control. (15.85)

Having meditated upon Goddess Sindhu-Durgā— who resembles the autumn moon, who bestows supreme bliss, and who holds a noose and a goad— one [should worship her] with the finest sacrificial fuel sticks.
One should offer oblations with reeds sprinkled with honey for the sake of attaining the power of vision [to see hidden treasures].
She holds a skull, a trident, a noose, and a goad in her hands. (15.87)
One should meditate upon Agnidurgā, who resembles the flower of the hibiscus;
having offered oblations with a salt-figurine mixed with the three sweets.
Thus, one who knows the mantra should meditate upon the desired objects; there is no doubt in this matter.
The syllables beginning with *ati-durgāṇi* are said to be threefold. (15.89)
That which begins with *durgā* and ends with *ṛṇa*, followed by *gālī* and so forth, is proclaimed as *Gālidurgā*.
That which begins with the bindu (*bindu*) and ends with other syllables is celebrated as *Viśvadurgā*. (15.90)
That [line] beginning with "Sindhu" and ending with "va" is called Sindhudurgā; the wise know that same line, when beginning with "agni" and so forth, as Agnidurgā. (15.91)
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the courtyard, one should daily worship the Goddess with fragrant flowers and other offerings, following the very path previously described.
One should offer the bali-oblation with caru at night for the sake of all accomplishments;
this shall destroy malevolent spells, disease, fear, injury, spirits, and enemies. (15.93)
Having worshipped the fire appropriately with excellent and pleasing flowers,
the mantra-practitioner, standing before it with undistracted mind, should recite the mantra.
This recitation leads to all accomplishments; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
One should perform oblations facing west with salt sprinkled with honey. (15.95)
By means of the number of syllables in the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should bring even an enemy under his control.
Having washed the śālī rice and purified it, he should prepare the clean grains. (15.96)

Having recited [the mantra] over the fire consecrated with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the wise one should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru); then, having removed it from the fire, he should again recite the mantra.
Having worshipped the Goddess who removes poison as before,
one should offer eight thousand oblations of this sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter into the fire.
While performing the pouring of the remnants into the vessel, he should have the person to be treated consume that [medicine] again;
he should bury the remainder at the door and the poured residue within the courtyard.
Malevolent spells, diseases, along with the afflictions caused by spirits and planetary grahas, are destroyed;
furthermore, a spell cast by an enemy shall devour those very enemies themselves. (15.100)
With rice grains, sacrificial offerings, milk, the best fuel-sticks of milky trees,
and clarified butter mixed with the three sweets— one should perform these separately one thousand times each.

One who performs the oblation becomes a certain ground for success; the practitioner certainly becomes so on an auspicious day when the Sun is situated in the sign of Aries and the knower of mantras acts accordingly. (15.102)
In a river flowing toward the ocean, which always possesses abundant water, one should take up sand, lift it out, and having cleansed it, purify it thoroughly. (15.103)
Having placed them in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and upon the consecrated sacrificial fire,
one should fry them with a ladle made from the wood of the Brahma-tree, using the mantra for the sake of success.
When the sun is situated in Leo, Pisces, or Sagittarius, during the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight, and under the asterisms of Viśākhā, Kṛttikā, Mūla, Hasta, the Uttarās, or Maghā. (15.105)
On the Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa nakṣatras, or on days presided over by Saturn or Jupiter,
a wise person should perform the installation of the sand, avoiding all other times.
These auspicious [measures] have been prescribed for the protection of houses, villages, and kingdoms;
furthermore, they are applied to pits of medium size and so forth, measured by *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, and *ghaṭa*.
Having recited [the mantras], the preceptor should cast them into the nine [vessels] and worship them in sequence,
beginning with the mantras of the goddesses in the center and ending with those of the skull-bowl (kapāla).
Having worshipped the discus, conch, sword, shield, arrow, bow, trident, and skull-bowl with their respective mantras, one should finally offer the bali-oblation.
One should offer oblations to the lunar mansions, the planets, the zodiac signs, and the lords of the worlds;
where this protection is established, there prosperity increases. (15.110)
Minor planetary afflictions, great diseases, thieves, malevolent spirits, and reptiles—all these go to destruction by this rite; of this there is no doubt. (15.111)
The wise man should place one *kuḍava* measure of purified sand,
combined with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), in a vessel fashioned from the wood of the *brahmavṛkṣa*.
Having deposited [the seed] there according to the prescribed rite, one should establish it; therein, riches increase day by day along with timely rains and other such blessings.
Great portents, malevolent spells, treachery, and powerful planetary influences are destroyed;
one should consume the five products of the cow and perform the installation according to this rite.
The cow urine should be one *prastha* in measure, and the cow dung half of that;
the milk should be seven times the amount of clarified butter, and the curd three times the amount of cow urine. (15.115)
Clarified butter should be mixed with cow urine in equal parts, or all [the ingredients] may be said to be in equal proportions.
The cows should be of the Kapila, white, smoke-colored, ash-colored, or reddish-brown hue. (15.116)
In the absence [of these], all [the lines] are said to be equal to that arising from Kapila;
[they are drawn] upon a board consisting of forty-nine squares belonging to the Brahma-lineage.
Having left the corner squares and having written the [mantra] beginning with Śakti and ending with Jātavedas in the central squares, one should worship the deities therein.
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should bury it level with the surface as before;
one should offer the sacrificial fee (bali) as previously prescribed—the fruit of this has been stated above.
In the center, having placed eight feet within the eight squares of the *māyā* [triangle], this yantra is surrounded by the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
Situated within the form of the earth, it destroys all diseases of living beings and bestows protection, longevity, prosperity, and fame. (15.120)
The three worlds are under the control of that man who, instructed by his preceptor, knows the rites of discharging and withdrawing the fire-weapon (āgneyāstra). || 15.121 ||
Whether it be a king of mature wisdom, or one who possesses wealth, or likewise an enemy;
such is the power of sound, as it is traditionally taught in the Jñānavedā.
We ourselves worship the God, the Lord of the Universe, the imperishable Supreme Self who abides in the form of Fire, with Soma. (15.123)
O Arāti, O beloved of Hara, take away my wealth, my knowledge, all my sons beginning with Dakṣa, and likewise my perfect wisdom. (15.124)
Having bestowed [this], the divine Four-Hari, the grandfather of all the worlds, he who properly practices hostility toward all the worlds; 15.125.
May Mahādeva, the one of variegated splendor, who awakens one to the goals of human existence, dispel my hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions. 15.126.
Just as a boat crosses a river difficult to cross, so too [the practitioner] crosses over without a doubt;
and one-tenth of the oblations of clarified butter should be offered to him along with marks of honor.
Having touched an aśvattha tree on a Saturday, one should perform recitation;
one obtains the fulfillment of desired goals, and fear is swiftly destroyed. (15.128)
He who recites this a thousand times daily attains Brahman, of this there is no doubt;
he who, ever vigilant, constantly remembers this mantra amidst all difficulties.
One shall immediately cross over all difficulties; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame, longevity, health, and the increase of nourishment. (15.130)
What is the use of saying more in this regard? By taking refuge in the temple of Durgā, the wise accomplish the four aims of human life. (15.131)
Durgā, when accompanied by Sāvitrī, is remembered as the bestower of great success;
when worshipped according to the prescribed rite, she grants all that is desired. (15.132)
If not worshipped, she will indeed grant what is undesirable to everyone;
however, by offering a hundred oblations of Apāmārga, she becomes a bringer of peace in the cow-pen.
Now, by means of salt, one may bring all [these] under one's control:
on a difficult path, in fear, in gambling, in legal disputes, in water, and in battle. (15.134)
In captivity or in calamity, one should mentally recite the mantra of the King;
by mere recitation, one shall accomplish everything, just as for the Brahmins. || 15.135 ||

For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, [the desired result] is always attained through recitation, fire-oblations, and consecrations; whatever a Brahmin recites with a specific person in mind, that person undoubtedly obtains it. (15.136)
Standing in water reaching up to the knees and beholding the solar disc until its setting, a brahmin shall attain all his desires. (15.137)
A Brahmin may overcome any calamity, whether his own or that of another, by meditating upon the auspicious Durgā, the remover of difficulties, who dwells within the solar orb. (15.138)
She holds a conch and a discus, is serene, and bears the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she has four arms, three eyes, a reddish luster, and the brilliance of fire. (15.139)
Having meditated upon the Mother of the World and beheld the solar orb,
standing in water reaching up to his mouth, he should recite [the mantra] with his mind fixed upon that.
By reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, one shall obtain all desires, [becoming free] from all great sins, sins, and minor offenses. (15.141)
And one is liberated from terrible sins as well as from diseases, fears, and so forth;
the practitioner of mantra should offer water into the circle of water with this [mantra]. 15.142.
Beginning on a Sunday, a wise practitioner of mantra who recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times obtains gold and, immediately, gems in their true form. (15.143)
Standing in water reaching up to the navel and facing the mandala himself, he should contemplate that he is being consecrated by the Goddess, even with great effort. (15.144)
One should sprinkle one's own body with waters consecrated by mantras;
that water bestows long life, health, sovereignty, the destruction of enemies, and [prosperity]. (15.145)
One obtains good fortune and unshakable prosperity; there is no doubt in this matter—having established and kindled a fire with abundant fuel, one should remain restrained in speech.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in the eight directions and in the center;
in the east, one should worship Agni Mahādurgā, the presiding deity of the mantras.

Having worshipped Śivā with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, or even mentally, one should visualize her holding a conch, a discus, a bow, and an arrow, while brandishing a finger in the gesture of threatening Death.
One should recite the Gāyatrī as a young maiden, pure and mounted upon a lion, holding in her left hand a discus, a sword, and an arrow, and equipped with various weapons. 15.149.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Śivā, who is three-eyed, mounted upon a lion, and the bestower of the desired accomplishment.
While meditating, one should mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times and repeatedly cast wooden splinters into the blazing fire.
All undertakings are accomplished and all fears are destroyed. || 15/150 ||
What is the use of saying more in this matter? One who desires sovereignty, though it has been seized by an enemy, and who desires long life and health, should kindle the sacrificial fire. (15.151)
One should worship Durgā, the presiding deity of Agni in the eastern direction, with scents and other offerings;
likewise, one should offer oblations to Durgā and her attendants, one by one in sequence.
Then, on both sides, one should likewise offer oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter to Durgā and her attendants in due order, followed by the Vyāhṛtis.
For the destruction of malefic planets, the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations into that fire using thorny wood smeared with cow’s urine; thus, every malefic planet is destroyed.
The Aśvattha is to be known as the first; the second is said to be the Vaṭa;
likewise the Udumbara and the Plakṣa—this is declared to be the sequence of the trees. (15.155)

One should perform oblations in sequence in the presence of four milk-exuding trees; by using all of them smeared with honey, [the targets] shall become subject to one's will until the end of their lives.

In that same manner, one should bring the city, the country, and the kingdom under control; likewise, the four social orders (varṇas) should be brought under subjection in their proper sequence. (15.157)
Having touched a palāśa tree with the five essences of mantra,
one should cut it with an axe and split it into five parts in succession.

In the east, the southeastern portion, and likewise the western portion, as well as the northern portion—at the beginning of the twilight and so forth—one should then [consider] the month, the fortnight, and the day. (15.159)
Having taken up the conch, the discus, the lotus, and likewise the Kaumodakī mace,
with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), according to the prescribed rule and their respective mantras.
Having invoked you there, purified you, and worshipped you in due order,
one should likewise recite the mantra a hundred times for each step in this very sequence.
One should conclude the four conch-vows in due order upon the conch and other vessels,
having worshipped the Goddess of the Gods with devotion by means of this mantra.

One should not recite the mantra while merely remembering it; rather, one should consecrate it with devotion, sequentially [applying it] to the village, the city, the field, the house, the rampart, and so forth. (15.163)
Having dug a pit one cubit deep in the four directions and in the center,
one should pour in the five products of the cow and likewise place conch shells and other items.
Having worshipped and honored each [deity] in its own respective place, as well as the petals,
one should meditate upon Durgā, mounted upon her lion, in every direction according to the prescribed rite.
In whosever kingdom he performs [this rite], that country shall be free from calamity,
prosperous with wealth and grain, and forever free from thorns.
That which consists of five faces does not exist, nor could it possibly arise in any way;
having taken five white lotuses, one should proceed in the same sequence as before.
Having thus propitiated [the deity], the practitioner should bury it for the sake of universal pacification;
or else, as before, the practitioner should [use] that which is consecrated with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should bury [the image] amidst those desiring great knowledge for the sake of all-pervading peace;
thus has the ritual application of the five Durgās been declared. (15.169)
Having offered a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with clarified butter, one should present the oblation;
likewise, by offering blue lotuses, one obtains gold and attains prosperity.
The practitioner of mantras shall obtain garments according to the color of the flowers;
by offering white flowers smeared with honey and clarified butter, one shall attain all desires.
Having prostrated, one should again stand before the Sun while anointed with clarified butter;
by reciting [the mantra] ten thousand or a thousand times, one shall attain liberation, without a doubt.
One who desires spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer oblations of palāśa fuel-sticks;
having offered oblations of nyagrodha fuel-sticks, one shall obtain wealth and grain.
By offering oblations of *udumbara* fuel-sticks, one becomes possessed of wealth and food;
by offering oblations of *aśvattha* fuel-sticks, one shall swiftly accomplish whatever task is to be done. (15.174)
Performing the expulsion of delusion at night, naked and restrained in speech, one should [use] sugar with the Durgā-bīja in the nine locations of Durgā. (15.175)
As long as one has thus made [the enemy] an adversary and casts him into the midst of enemies, they will then suddenly and immediately flee from one another in fear. (15.176)
Having encapsulated the seed-syllable of Durgā with the Sāvitrī mantra, one should place it evenly;
the desired accomplishment occurs swiftly—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (15.177)

Whether afflicted by disease or other ailments oneself or even another, the mantra-practitioner, having commenced [the practice], shall recite the mantra; one is immediately and instantly liberated. (15.178)
From an oblation of grain one obtains grain; by means of milk, one becomes possessed of cattle;
through bilva fruits one attains prosperity (Lakṣmī), and likewise through śrī flowers.
With its leaves smeared with Madhūka resin, one shall bring the entire universe under one's own control;
having first visualized the enemies upon the earth in front of the solar disc.

While standing in water reaching up to the knees, with his face turned downward, he should burn away his impurities with flames while meditating on the water as being composed of fire, exhaling air through the lower opening. (15.181)
Having taken water in his joined palms with the mantra "atidurgā," he should,
filled with wrath, cast it a thousand times into the body of the enemy.
Having ignited the heart with his hands using *śataparṇī* and other substances, he should effect the slaying of the enemy by means of the sprinkling of water alone. (15.183)
Below the solar disc, [the enemy] is pierced by fire;
situated between those two, the enemy is enveloped by a mass of blazing flames.
An enemy meditated upon [with this mantra] shall perish; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (15.184)
Thus are the eight Durgās, beginning with Jātavedā.
Now I shall describe the Dināstra and the Kṛtyāstra, which crush the enemy.
Those most proficient in mantras declare that the Atidurgā mantra is the Dināstra.
This mantra, when recited in reverse order, is declared to be the Kṛtyā-weapon;
they know that the six limbs of the Dināstra are likewise arranged in reverse order.
The wise practitioner should contemplate the enemy situated within the orb of the sun, face-down and struck by poison, being devoured by the Kuṇḍalī rising from the base (mūlādhāra). 15.187.
One should cast [the mantra] into the Mūlādhāra, where the fire of Time blazes instantly; within three days, the enemy, overcome by fever, shall relinquish his life-breaths. (15.188)
One should visualize the enemy, his limbs pierced by the weapon of Time (Dināstra), situated within one's own seat (svādhiṣṭhāna),
with his body consumed by the fire kindled by the five vital winds.
Meditating thus, one should mutter the mantra; immediately he becomes as beloved to Yama as a foe situated in Maṇipūra whose body has been consumed by fire. (15.190)
Meditating thus, one should recite the Dināstra mantra;
that enemy, who has been placed within the Unstruck (anāhata), shall fall under the power of death, utterly consumed by the fire of the mantra.
Bound with a swift noose by the servants of Yama, the enemy, though residing in a pure station, is led away, tormented by the five arrows of the day. (15.192)
If [the victim] is visualized with his face turned downward, his life will swiftly end within three days.
One should mentally burn the enemy, struck down at the Ājñā-cakra, with a blazing fire. (15.193)
Having abandoned son, friends, wife, and others, one should approach death;
standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should meditate upon the form of the Sun.
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over an enemy whose entire body has been burnt;
within seven days, he goes to the realm of Yama.
Beginning from Sunday, one should recite the mantra for a week, starting from sunrise until sunset. (15.196)

The enemy, afflicted by a fever of the three humors (sannipāta) and seized by Yama, shall be [subdued] if the practitioner of mantra stays in a temple of Durgā for three nights, abstaining from food. (15.197)
Contemplating the enemy whose body has been pierced by the arrow of the day, one should recite this mantra; the enemy, afflicted by fever, shall go to his death. 15.198.
Having touched the image of Durgā, one should recite the mantra while mentally visualizing for three days one's own enemy as impaled upon a trident and tormented by the weapon of Time (Kālāstra).
Overcome by a great fever, he becomes a guest of Yama;
his enemy, who has entered the solar orb, is bitten by the serpents on his chariot.
Meditating on one whose entire body is consumed by the fire of poison, one should satiate them with warm water;
by doing so for five days, that person shall become a favorite of Yama.
Having visualized the enemy’s body seized by flames issuing from the solar disc, one should recite the mantra; he shall sport in the presence of Yama. (15.202)
Having perceived his own enemy stationed within the solar disc conjoined with the planets and pierced by arrows consisting of mantras, the best of mantra-knowers should perform the recitation.
The messenger of Yama swiftly leads the enemy to the abode of Yama,
appearing like the fire of universal destruction or like another Kālarātri.
Terrible, bearing a trident and a noose, seated upon the shoulders of a lion,
she dwells within the orb of the sun, with three red eyes blazing forth.
Scorching her enemies with sparks as their bodies were thrown into turmoil, she displayed her fangs and lips, her face contorted by dancing eyebrows and a furrowed brow. || 15.206 ||
Threatening her own enemy with a terrifying forefinger,
she illuminated the ends of the quarters with the flame-like radiance of her fangs.
Visualizing herself as terrifying, tearing open the chest of the enemy with a trident, the practitioner of mantra should recite for three days; he shall cause the death of his own foe.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the weapon-mantras, [he visualizes her] possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction,
wearing red garments, cruel, and endowed with three red eyes.
Mounted upon a lion, she was rushing toward her fleeing enemy;
having severed his head with her sword, she vanished in an instant into the expanse of the sky.
Having meditated upon Durgā, the reciter of mantras should chant for three days while abstaining from sitting on a seat;
by this very procedure, the enemy shall become dear to death.
One should perform these rites during the day, but not at night;
before a lifeless liṅga facing westward, there should be a living buffalo.
Having placed a vessel upon his head and fashioned a triangle there, the most excellent preceptor [performs the rite] in that kindled fire according to the rules. (15.213)

One should offer excellent fuel-sticks of the *kāraskara* tree, smeared with goat's blood, inscribed with the syllables of the mantra and joined with the name of the person to be accomplished. (15.214)

Having meditated upon the Goddess as being like the fire of universal dissolution, terrible, and adorned with thirty-two arms, one should offer a thousand oblations while she is visualized within the orb of the sun.
She was dancing upon the head of a lion, blazing with upraised weapons;
she possessed great fangs, was most terrifying, had flaming hair, and her mouth was roaring.
With a face of flesh wet with blood and three fierce, rolling eyes,
by this ritual, the enemy shall be tormented by a great fever.
The practitioner, having suspended the serpent [image] with warm water above, releases his own body along with his sons, friends, and others. (15.218)
Durgā, who is situated within the solar disc, resembling a thousand suns,
possessing a thousand hands and feet, and a thousand eyes, heads, and faces.
One should meditate upon her whose limbs are bound by a thousand serpents, terrifying the three worlds; with the root mantra, one should satisfy her serpent-mouthed form with warm water.
Bound by the noose of time, an enemy may deprive one of a well-lived life;
yet [one should remember] her who roars like Narasiṃha, resembling ten thousand midday suns. (15.221)
Meditating on her as seated upon a fierce lion, with a most terrifying appearance, and impaling her enemies upon a trident, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. (15.222)
If one offers warm water at the mouth of a serpent for three days, that enemy shall go to the abode of Yama; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having cast an image of a bear or a tree, from which breath has departed, into hot water according to the ritual procedure, one who is rich in poison [should proceed]. (15.224)
Resembling the sun, the moon, and fire, she holds a sword and a shield,
with hundreds of sparks issuing from her three eyes as if they were bolted shut.
Meditating upon her seated upon a lion, richly adorned with serpents, inspiring fear in the three worlds, and brandishing a sword and a kṛtyā weapon, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
By this rite, the enemy becomes seized by death.
Having prepared an excellent triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in a temple of Durgā, [one should proceed]. (15.227)
There, when the fire has been kindled, one should [cast] an effigy made from buffalo dung, smeared with the blood of a goat, and into which breath has been instilled. (15.228)
Having repeatedly cut [the victim], one should offer oblations at night to those who are unaging and impassioned,
while meditating upon Durgā as she dances upon the breast of Mahiṣa.
She was of terrible appearance, piercing the body of Mahiṣa with her trident,
and terrifying the armies of the Asuras with incessant bursts of loud laughter.
Resembling the fire of universal dissolution, endowed with three blazing eyes,
her lower lip bitten by her fangs, her lotus-face terrifying with its tusks.
Accompanied by maidens holding swords and shields,
the enemy goes to the presence of Yama by means of this rite.
This weapon of Time has been described, which effects the subjugation of enemies;
the best among those who know mantras should perform all the ritual applications prescribed for magical rites (kṛtyā). || 15/233 ||
The goddess Kuṇḍalī, who has the form of a serpent, having risen from the foundation (ādhāra),
then proceeds through the path of the aperture of the Suṣumnā to the region of the void (vyoma).
Visualizing her as having seized the enemy with her mouth and returning toward her own home, blazing with the fires of the cosmic dissolution (Kālānala), one should recite the mantra. (15.235)
Deluded by this, the enemy meets death within seven days;
on a Tuesday, [one should offer oblations] into a funeral pyre fire mixed with mustard oil.
One should perform oblations for half a month with *siddhārtha* seeds mixed with jaggery, as prescribed;
the enemy, consumed by the blazing weapon of the *kṛtyā*, shall go to the city of Yama. (15.237)
Then, on the fourteenth day at midnight, the practitioner should take bones from a funeral pyre,
smear them with oil from a wound, and offer them as oblations into the fire of the funeral pyre.
By this rite, the cowardly enemy shall meet his death;
[one should fashion] an image of the enemy made from husks and bones, drenched with oil from a wound. (15.239)
At night, the practitioner should offer as oblation an effigy into which life has been infused;
by cutting it again and again with the blood of an aged person, the enemy dies within seven days. (15.240)
Having touched sand from a cremation ground mixed with unbroken grains, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should then scatter that [sand] into a pond or similar body of water, along with water boiled with the weapons-mantra of the Kṛtyā.

The yellow pepper belonging to that [deity], when empowered by the ashes of a *preta* consecrated on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight with charcoal from a funeral pyre, destroys all people. (15.242)

Having fashioned these pills from buffalo ghee, stirred together according to the number of syllables in that mantra, and having properly consecrated them with breath-recitation (*samīraṇa*), [one should employ them]. (15.243)
With a firm mind, one should offer oblations into a fire kindled with wood from a funeral pyre;
within three days of the fourteenth lunar day, the enemy shall fall under the power of death. (15.244)
One should cast cemetery ashes and white mustard seeds into the five products of the cow;
one should then meditate upon the Goddess, possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction, within the buffalo-dung [mixture]. (15.245)
One who knows the mantra should roast [the offerings] while reciting the mantra over a funeral pyre fire made of *graha* wood;
in a temple of Durgā, one who knows the mantra should offer oblations ten thousand times with this [mantra].
Taking that ash again, one should throw it into the enemy's army;
that army will be split in many ways, deluded by the disease of fever. (15.247)
If one casts [the mantra] upon weapons at the time of battle, the enemy flees;
if cast upon houses, villages, and so forth, it effects expulsion in an instant. (15.248)
On the seven days of the week, during the periods of the Kulika, one should take sugar and a thunderbolt from the dwellings of Durgā located in the northeast direction, and then recite the mantra.
One should roast them according to the prescribed rite in the five products of a buffalo;
having recited the mantra over them once more, one should scatter these [remnants] throughout the house, the village, and the city.
That region quickly perishes by the fire born of the burnt mantra:
the *brahmadaṇḍī*, the *markaṭikā*, and the triad of *karakrośanikās*. (15.251)
On Saturdays, when the *kulika* occurs, one should take hold [of the ritual] and recite the mantra;
on the fourteenth day, one should cast a pestle into the house of the enemy while reciting the mantra.
The enemy’s destruction occurs together with his sons, wife, and others;
or, by digging even one [of these], the practitioner of mantra obtains that same result from the mandala. (15.253)
One should bury six sets of six dots along with sun-leaves within a doll;
having touched it, one should recite the mantra starting from midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
One should bury this [mantra], joined with the name of the enemy, in a cremation ground;
then that enemy, along with his kinsmen, will quickly give up his life.
The practitioner of spells [should fashion] slabs from skulls, numbering as many as the syllables of the *kṛtyā* weapon-mantra.
Having touched it, one should mutter the Astra mantra preceded by the rite of establishing the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana).
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at a cemetery, [one should do this] near a poisonous tree.

One should offer oblations of [substances] smeared with red lac; struck by the blazing flames of the *kṛtyā* weapon, the enemy, utterly deluded by a great fever, shall go to the city of Yama. (15.257)
One should place this [substance] into a jar filled with blood,
cover it with a skull-cup, and conceal it with a red cloth.
One should worship with red flowers and other offerings, and having touched it,
one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times on a Tuesday at midnight, using fuel from the *kāraskara* tree.
One should offer oblations into the fire of a cremation ground, and the enemy shall go to the city of Yama.
Having fashioned a jar from the wood of the tree corresponding to the victim’s birth-star, one should fill it [with the enemy's substances]. 15.260.
One should place that Virāja there with the five products of the buffalo;
one should perform all rites, such as recitation and worship, exactly as before. (15.261)

When the fire has been kindled with the *kṛtyā* mantra during the state of the *kāraskara* wood, one should offer ten thousand oblations of wound-oil; at the conclusion, that jar [should be treated] again.
Having uprooted [the plant] from its base to its tip, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
by performing the oblation according to this rite for three days, the enemy shall die.
One should cause a handsome son of a buffalo-cow, who has fasted for one night, to drink a *prastha* measure of buffalo ghee consecrated with the mantra. (15.264)
With all his limbs bound with *kuśa* grass,
he was immediately placed upon a fire kindled with *kāraskara* wood by the knower of mantras, who used wound-oil.
Having performed the fire sacrifice, the mantra-practitioner, with a restrained mind, should offer ten thousand oblations;
then, within a single day, the enemy shall go to the city of Yama.
When the fire has been placed in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and kindled with the mantra,
and has been worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform ten thousand oblations (ayuta) in due order.
Then, for seven days, one should apply a mixture of rājī, bhallātaka,
and sesame oils to a buffalo that has reached the time of parturition and whose wind (vāyu) has been stabilized.

Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should recite that mantra while touching it with the *kūrca* brush, mentally recollecting the calf from its head down to its vulva. (15.269)
Having drawn it forth, one should offer into the kindled fire that which has fallen into the hand.
When this is done, a Kṛtyā arises, blazing from the sacrificial fire.
She devours the enemy before long, even if protected by the Lord;
furthermore, she enters the fire, protecting even her own performer.
The best of mantra-knowers who performs such rites should recite mantras such as the Mṛtyuñjaya for the sake of self-protection.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the section on the nine Durgās beginning with Jātavedas in the venerable Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The sixteenth chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
Now, the ritual procedure for the mantra of salt is being declared.
This mantra, which brings about all peace, is accomplished from the very moment of its grasping. || 16/1 ||
Without the observances of vows, fasts, and restrictive rules, such as the *puraścaraṇa* and others; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, the deity is Mahārātri-Bhadrakālī. (16.2)

The *Ṛk* and others were previously described as being in the eastern salt ocean; those beginning with the second [ocean], such as the salt ocean and so forth, are proclaimed as being in the south and other directions. (16.3)
The fourth [verse] is "saṃdahatyā," and when it has passed, the fifth is "pūrvārtha.
The sage is declared to be Aṅgiras, and the meter is cited as Anuṣṭubh. (16.4)
Agni, Rātrī, Punardurgā, and Bhadrakālī are the presiding deities;
with a concentrated mind, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the syllables of the *ciṭi* mantra.
The heart is said to consist of five [syllables], the head is remembered as having three syllables;
the crest-lock is said to have five syllables, and the armor consists of six syllables. (16.6)
The Eye is proclaimed with five [syllables], the Weapon with a pair;
then the Tāra (Om), followed by two Ciṭis, and after that, Cāṇḍālī.
One should utter "mahāpadādyām" (beginning with mahāpadā), then "tām" (her), followed by "amakaṃ me" (make [him] mine);
then "vaśamānaya" (bring under control) and the pair of "ṭha" syllables—this is declared to be the *ciṭi* mantra. (16.8)
Consisting of twenty-four syllables, it bestows the fruits of all desires:
(Oṃ ciṭi ciṭi cāṇḍāli mahācāṇḍāli, bring so-and-so under my control, svāhā).
I worship the Fire-god, who resembles fresh saffron, who has three eyes, and who is adorned with hundreds of beautiful ornaments.
Holding a *śruva* ladle, a spear, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in his arms, he is seated upon a red lotus.
Thus is the meditation on Vahni:

I bow to that youthful woman, who has the luster of a dark rain cloud, whose breasts are beautiful and adorned with strings of pearls, who holds a skull, a noose, a goad, and a trident in her hands, and who is clad in blue garments. 16.10.
This is the meditation on Vahnistrī:

one should meditate upon Durgā, who is capable of shattering all fortresses; she has the luster of a dark blue cloud, her hands are enriched with a sword, a conch, a trident, and a scimitar, she bears the crescent moon as her crest, she is formidable, possesses three eyes, has conquered the host of enemies, and is skilled in breaking through difficulties. (16.11)

May Bhadrakālī be for my prosperity— she who bears the axe, the skull-bowl, the hand-drum, and the trident; who is adorned with a crescent moon, whose hair is tawny and upright, and whose eyes are like white smoke.
One should properly recite this five-verse hymn of meditation on Bhadrakālī ten thousand times,
and then offer oblations into a kindled fire one-tenth that number, using clarified butter from a buffalo as the libation.
Having thus performed the preliminary ritual (*puraścaryā*), one becomes skilled in practical application (*prayoga*).
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), the two [deities] should be meditated upon as being like fire and lightning. (16.14)
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon Durgā Bhadrakālī during the rite of slaying;
standing in water reaching the knees, he should recite the mantra at night.
By this, the desired object to be accomplished becomes a servant in an instant.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, the wise one should recite this mantra. (16.16)
For one who recites it one thousand and eight times, the object of his practice shall come under his control.
The practitioner of mantras, standing in water reaching up to the neck, should mutter the five verses.
One shall bring [the target] under control within seven days by means of this procedure:
having written that [target], with the name of the person to be subdued interlaced [with the mantra], upon a palm leaf.
Having cast it into water mixed with milk, one should boil it during the night;
that person to be influenced will become submissive—there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Having written this on a palm leaf, one should bury it in the house of Bhadrakālī;
this is declared to be the practice for bringing all living beings under one's control.

Having inscribed the mantra interwoven with the name of the person to be influenced upon a copper plate, one should heat it in a fire of khadira wood; within a month, that man shall become submissive.
Having properly prepared a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the characteristics prescribed in the scriptures,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) therein upon the consecrated bearer of oblations (the fire).
Having washed [the substance] with cow's milk and added salt, the wise one should offer it as a ground powder into the fire; within seven days, he shall bring people under his control.
Likewise, one should offer oblations with rock salt sprinkled with curd, honey, and clarified butter;
by this, one may subjugate all the gods in no time, let alone kings.
One should take one *prastha* of pure salt, divide it into five separate portions, and with devotion offer each portion with a single verse for five days. (16.25)
By means of this very [mantra], he over whom it is recited shall become submissive; of this there is no doubt.
Taking pure salt mixed with honey, one should offer it as an oblation. (16.26)
By forty-nine oblations, one brings the desired object under control;
by constantly offering pure salt, one should bring an enemy under control.
One should offer oblations with salt well-ground and combined with the three sweets; thus one may bring women, men, and even kings under one's control.
One should recite the mantra beginning from the third day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day.
One should fashion five effigies that are uniform, auspicious, and complete with their primary and secondary limbs.
One [type of] effigy is prescribed for the sequence of accomplishment;
it is made of salt produced from a mine, ground, and thoroughly purified. (16.30)
One should sprinkle the *kuḍara* with milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey in sequence;
then, with water thoroughly mixed with jaggery, clarified butter, and honey.
One should fashion a gentle effigy, beautiful in all its limbs;
one should then place into their heart the mantra of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the prepared yantra.
Having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in these [vessels], one should worship them with flowers and other offerings;
afterwards, on the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight, when only one watch (*yāma*) remains.
Having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, immediately thereafter the Mantra-nyāsa,
consisting of twenty-four [syllables] originating from the Ciṭi-mantra.
With a concentrated mind, one should place the phonemes beginning with *tā* in these locations:
on the crown of the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, and the chin. (16.35)
Having placed [the syllables] upon the throat, heart, pair of breasts, belly, navel, the two hips, the penis, and the anus, one should assign the remaining four phonemes [to the feet].

Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the two thighs, the pair of knees, the pair of shanks, and the two feet—and likewise upon all the limbs—one who is adorned with red garlands and unguents [should proceed]. (16.37)
Pure, wearing red garments,
he should dig a wooden effigy carved from hard wood face-down into the sacrificial pit, beneath the seat made of flour.
One should place an earthen image at the location of one's feet;
likewise, one made of beeswax should be suspended in the sky above the sacrificial pit.
Thereafter, while touching the effigy made of salt,
one should recite the five verses eight hundred and eight times according to the prescribed rule.
Having performed the equalization, one should again place the *ciṭi*-mantras upon her body:
on the finger-joints, the forefoot, the calves, the thighs, the knees, and the anus.
Furthermore, [one should place them] at the region of the *liṅga*, the navel, the abdomen, the lotus of the heart, the two breasts, the shoulders, the chin, and again the face. (16.42)

Having taken fire and kindled it with wood corresponding to the birth-star of the person to be acted upon, [he should place it] sequentially on the two nostrils, the two ears, the two eyes, the forehead, and the head. (16.43)
Having worshipped the deity mentioned in the mantra upon that wooden leaf,
the wise one should offer the *arghya* with *kusīta*, *rāji*, and *puṣpa* flowers and then prostrate.
With these mantras, at the beginning and end of the ritual application, one whose mind is fully restrained [should recite]:
"Oṃ, O slayer of enemies, O bearer of oblations, by this [mantra] as well, [be present] in the night. (16.45)
O Jātavedas, O Mahādeva, you who possess the luster of molten gold, be satisfied with this oblation offered with mantras along with her.
O Lord of Svāhā, consumer of all things, burn the salt, O slayer of enemies!
Om! By you, the Sovereign, through all [powers], the entire world is held together with its devouring [nature]. 16.47.
O Great Goddess, salutations to you; be the granter of boons and the fulfiller of desires. Oṃ, O Great Goddess consisting of darkness, O lady of excellent vows of the Great God! (16.48)
Having offered a human sacrifice at the three watches [of the night], bring him under my control and give him to me!
Oṃ Durgā, you who are free from all difficulties, you who are filled with the awakening to the insurmountable! (16.49)
O Goddess who bears the conch and the discus, O terrifier of wicked enemies!
Oṃ, salutations to you; burn my enemy and bring him under my control, O Caṇḍikā!
O Śākambharī, Great Goddess, O sinless one, be my refuge!
Oṃ, O Bhadrakālī, O greatly fierce one, O bestower of auspicious success! (16.51)
Slay my rivals! Strike them, burn them, dry them up, and scorch them!
Having repeatedly torn them apart with spears, swords, javelins, thunderbolts, and other weapons, kill them! 16.52
O Mahādevī Mahākālī, protect us, O you whose nature is invulnerable!
Having consecrated and prepared the effigy, one should then [perform the rite] seven times. (16.53)
Having recited the five *ṛg* verses, one should offer oblations into the kindled fire:
first the right foot, and immediately after that, the hand.
The third is declared to be the head; beyond that is the neck (vāhasta).
Above the middle [of the body] is the fifth, and the sixth is said to be half a part (ardhāṃśa). || 16.55 ||
The seventh [division] shall be the left foot; such is the sequence of divisions remembered.
Or, among those previously mentioned, there may be a division of seven by seven according to the rule. (16.56)
Having thus offered oblations and worshipped the fire, the sacrificer should then prostrate himself like a staff;
he should honor his own preceptor with wealth and grain.
By this method, the practitioner of mantra shall subjugate asuras and gods;
how much more so humans, kings, and women, beginning with their names? (16.58)
Then, for the rite of killing, the practitioner should place the four effigies previously described according to the former procedure and the prescribed rule.
One should prepare other [substances] according to this method that will be described:
with the dung of a boar and a pigeon, sesame, wood, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and asafoetida (rāmaṭha).

One should apply the resin of *nimba*, which causes ulcers, ground together with the dust from the left foot of the person to be affected, mixed with buffalo urine and the previously mentioned salts. (16.61)
Having properly fashioned the effigy, one should begin the rite of infusing life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā);
thereafter, one should perform the recitation of mantras (japa), worship (pūjā), and other rites according to the previously mentioned method.
Then, at night, having duly worshipped either Durgā or Bhadrakālī in the fire kindled in the previously mentioned sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), [one should proceed].
Holding a sharp weapon in his left hand, the practitioner, beginning with the left foot and ending with the right foot, [should perform the dance]. (16.64)
Having cut [the wood] again and again, one who has conquered his senses and abstains from food should offer oblations,
beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
With this very procedure, one who has conquered the senses should perform the fire-oblation;
by practicing it for three weeks, he shall cause his own enemy to die.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, she is Raudrī, the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals;
her seer is Vāruṇa, named Varuṇa, who is himself movement. (16.67)
Whoever should recite it a thousand times, the world shall become subject to him;
standing in water reaching the knees at night, he should remain absorbed in meditation. (16.68)
With whomsoever one recites the mantra while aiming [at them], that person will immediately come under one's control;
having propitiated Bhadrakālī with red flowers, one should touch [the person] while reciting.
Whether meditating on a hundred or a thousand [times], he will come under one's control immediately.
One should write the mantra, interwoven with the name of the person to be accomplished, on a palm leaf. (16.70)
Having recited [the mantra] a hundred or a thousand times, one should dig at the house of Bhadrakālī;
he will become like a servant for as long as he lives, without a doubt. (16.71)
Holding red flowers, wearing red garlands and unguents, the practitioner,
being well-disposed, should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) and offer oblations upon the ground.

When one watch of the night has passed, seated upon an auspicious seat made from the wood of the *sādhya* tree, which is inscribed with the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), he should sit upon a higher seat.
Having prostrated before the fire in the middle of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), or on a mound (*sthaṇḍila*),
one should spread lotus flowers and also *kuśa* grass made of reeds.
Having propitiated the fire during the great night, one should worship the fire in the eastern direction;
with a red cloth and salt, one should fashion an auspicious image.
Then the wise practitioner should place the syllables of the mantra upon that [seat], which is smeared with honey, possesses a moving lap, has been worshipped, and is endowed with the senses.
Then, having kindled the fire with clarified butter, one should offer oblations with the *praṇava*,
and likewise with the syllables of the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively.
Starting from the left foot, this continues until the hand is filled.
Having taken it with that very hand, which has been consecrated, || 16.78 ||
The practitioner of mantras, established in meditation, should offer oblations seven times with the mantra beginning with the *praṇava* that has been perfected through the guru’s instruction. (16.79)
Furthermore, one should offer clarified butter with the vyāhṛtis and with the praṇava;
at the conclusion of the oblation, the wise person should always perform the offering of bali.
The best of practitioners should gradually place on the ground food mixed with sesame, parched grain, and so forth, along with barley meal and curd, two or three times.
Oṃ, homage to the hosts of night-walkers who bring all under control!
May they accept this offering for the sake of subduing all and for all peace, svāhā!
Having offered the bali-oblation, the wise practitioner should further recite the mantra beginning with "lavaṇa. (16.82)
Having sprinkled water around the fire and likewise worshipped it during the dead of night, the wise man should complete the remainder; he will immediately come under control.
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight,
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of land or gold according to the prescribed rule.
One should give [the fee] to the officiating priests or to the preceptor, or feed a Brahmin;
he who performs the fire-oblation (homa) in this manner according to the instruction of the Guru and the scriptures. || 16.85 ||
That mortal comes under the power of death; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, one who desires to perform attraction should stand in water reaching up to the navel. (16.86)
