With an undistracted mind, one should constantly meditate for a thousand [repetitions] or even more, according to the specific requirement; during the great night, one should recite the mantra tirelessly.
The subject to be accomplished, bound by fetters, is under restraint in the presence of the Mothers;
[one should visualize] Mahārātri, resembling a garland of flames, possessing great arms.
Having propitiated Bhadrakālī with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order, he will immediately bring her, whose face is formidable with fangs, under his control.
Reciting [the mantra], one should cast a thousand red flowers at each repetition while meditating upon the Great Goddess; that man will come immediately. (16.90)

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished interspersed with the words "enemy's son," man, or woman, one should cast it into water mixed with milk and boil it while remaining absorbed in meditation. (16.91)

If one recites [the mantra] a hundred or a thousand times, he will come immediately; may Aruṇa protect you— he who is accompanied by the Dawn and the Aruṇa-lotus, whose hands are joined with the sacrificial ladle (sruva), the spear (śakti), the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and whose three stainless, radiant eyes are like nectar-born lotuses.
May she who has a face like the rising moon, who wears deep blue garments, whose body is as dark as a forest of golden *nīla* trees,
whose heavy breasts are closely set, and who holds a goad, a noose, a trident, and a skull-bowl— may she protect you eternally. 16.93.
Oṃ! She whose hands shine with the discus, conch, sword, and trident;
who has torn apart many demons with her resplendent crown;
whose body is adorned by three eyes; and who possesses the brilliance of the sun.
May Kātyāyanī, whose limbs resemble the branches of a tree shaken by the wind, protect you.
Oṃ! Svaraudrasṛtadaṃṣṭrikā, three-eyed, with hair standing erect, filled with a shield, skull-cup, axe, *ḍamaru*-drum, sickle, and trident;
dense, resembling a dark cloud, dripping with blood, adorned with a garland of small bells.
May Bhadrakālī abide for a long time for the accomplishment of worldly existence. || 16/95 ||
Holding a shield, sword, mace, spear, skull-bowl, javelin, noose, and trident, with fierce fangs and adorned with three eyes, she is to be meditated upon.
Having offered oblations with salt mixed with clarified butter, one will certainly achieve victory;
having mixed sesame oil and offered it as an oblation, one will become possessed of prosperity.
By offering oblations mixed with *punnāga* flowers, one shall obtain a son;
by using even the fruit of the *mātuluṅga*, all pacification will certainly occur.
By means of the homa of mad-offering seeds, one becomes intoxicated; it is not otherwise.
With salt combined with neem oil, death occurs swiftly. (16.99)
Or, by offering oblations with salt, lost property is quickly recovered.
Furthermore, there may be a *dhātrī* tree originating from *kāraskara*, or an *udumbara* tree. (16.100)
Those known as Jambū and Khadira, those named Vaṃśa and Pippala, those called Nāga and Rohiṇa, and those designated as Palāśa and Plakṣa. (16.101)
The Jambu, the trees known as Vilva, Arjuna, and Vikaṅkata; the Bakula, Sarala, Sarja, Vañjula, Panasa, and Arka. (16.102)
The practitioner of mantras should perform all the rites for self-protection and so forth, as previously described, using the Śamī, Kadamba, Āmra, Nimba, Madhuka, and Ṛkṣa trees.
In the perfect accomplishment of desired fruits through this method, there is no other mantra equal to it; this is the truth indeed, and not otherwise. (16.104)

"Performing the rite," [it means] that having offered one hundred and eight oblations each of *apāmārga* stalks, *mṛdvī* stalks, and *rājī* stalks with the *praty-aṅgirasa* mantra, one should offer the *bali* in the ten directions with these mantras while effecting protection for oneself from the destruction of others' spells (*parakṛtyā*). || 16.105 ||

For example: "Whatever evil has preceded me, by what cause or action here may you, Indra, king of the gods, crush it, paralyze it, delude it, dry it up, cast it down, scorch it, melt it away, terrify it, consume it, destroy it, kill it, and deliver it as an offering! (16.106)
May it be auspicious for me, may it be welfare for me, may it be peace and prosperity for me— that [merit] of mine which has gone to Agni,
that which has gone to Īśa, that which has gone upwards, that which has gone to heaven, and that which [remains] here because of my sinful action.

O Sūrya, King of the Gods, may you crush, paralyze, delude, scorch, and terrify [the enemy]; deliver the offering to her; whatever has been done for me, may it be auspicious and propitious for me—my peace and my well-being—you who are omnipresent to me.
In this manner, one should offer bali to the deities in the ten directions;
when this rite is performed, the magical spell (kṛtyā) of enemies is swiftly destroyed.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Salt Mantra," in the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*, the supreme king of tantras within the glorious Western Tradition (*Paścimāmnāya*).
The seventeenth chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
The substances for writing mantras are sandalwood, gorocanā, and turmeric.
Household smoke, charcoal from a funeral pyre, and poisons [are used] in rites of killing. || 17.1 ||
Soma, fire, a lump of salt, and the juice of *dhustūra*—
along with house-soot and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*)— are declared to be the eight poisons (*viṣāṣṭaka*).
Now I shall describe the varieties of yantras, concealed within the tantras, by which practitioners of mantra constantly accomplish their own desires. (17.3)
One should write the mantra of Dhūmāvatī in sequence within a pair of fire-squares marked with tridents;
in the intermediate corners starting from the center, one should place those residing in the wind-square.
The yantra is colored like fire and wind—red and yellow. || 17/4 ||
The mantra of Dhūmāvatī consists of the word *dhūmāvatī* with the seed-syllable *dviṭha* (hūṃ) placed before it;
Dhūmāvatī is known as Kālī, the subduer of enemies. (17.5)
One should bury this [image] in a cremation ground along with poison and water from a golden vessel made from a ghost's rags; this will certainly drive the enemy away.

Having written the syllable *dhūṃ* together with the object of the rite in the center of the six-cornered *vajra*, one should write "O *Dhūmāvati*, svāhā! within each of the corners starting from the east inside that six-cornered figure. || 17/7 ||
And *svāhā* in a triangle; outside of that is the abode of Mātariśvan (Wind), marked with six dots. Thus is the house of Vāyu. || 17/8 ||
Outside of that, one should encircle it with two lines of the color of wind (blue).
Having written the name [of the practitioner], the knower of mantras should write Dhūmāvatī, together with the letters Ña, Ṇa, Na, and Ka-sa, within the squares of the pair of *ma*-cells on the leaf.

This supreme machine, covered with a cloth, a skull-bowl, and so forth, and enclosed by wind, mountains, and houses, when placed in a ground frequented by spirits at its edge, shall cause hatred among enemies. (17.10)
First, the pair *gharmaṭikā*, then the pair *varmaṭikā*;
[O goddess] who causes terrible hatred, who causes the agitation of hatred! (17.11)
Then, for the two [mantras] Ghorā and Aghorā, [the mantra] "amukāmukau vidveṣaya huṃ phaṭ" is declared by Gharmaṭika as the Vidyā.
Within the eight petals, one should write the letter *ma* joined with two squares below two filaments (*kesara*).

Inside those two squares, in the center, is the name; within the letter *ma*, having written *ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma* starting from the northeast corner (*īśakoṇa*) in the four corners, one should place the mantra of Dhūmāvatī on the eight petals and surround it externally with the Gharmaṭikā mantra.
One should encircle the house of wind (the letter Ya), which is marked with six dots, with three [circles].
One should draw four clear lines according to the rules— east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east—
forming a square with a trident rising at each corner and joined by pairs of side-arms, starting from the center and extending to its end; then,
having written the syllables of the mantra beyond that, one should inscribe eight syllables in the gaps of the eight squares.
The twelve-syllable mantra of the King of the Dead (Yama), which arises from the trident and has been duly declared, [is as follows]. 17.14.
Yama, the King of Death, who is immeasurable, whose fierce rising is terrible;
he in whom the three wombs are contained, and who is free from disease—this eight-syllable mantra, "ukto dhūmāndhakārāya svāhā," has been declared. (17.15)
The syllable *praṇava*, then *uṣṭrām*, then *daṃṣṭrām*, and after that *vikṛtam*; [the word] *ānanāya* and *vadhūḥ* for the fire—this is the twelve-syllabled mantra.
Having drawn this on a board made from a poisonous tree, or on human skin, or on a cloth,
using the eight poisons, one should bury it in a cremation ground at night.
Overcome by a great fever, his mind agitated by fainting, the enemy goes to the realm of Yama within a fortnight; of this there is no doubt.

In this diagram (*cakra*), having drawn a twelve-syllable wheel in the form of *kuṇḍalinī*, having marked the four lines extending to the corners with tridents, and having placed four circles below the tridents, one should write "Yamarāja" and so forth from the center to the edge; then,
starting from the southeast square located at the corner below the central circle, one should write up to the eight syllables ending in "dhūmāndhakārāya svāhā."
In the four tridents, one should write the mantra of the fangs starting from the first trident. || 17/19 ||

In the eighty-one squares, one should write the *sādhya* (the name of the target) in the central fire-square. Then, one should write the seed-syllables *kṣīṃ śrīṃ dhruṃ* in the rows situated in the cardinal directions.
In the remaining squares, beginning from the northeast and moving toward the southwest, one should write the mantra of Kālī row by row.
Outside of that, one should draw the Yantra consisting of the seed-syllable of Yama and the seed-syllables of fire and wind.
O Kālī, Māra, Ramā, Vāṇī, Nīla, Mokṣa, Kṣama, and Nalī; may you rejoice, O Umā, and protect me, for you are the imperishable essence of all those respective functions.
This is declared to be the mantra of Kālī, [known as] Kālarātri, for her own enemies:
*yamā pāṭa ṭamā māya māṭa moṭa ṭamo ṭamā*. (17.22)
*vāmo bhuvi vibhū movā ṭaṭavīstvaṭavī ṭaṭa*—this verse, which consists of the syllable *yam*, is proclaimed as the destroyer of enemies. (17.23)
One should write this diagram called Nigraha on a piece of cloth using crow feathers and soot made from the resin of the eight poisons and the *nimba* tree. (17.24)
At midnight, when the wind blows from the south, the practitioner of mantra should bury [the object] beneath a Vibhītaka tree, an anthill, a cremation ground, or at a crossroads.
In every way, the enemy shall meet death within seven days by this [rite];
he will be seized by great diseases or he shall fall down.
This wheel is fashioned upon a stone or a brick,
smeared with *markaṭī*, poison, and *daṇḍī* plants, and turned face downwards.
One should dig a yantra there in the ground at night; otherwise, one will encounter further misfortune.
[Draw] ten lines vertically and ten lines horizontally. (17.28)

Having thus drawn the wheel consisting of eighty-one squares, one should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) together with the ritual action (*karman*) within the triangle in the fifth central square.

Then, in the four directions, starting from the square adjacent to the central square containing the target and proceeding in a clockwise outward sequence, one should write *dhū*, *kṣīṃ*, *śrū*, and *hrūṃ* in the first square of each direction. Starting from the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*), one should [continue] in the first row across the eight squares.

Having written "nīlāmokṣakṣamālinī," below that "māmodeta," below that "tadevomā," below that "rakṣa" [repeated] with "tattatkṛtakṣara" after each, below that "hrūṃ" and so forth, below that "rakṣa" [repeated] with "tattatkṛtakṣara" after each, below that "māmo deta," below that "tade momā," below that "nīlāmokṣakṣamālinī," and below that "kālī māra ramā vāṇī," and having performed the invocation starting from the northeast corner (īśakoṇa) with "yamāpāṭaṭamāmāya."

Having written "māṭa moṭa ṭamo ṭamā" in the east, "vāmo bhuvi vibhūmo vā" in the south, and "ṭaṭavīstvaṭavīṭaṭa" in the north, and having drawn a circle, one should encircle its exterior with fire and wind. || 17/29 ||

Thus one should write it within sixty-four squares, encircling it with the verse beginning with "Aṣṭamī, Īśāna, Niśā, Kālī, etc., and Yama," and one should fashion this yantra surrounded by the seed-syllables of fire and wind. || 17.30 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Dhūmāvatī Siddhi Yantra," in the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra* of the glorious Western Tradition (*Paścimāmnāya*).
The eighteenth chapter.
Śrī Śiva said:
The man who worships a mantra having encased it within the *bhūtalipi* [alphabet-matrix], [attains success].
By reciting it one hundred times in both forward and reverse order, his mantra becomes perfected.
With breasts full and high, resembling ten million crescent moons,
her head marked by the half-moon, her three eyes rolling with the intoxication of wine,
she constantly bears in her hands a boon, a rosary, a lore, and a skull-cup.
I take refuge in Vāgīśvarī, who is resplendent, proud of her youth, and whose body is inscribed with letters. 18.2.
The five short vowels are the phonemes of conjunction: space, air, fire, water, and earth;
they correspond respectively to the last, the first, the second, the fourth, and the middle [consonants]. (18.3)
There should be five-colored syllables at the end, together with white moons;
this is declared to be the *bhūtalipi* consisting of forty-two syllables.

a i u ṛ ḷ e ai o au ha ya va ra la ṅa ka kha gha ga ña ca cha jha ja ṇa ṭa ṭha ḍha ḍa na ta tha dha da ma pa pha bha ba sa ṣa śa sa ṣa śa ba bha pha pa ma da dha tha ta na ḍa ḍha ṭha ṭa ṇa ja jha cha ca ña ga gha kha ka ṅa la va ra ya ha au o ai e ḷ ṛ u i a.

Having meditated and recited [the mantra] one hundred times according to the method of both direct and reverse order, one becomes perfected, endowed with knowledge and realization; of this there is no doubt. (18.5)
In direct order, they begin with earth and end with the beginning; in reverse order, they go from the beginning to the end.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule and recited the *bhūtalipi*, a person—

By reciting this one hundred times in both forward and reverse order, a person shall obtain all desires; indeed, that man who recites this mantra while encasing it within this [mantra] shall achieve his aims.
Through one hundred repetitions performed in forward and reverse order, his mantra becomes perfected.
[The syllables] Śakti, Vāṇī, and Bindu are adorned by being enclosed within Pāśa and Aṅkuśa. (18.8)
The first seven [syllables] ending in *sa* are *vyoma* (ha) conjoined with *satya* (la) and *indu* (sa)—[namely:
ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa].
At the end of that should be the *haṃsa* mantra; after that, the word *amuṣya* follows. (18.9)
One should say "the vital breaths" (prāṇāḥ), and thereafter "here the vital breaths"; then "the soul of so-and-so is situated here," and the word "of so-and-so" (amuṣya) should follow. (18.10)
At the end of this [mantra], all the senses— speech, mind, and sight,
as well as hearing and smell— having come here to the place of the vital breaths, may they remain for a long time in happiness.
Let the fire-bride remain at the end; this is declared to be the Prāṇa-mantra. || 18/11 ||

One should employ the noose and other [weapons] preceded by the word "amuṣya" (of such-and-such a person); this great mantra, known as the "Life-Extractor," is proclaimed for ritual applications. 18.12.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Instruction on the Vitalization of the Earth-Alphabet," in the glorious *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*, the supreme king of great tantras.
The nineteenth chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
The ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of mantras, which bestow accomplishment (siddhi), are now being described.
First birth, then life, followed by striking and likewise awakening.

Now, consecration (abhiṣeka), purification (vimalīkaraṇa), nourishment (āpyāyana), satiation (tarpaṇa), illumination (dīpana), and concealment (gupti)—these ten are the purificatory rites of mantra (mantrasaṃskriyā). (19.2)
Indeed, all mantras become bestowers of accomplishment when purified;
the extraction of mantras from within the Mātṛkā is known as their "birth. (19.3)
The wise one should recite the syllables of the mantra interspersed with the *praṇava*;
those proficient in mantra and tantra call this "the life" (*jīvana*) of the mantra. (19.4)
Having written down the syllables of the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should strike each one with sandalwood water; that is declared to be "striking" (tāḍana) by means of the wind-mantra.
Having written that mantra, the practitioner of mantra should diligently perform its awakening by striking it with *karavīra* flowers equal in number to the syllables of that mantra. (19.6)

Following the procedure prescribed in the *Svatantra*, the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the mantra with the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, equal in number to the syllables of the mantra, for the sake of purification. (19.7)

Having reflected with his mind, the practitioner of mantra should, according to the prescribed rule, burn away the three impurities at the root and center of the *suṣumṇā* by means of the light-mantra.
The practitioner of mantra should purify the three impurities within the mantra; this is the purification.
The *jyotirmanu* is considered to consist of the *tāra*, followed by *vyoma-agni-manu-yuk* (the syllable *hrauṃ*), and the *daṇḍin*. (Oṃ Hraum).
With water from *kuśa* grass over which this has been recited, one should sprinkle each individual syllable of the mantra.
This nourishment is prescribed according to the rule by means of that mantra;
the practitioner of mantra performs the libation with the excellent mantra—this is known as *tarpaṇa*. (19.10)
The union of Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā is called the illumination of the mantra;
the concealment of the mantra being recited, however, is its non-disclosure.
Ten consecrations (saṃskāra) have been proclaimed, hidden in all tantras;
by performing them according to the tradition, the mantra-practitioner shall obtain his desire. (19.12)
Thus, there are ten types of purificatory rites for the removal of defects in mantras.
Now, the measure of the substances for the oblation (homa) is stated here: one karṣa of ghee is prescribed for the oblation, and milk is recorded as being one śukti in measure. (19.14)
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) have been described by the wise as being equal;
honey and milk are declared to be equal to them, each in the measure of a barley grain.
The curd should be the measure of a handful (prasṛti); the parched grains (lāja) should be equal to a fistful;
the flattened grains (pṛthuka) should be the same as those, and the roasted flour (saktu) is likewise prescribed.

Jaggery should be half a *pala* in measure, and sugar is likewise prescribed as such. A portion of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) should be half a mouthful; sugarcane is prescribed up to the length of a joint.
One should offer each leaf, flower, and so forth, as well as incense and other offerings, one by one. (19.17)
They know that plantains and oranges are each [offered] individually;
a citron is divided into four pieces, and a jackfruit is traditionally held to be tenfold.
The wise know that coconuts are cut into eight pieces;
the wood-apple fruit is made into three parts, and the wood-sorrel is cut into two.
In the fire-oblation (homa), the fruit of the urvāruka is prescribed when it is split into two pieces;
other fruits should be cut into pieces, and the fuel-sticks (samidh) should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, along with four finger-breadths of guḍūcī;
there should be a handful of rice, as well as mudga beans, māṣa beans, and barley.
The rice grains should be half that amount, while the kodrava grains are measured by a handful; likewise, the wheat and red kalama rice are prescribed at the measure of one handful each. (19.22)
Sesame seeds should be the size of a small frying pan; mustard seeds are of that same measure. Salt should be the size of a śukti, and there should also be twenty black peppercorns. (19.23)
Pura, varada, and māna are synonyms; rāmaṭha is considered to be the same as those.
So too are sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron. (19.24)
The teachers have specified that [the size of the offerings] should be equal to the seeds of the tamarind;
however, when no specific sacrificial substance is mentioned, sesame and clarified butter are said to be the sacrificial offering.
Now, O fair-faced one, hear the fruit of the sacrificial substances used here:
by means of palāśa flowers sprinkled with the three sweets, a person obtains all desires;
and through the oblation of campaka, pāṭala, bakula, and other such flowers, one attains the triad [of goals].

External [obstacles] are removed by drops and petals, as well as by fruits; likewise, sovereignty by lotuses, longevity by barley sprouts along with jaggery, and peace by sesame seeds with clarified butter.
By offering wealth with the Aghora mantra, one obtains riches;
with white mustard seeds (siddhārtha), one gains affection; with molasses, sons; and with fruits, a man attains happiness. (19.27)
Through oblations of parched grain one gains good fortune; through other grains, prosperity;
through *kādamba* flowers, sovereignty over the world of the Yakṣas; and through *punnāga* flowers, a mortal attains the status of a Vidyādhara.
With *mālatī* flowers, one [reaches] the worlds of the Siddhas and Gandharvas. || 19/28 ||

The summoning of yakṣiṇīs occurs through *arjuna* flowers and mustard seeds combined with the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*). Through oblation (*homa*) with *jaya*, *ripu*, and *kusuma* flowers, as well as *kiṃśuka* flowers, Vaiśyas shall become submissive. Through *karṇikāra* flowers, the gods of the earth—the Kṣatriyas—shall become submissive; likewise, through *kāśamarda*.
The Vaiśyas were subdued by the Kirātas like a host, and the Śūdras by the Pāṭalas. || 19.29 ||
Through a fire-oblation of the flesh of a goat or a wild animal, the entire enemy kingdom shall come under one's own control;
furthermore, the enemy force shall turn its back [in retreat] by means of an oblation of sweetened human flesh.
By performing oblations at night with the three pungents, neem leaves, hair, jaggery, and mārapala,
mixed with mustard oil, enemies die within three days of the sages (nine days).

It is said that a fire sacrifice performed with *lagnajit*, *ajara*, hair, turmeric, and pieces of fingernails effects the immobilization of the powerful army of hostile kings within seven days. (19.32)
Through oblations of black gram (māṣa), there is dumbness; through kodrava grains, affliction by disease; and through peas (kalāya), there is the onset of a fatal illness.
Through sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) from an *unmatta* tree, there is madness; and through those from the *śālmalī* tree, death occurs within seven days.

A person who, with a concentrated inner self, offers oblations at night in a six-cornered sacrificial pit using barley, wheat, and sesame seeds mixed with the ghee of a tawny cow, certainly attains the power of moving through the sky.
Having kindled the fire-eater with wood from the palāśa tree and sprinkling it with sandalwood and bandhujīva flowers, || 19.34 ||
All beings shall become submissive through oblations made with priyaṅgu flowers;
likewise, by offering various kinds of food, edibles, grains, and drinks, a person shall attain supreme prosperity in this world. (19.35)
One should desire [to adorn] with sprouts of the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and other trees combined with sweet-flavored ingredients; through *mallikā* flowers, fame shall be attained.

Satisfaction results from oblations of blue lotuses; nourishment comes from *saugandhika* flowers; affection for the people arises from white water-lilies; and sons are obtained through *mallikā* blossoms. (19.37)

Whatever indeed may be most desired by the minds of men upon the surface of the earth, all that shall be attained without delay through the oblation of the three sweets, provided it is endowed with one's own power. (19.38)

The oblation of clarified butter is made with ladles sixteen finger-breadths wide and twice that in length; here, the medium height is half of that, while the inferior is eight finger-breadths high. Likewise, an oblation of sesame or honey may be offered, combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One small measure each of milk, curd, and likewise of gruel; and a quantity equal to a single cluster of cakes, a portion of milk-rice, and a mouthful of food. (19.40)
One each of plantain fruit, citron, and orange;
the jackfruit should be divided into ten pieces, and the wood-apple fruit should be in pieces of jaggery.
Then, by means of the prescribed ritual, all such substances as sugar-cane pieces, jaggery fragments, and unbroken petals, flowers, and fruits should be offered into the fire;
one thereby attains complete pacification—of this there is no doubt. (19.42)
Oṃ tat sat. Oṃ peace! Oṃ peace!

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Number and Other Details of the Ritual Substances for the Fire Offering and the Ten Purificatory Rites Beginning with Birth," in the *Phetkāriṇī-mahātantra*.
The twentieth chapter.
Śrī Śiva said:
On the ground divided into nine parts, one should place the vowels in order in the center.
One should also [recite] the seven syllables beginning with *ka* at Īśāna for one hundred thousand times.
In the three squares starting from the field (kṣetra), the place of the lamp is called the "mouth";
the two hands, the two flanks, and the two feet are declared to be the "tail" for the remainder.
Through the recitation of the Kūrmatanu mantra, there is accomplishment in his hand, short life and indifference on the sides, suffering in the feet, and pain in the tail. (20.3)

Starting from the first letter of the name up until the first letter of the mantra, divide by seven; the remainder is multiplied by three. Any resulting debt (negative value) that is positive in nature must be discarded. (20.4)

Starting from the first syllable of the mantra up until the appearance of the beginning of the name, one should divide [the syllables] by three; the remainder of seven is that which is to be grasped by oneself, consisting of such a nature.

One should not worship the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha, nor the Praṇava of the temple, nor mantras consisting of syllables along with their seed-syllables (piṇḍa) if they are either enemies or friends [of the practitioner]. // 20.6 //

O fair-faced one, one should not worship a mantra consisting of a single syllable, one with three peaks, or a garland-mantra (mālāmantra), whether obtained in a dream or given by a woman, if it belongs to a friend or an enemy.

The fourfold results—Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Ari—become clearly manifest at the door and the spokes in the [alphabetical] sequence beginning with *ka*, *ṭa*, *pa*, and *ya*, for those seeking knowledge, food, and the application of mantras. (20.8)
The *siddha* [day] is established in the ninth, first, and fifth; the *sādhya* in the sixth, tenth, and twelfth;
the *susiddha* in the third, seventh, and eleventh; and the *ari* (enemy) in the second, eighth, and fourth. (20.9)
In a four-compartment grid, one should write the vowels and consonants in the order starting from the northeast (Īśāna).
In the wheel, the sequence "a-k-a-tha-ha" is stated for the names and syllables in the [sections] beginning with Siddha.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Kūrma-cakra and the Designations of the Ṛṇin, Dhanin, Siddha, and Sādhya," in the Phetkāriṇī-tantra of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya).
The twenty-first chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
One should recite the Krodha-mantra one hundred thousand times; it possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Laughing with a loud, terrible laugh, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, and possessing great radiance. || 21/1 ||
On the right, joined with a vajra, and with the threatening gesture (tarjanī) of the left hand,
[he holds] the great mantra of the King of Wrath, the Vajra-weapon of the wrathful deities such as Viṣa.
Having taken the word *viṣaṃ hanapada*, then the word *vidhvaṃsaya*,
and having uttered the word *nāśaya*, [one should employ] the noose (*pāśa*) conjoined with the weapon of wrath (*krodhāstra*).
Then, with the Vajrajvāla [mantra], one should strike the pair of eyes;
thereafter, for all spirits, the Kūrca [mantra] at the end of the Astra [mantra] effects the destruction of the spirit.
Having bowed to Krodhādhipa, Vyomavaktra, Vajrapāṇi, Surāntaka, and Kālakalpataru, the accomplishment of Bhūtinī is now described. (21.5)
The first is the goddess Vibhūṣiṇī, the supreme Kuṇḍaladhāriṇī,
then Tāriṇī, Siṃhinī, Haṃsinī, and thereafter Naṭī.
(“Oṃ hana vidhvaṃsaya nāśaya ā hūṃ phaṭ”).
Ceṭikā is said to be Kinnarī, while Bhūtinī is fond of Rati.
At the end of the names of the two wrathful weapons, [one should add] "Bhūtavīrya" followed by three *kūrca* syllables (*huṃ*). (21.7)

Adorned with the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the two *lajjā*s (hrīḥ hrīḥ), and the two *astra*s (phaṭ phaṭ), this mantra of Vibhūṣiṇī consists of two wrathful syllables. Thus has the mantra of Vibhūṣiṇī been proclaimed. (21.8)

(OM VAJRAJVĀLENA HANA HANA SARVABHŪTĀN HŪḤ PHAṬ) With a flaying knife in one hand and a human head in the other, she is of towering form and terrifying appearance, with hosts of spirits gathered amidst her teeth, flesh, blood, and fat.

May she, whose entire earth is filled with masses of hair from which the backs of her limbs hang down like the branches of *śāla* trees made terrifying by black serpents, protect us as far as the edge of the mountains.
Having gone to the foot of a single tree and dwelling there for three nights during the night,
one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times while meditating with a one-pointed mind.
At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed worship by name and offered incense before her, one should recite at midnight; then she, adorned with ornaments, arrives.
When the *arghya* is offered mixed with sandalwood water, she is certainly pleased;
whether she be a mother, a sister, or a wife, she becomes satisfied and fulfills one's desires. (21.12)
Having made the three worlds her hand-apple, she becomes their mother and bestows the collyrium-ornament upon the retinue of one hundred and eight.
If the illustrious sister brings a woman even from a distance of a thousand yojanas and bestows upon her a divine elixir of essence, [she shall be liberated]. (21.14)
If one's wife mounts his back, she leads him to heaven and bestows a thousand dīnāras, as well as mercury and an elixir of immortality.
The Goddess, ever adorned with splendor, fulfills all hopes;
she is declared to be the wearer of earrings through the two powers of Dhruva and Māyā. 21.16
The mantra of Kuṇḍaladhāriṇī is declared to consist of three *kūrca*s and the weapon (*astra*):
(Oṃ Oṃ Hrīḥ Hrīḥ Phaṭ Phaṭ Kuṇḍaladhāriṇī Hūṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ).
She who wears earrings on her ears is moon-faced and is fully endowed with a lute.

May she who adorns the three worlds with joy— she whose waistband hangs from the slope of her mountain-like hips, who sports with pearl necklaces, whose high, swelling breasts shine forth, and who wears earrings— protect us. 21.17
One should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times at night in a cremation ground; Kuṇḍaladhāriṇī arrives, and an offering of blood must be presented to her; being pleased, she even grants [boons].
"What must I do, my child? Become a practitioner (sādhaka), O Mother;
for five hundred days, even the three worlds shall grant [your desires]. (21.19)
The mantra of Sindūrahāriṇī is declared to consist of two Krodhas,
two Astra-mantras, and three Kūrca-mantras, ending with the word *sindūrahāriṇī*.

(HŪḤ HŪḤ PHAṬ PHAṬ SINDŪRAHĀRIṆĪ HŪḤ HŪḤ HŪḤ PHAṬ) She who wears a golden ornament, whose garment is the swaying branch of a trembling leaf, whose body is made beautiful by longing, who is radiant, white-robed, and smiling.

May this creeper-like Rāhu, who steals the vermilion from her beloved’s feet—darkened by the continuous luster within yet possessing the beauty that has become the ornament of the three worlds—grant protection. 21/21.
Having gone to an empty temple, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
she quickly arrives, and having come, she becomes the desired wife.
Adorned with garments and ornaments, the goddess Sindūrahāriṇī protects twelve people for twenty-five dīnāras. (21.23)
From the two *lajjā* [seeds], the pair of weapons, and then the word *siṃhinī*, and from the three *krodha* seeds, the *siṃhinī-mantra* is said to be born. (21.24)
(Hrīḥ hrīḥ phaṭ phaṭ siṃhinī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ) She who stands upon the Daityas within the mountain peaks, trees, fortresses, jagged caves, and inaccessible gorges;
she whose feet tread upon the entire universe as it falls from her hair, and whose moon-throne has slipped away.
May she—whose forest of teeth gleams like a multitude of stars, who agitates the Siddha women, and who is adorned with a garland hanging from her entire head—protect all. 21.25.
Having gone to Ekaliṅga at night, one should mutter the mantra ten thousand times;
then, being pleased and highly propitious, Siṃhinī comes when she has been worshipped.
"What shall I do?"—thus speaks the wife who has become beloved, as she offers a dināra, a pair of garments, and flavorful elixirs. (21.27)
*Tāra*, *trimūrti*, *astra*, *trayuga*, then *haṃsinī* and *bhūtinī*, followed by the *trikūrca-astra*; thus is declared the supreme *haṃsinī-mantra*. (21.28)
(OM OM PHAṬ PHAṬ HAṂSINĪ BHŪTINĪ HŪḤ HŪḤ HŪḤ PHAṬ) Her eyes resemble white and dark lotuses; serpents hang from her neck;
she is respectfully attended by the wife of Mādhava, who is captivated by the sound she has begun to utter.

May the illustrious Haṃsinī protect you— she whose side-glances are slightly cast askance, whose face bears the look of one initiated into the state of supreme enchantment, and who wears a shimmering necklace of pearls strung together like a creeping vine.
Having gone to the abode of Vajrapāṇi, one should paint a beautiful image;
having worshipped it with Hayamāra, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Until midnight, the goddess certainly comes in the form of a female swan;
delighted by the offering of sandalwood and water for honor, she speaks to the practitioner.
"What should I do for you today? O practitioner, become my servant! I shall provide clothing, ornaments, food, and so forth for your expenses. (21.32)
Because there is no expenditure at all, he does not give and becomes angry; from the three syllables of the weapon-mantra *tāraṃ* (OM), one should extract the word *naṭīti*. 21.33.
This mantra of Nartakī, ending with three *kūrca*s (*hūṃ*) and three *astra*s (*phaṭ*), has been declared.
(Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ naṭī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ).
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme sādhana of Coṭikā, by obtaining whose grace a person attains all that is desired. (21.34)
One should extract the pair of syllables *tārā-cakra-ādhāra* followed by the word *naṭī*;
ending with the three *kūrca*s and *lajjā*, this is declared to be the mantra of Nartakī. (21.35)
Her face is as beautiful as a full-blown blue lotus, her breasts are like lofty water-jars,
her eyes are like a pair of sporting khañjana birds or fish, and her smile bestows bliss;
she is a woman who dwells upon the shores of the Ocean of Milk, clothed in dark blue garments.
[She is] one who devours with teeth as bright as the rising moon, and who is distinguished by the utterance of the collection of jewels.
Having gone to the house of a woman of low caste and having performed recitation and worship for seven days,
one should also recite [the mantra] with sandalwood incense at sunset.
That dancing girl becomes a wife who provides sensual enjoyments;
she departs after spending one *pala* of gold for her expenses. (21.38)
Day by day, the goddess Naṭī certainly becomes stable; then follow the two Tārakūrca-mantras and the two Astra-mantras as her attendants (ceṭīs). 21.39.
Then, having bestowed two *krodhas*, this is considered the supreme mantra for the *ceṭī*:
(Oṃ hūḥ hūḥ phaṭ phaṭ ceṭī hūḥ hūḥ).
She goes along, speaking measuredly, with a moon-like face, her upper garment fallen away.

May the maidservant protect you for a long time— she who bears a stainless lotus in her jar, a golden line parting her hair, her pure body anointed with sandalwood and other unguents, and whose braid of hair, though slightly curled, is graced by its fragrance. 21.40.
In any terrifying place, by the mere utterance of her name, she certainly comes and even performs the work of a maidservant. (21.41)
Alternatively, one should perform recitation for three nights at the door of one's own house;
having arrived at the dwelling, that goddess performs the work of a servant.
The pair of *tārakūrca* (the two *hūṃ*s), followed by *kāmeśvarī-bhūti*, and finally the two *krodha*s (the two *phaṭ*s)—this is declared to be the mantra of Kāmeśvarī. (21.43)
(OM HŪḤ PHAṬ PHAṬ KĀMEŚVARĪ BHŪTINYAI HŪḤ HŪḤ) She has come to the battle of passion; she is sweetness endowed with vernal flowers;
she sings with a sweet voice, her face smiling, holding a lute, and full of grace.

May this Kāmeśvarī Bhūtinī—whose eyes are like red lotuses, who is endowed with the intoxication of honey, who wields a bow of flowers, and whose face is sweet as nectar—protect us from all sides. 21.44.
Having approached the mother’s place and partaken of meat,
and having offered meat and other oblations for seven days, [one should recite] a thousand times.
One should recite the mantra with self-restraint and offer blood as an *arghya* oblation;
Kāmeśvarī will become pleased and, as one's desired wife, she becomes his consort.
It certainly fulfills all desires and bestows sovereignty with certainty.
Having uttered "Tāra," "Lajjā," and the two "Kūrca" weapons, O beloved of Rati, the ritual procedure is as stated in the *Kāmeśvarītantra*, joined with the two "Krodha" mantras. (21.47)
(Oṃ hūḥ phaṭ phaṭ ratipriye hūḥ hūḥ phaṭ) In the midst of a golden enclosure, upon the surface of a celestial tree, she sits enthroned on a golden seat—
a youthful Yakṣī whose mass of braided hair is radiant with flowers of spreading fragrance.

Rich with full and lofty breasts, with eyes like blue water-lilies, red in complexion, holding two revolving red lotuses in her hands, bowed down by all the gods, and adorned with divine ornaments and necklaces; || 21.48 ||
One should extract the word "Devī" from between the two *krodha*s and the pair of weapons;
at the end, having taken the two *krodha*s, [one obtains] the unsurpassed mantra of Devī.
The maiden possesses a divine form, with a golden luster like that of celestial desire.
"Hūḥ hūḥ phaṭ phaṭ! O Goddess, hūḥ hūḥ!
She becomes a beloved wife, adorned with every ornament. (21.50)
Having gone to a temple at night, one should prepare a bed there;
one should offer white cloth, sandalwood, and jasmine flowers. (21.51)
Having prepared incense of guggulu, one should recite the mantra a thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, she comes under one's control, engaging in kissing, embracing, and other such acts.
"O Lord, let this chief of celestial women truly become my wife;
she shall grant eight days [of union], and at the end, a pair of divine garments. (21.53)
He will provide divine, wish-fulfilling food for his retinue;
furthermore, having brought wealth from the house of Vaiśravaṇa, he bestows it upon them. (21.54)
Having recited this [mantra] thousands of times, one certainly attains success at the conclusion of the recitation;
the Lord of Wrath (Krodhabhūpati) has said that one should recite the mantra again and again. (21.55)
This *kṛtyā*, which is the essence of all the Āgamas, has been taught by me in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*.
It should certainly be employed by the virtuous for the complete destruction and crushing of the enemy. (21.56)
For wicked men are like lions that cause suffering; they are like a malevolent *kṛtyā* spell that strikes others down.
Therefore, I have spoken [of her] in the *Phetkāriṇītantra* as the bestower of the desired success for those who recite it. (21.57)
The peerless and most terrifying Great Kṛtyā is remembered as the eternal destroyer of inauspicious enemies, presiding over creation, maintenance, and destruction. (21.58)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Sadhana of the Servant Maid," in the glorious Phetkāriṇī Tantra, within the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord.
And this treatise is completed.
